areas.area: Estimating what you have not found yet: capture-recapture in software inspection, species-richness / sample-coverage estimation, and the empirical literature on how many reviewers pay
areas.summary: Question 1 is largely a solved problem — but CDSFL is currently on the wrong side of the precondition that makes the solution available. Thirty-four years of software-inspection research (Eick et al. 1992 through Petersson et al. 2004) and a century of ecology and epidemiology have converged on a single mechanism: the overlap between what independent reviewers find is what estimates the size of what nobody found. Every estimator in the family — Lincoln-Petersen, Chapman, Chao, Burnham-Overton jackknife, Chao1/Chao2 — is a function of exactly two numbers: how many items were found by exactly one reviewer, and how many by exactly two. CDSFL records the first and has effectively destroyed the second. With Q1=2048 and Q2=2, the bias-corrected Chao2 estimate is 561,018 findings and the estimated sample completeness is 0.37%; the incidence jackknife on the same data says 3,688. Two estimators from the same family disagreeing by two orders of magnitude is not a hard estimation problem, it is a signal that the data lies outside the estimators' domain. The ecological and mark-recapture literature names this exact pathology: failure to recognise a previously-detected individual creates a "ghost", inflates the singleton count, and positively biases the abundance estimate (Yoshizaki et al. 2011; Link et al. 2010; Kodi et al. 2024). Two of 2,050 co-discoveries is therefore first a measurement of the finding-matcher, and only second a measurement of the panel. The single highest-value change is to stop treating identity as a by-product of deduplication and start recording, per finding, the full set of models that raised it — after which a large, mature, runnable body of method becomes available immediately, including a principled stopping rule, a marginal-yield estimator, and a way to make one-model and hundred-model deployments directly comparable. Two hard limits survive that fix and cannot be engineered away: the population size is not point-identified without an independence assumption CDSFL cannot make (models share training data), so the honest output is a confidence set rather than a number; and the number of unseen items can only be extrapolated about n log n beyond the sample you have, so a five-seat panel can say something about eight to twelve seats and nothing at all about five hundred.

techniques.name: Capture-recapture model taxonomy M0 / Mt / Mh / Mth and its estimators
techniques.source: Otis, Burnham, White & Anderson 1978 (Wildlife Monographs); Burnham & Overton 1978, Biometrika 65:625-633 (jackknife); Chao 1987 Biometrics 43:783-791 and Chao 1989 Biometrics 45:427-438; Chao, Lee & Jeng 1992 Biometrics 48:201-216. Transferred to inspections by Eick, Loader, Long, Vander Wiel & Votta, ICSE 1992, pp.59-65 (http://www.mdavidlong.com/estimating_software_fault_content.pdf). Definitive survey: Petersson, Thelin, Runeson & Wohlin, J. Systems and Software 72(2):249-264, 2004 (https://www.wohlin.eu/jss04-1.pdf)
techniques.what_it_does: Estimates the total population of defects in an artefact, including undiscovered ones, from the overlap between independent reviewers' find-lists. M0 assumes all defects equally detectable and all reviewers equally able; Mt allows reviewers to differ; Mh allows defects to differ; Mth allows both. Small overlap implies many remain; large overlap implies few remain.
techniques.assumption: Closed population (the artefact does not change during review); reviewers work independently and do not see each other's findings; and — the load-bearing one — that two reviewers reporting the same defect can be reliably recognised as reporting the same defect. Petersson et al. state this explicitly as a process requirement: before estimation, someone must identify which faults noted by different reviewers are actually the same.
techniques.why: The structural analogy is exact: a reviewer is a trapping occasion, a finding is an animal, the panel round is a closed capture experiment. Nothing about CDSFL's tool-confirmed ground truth breaks it — if anything it helps, because a tool-executed falsifier removes the false-positive contamination that inspection studies had to tolerate. But the method is unavailable to CDSFL today because the overlap it consumes is not recorded. This is a data-collection change, not a research problem.

techniques.name: Chao2 and the incidence (first-order) jackknife — the species-richness form of the same estimator
techniques.source: Chao 1987 Biometrics 43:783-791; formulas collated in Gotelli & Colwell, 'Estimating species richness', ch.4 of Biological Diversity (OUP 2011), Box 4.1 (https://www.uvm.edu/~ngotelli/manuscriptpdfs/Chapter%204.pdf); Colwell, Chao, Gotelli, Lin, Mao, Chazdon & Longino 2012, J. Plant Ecology 5(1):3-21 (https://academic.oup.com/jpe/article/5/1/3/1296712)
techniques.what_it_does: With m sampling units, Q1 items seen in exactly one unit and Q2 in exactly two: Chao2 = S_obs + Q1^2/(2*Q2); bias-corrected Chao2 = S_obs + ((m-1)/m)*Q1*(Q1-1)/(2*(Q2+1)); incidence jackknife1 = S_obs + Q1*(m-1)/m. Chao's estimator is a lower bound on true richness, not a point estimate, which is the right shape for a claim about how much you have missed.
techniques.assumption: Nearly homogeneous detection probability among the RARE items specifically (uniques and undetected), not among all items. Sampling units drawn independently. Correct identification of repeat detections.
techniques.why: This is the form that matches CDSFL's actual structure better than the classical inspection form, because CDSFL accumulates findings over rounds and models — a sample-based incidence design. I ran it on the stated figures: with S_obs=2050, Q1=2048, Q2=2, m=5, Chao2 (small-sample form) = 840,911, bias-corrected = 561,018, incidence jackknife = 3,688, estimated completeness 0.24-0.37% (verified twice, floating-point and SymPy exact rationals: 8415262/15). The two-order-of-magnitude disagreement between estimators in the same family is the diagnostic. Run these numbers as a permanent instrument health check, not as an answer.

techniques.name: Ghost individuals / misidentification models (Mt-alpha, latent multinomial) — the diagnosis of 2-in-2,050
techniques.source: Yoshizaki, Brownie, Pollock & Link 2011, Biometrics (model Mt,alpha); Link, Yoshizaki, Bailey & Pollock 2010, Biometrics 66:178-185 (latent multinomial); Fraysse, Choquet, Costantini & Pradel 2023, arXiv:2304.00885 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.00885); Kodi et al. 2024, Methods in Ecology and Evolution (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14326)
techniques.what_it_does: Models the case where the identity function fails: a previously-detected individual is not recognised as such and is recorded as a new individual — a 'ghost'. Ghosts inflate the singleton count, collapse the doubleton count, and positively bias the population estimate. The literature offers three fixes: (a) Yoshizaki 2007's conditioning on at least two captures, discarding all singletons; (b) explicit modelling of an identification probability alpha; (c) an informative prior on alpha when capture rate is low.
techniques.assumption: That you can independently measure or bound your identification (matching) accuracy. Fraysse et al. show that at per-unit capture rate 0.2 or lower, the model does not converge or is biased WITHOUT such a prior — exactly CDSFL's regime.
techniques.why: This is the most important item in the whole search. 2 of 2,050 is the textbook ghost signature. Two explanations fit: either the five models are near-orthogonal samplers (in which case the population really is enormous and the estimator is correctly telling you so), or the matcher under-merges. Ecology's own canonical example is instructive — divers surfacing and reporting fish sightings, where the same specimen seen by two divers produces 'illusory' duplicates or, in the other direction, illusory uniques. Before any estimator is trusted, CDSFL needs a measured matcher accuracy: take a sample of finding pairs, have a human or a tool adjudicate same/different, and report the rate. That number is a required input, not optional metadata.

techniques.name: Good-Turing coverage deficit as the marginal-value-of-one-more-reviewer estimator
techniques.source: Good 1953, Biometrika 40:237-264; identity proved in Chao & Jost 2012, Ecology 93(12):2533-2547, eq.6 and Appendix B (https://www.davidzeleny.net/wiki/lib/exe/fetch.php/vegecol:materials:chao-jost2012_ecology.pdf)
techniques.what_it_does: Estimated coverage deficit after m units equals exactly the slope of the accumulation curve: 1 - C_m = S_(m+1) - S_m. In words, the fraction of the population you have NOT yet covered is the expected number of new items the next reviewer will bring. For incidence data the working estimator is q0 = Q1/T (T = total incidences), and expected new findings from the next reviewer is approximately Q1/t.
techniques.assumption: That rare items have roughly homogeneous detection probability, and that units are exchangeable. Chao & Lee's practical guideline: the estimator is adequate when estimated coverage is at least 50%.
techniques.why: This is the sharpest answer to question 1, and it is far cheaper than estimating the total. You do not need to know N to decide whether to add a reviewer; you need the derivative, and the derivative needs much less data and much weaker assumptions than the asymptote. IMPORTANT CAVEAT I DERIVED AND VERIFIED, not stated in the sources: Q1/t is an UPWARD-biased estimate of marginal yield. Under the Bernoulli product model, E[new items in the next unit] = sum p_i(1-p_i)^t while Q1/t estimates sum p_i(1-p_i)^(t-1); the per-item ratio is exactly (1-p_i) (confirmed by SymPy symbolic simplification, by direct expectation computation over 20,000 items, and by 4,000-run Monte Carlo). At mean detection probability 0.14 the overestimate is ~20%; at 0.5 it is ~45%. This is the right direction for a stopping rule: if even the optimistic marginal yield is below your cost threshold, stopping is safe.

techniques.name: Coverage-based standardisation and the coverage-based stopping rule
techniques.source: Chao & Jost 2012, Ecology 93(12):2533-2547 (https://www.davidzeleny.net/wiki/lib/exe/fetch.php/vegecol:materials:chao-jost2012_ecology.pdf); optimal-stopping justification from Rasmussen & Starr 1979, 'Optimal and Adaptive Stopping in the Search for New Species', JASA 74(367):661-667 (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1979.10481667)
techniques.what_it_does: Instead of comparing samples of equal SIZE, compare samples of equal COMPLETENESS. Sample each community until the estimated coverage reaches a preset value, then stop. Chao & Jost show this is theoretically justified by optimal stopping theory, throws away less data than size-based standardisation, and more efficiently recovers the correct ranking of richness between communities.
techniques.assumption: Coverage is estimable from the data, which again requires the singleton/doubleton structure — i.e. requires overlap. Rough guideline: estimated coverage should be at least 50% for the machinery to be adequate.
techniques.why: This is the answer to CDSFL's scale-invariance problem, and it is a better answer than anything I expected to find. The harness should NOT define convergence as 'N models agreed' or 'K rounds elapsed'; it should define convergence as 'estimated coverage of the finding population reached target C'. A solo researcher with one model, a five-seat panel, and an institution with 500 models then all run the same gate, stop at the same statistically-defined point, and produce directly comparable results. The number of reviewers becomes an output of the process rather than a hard-coded assumption inside it. Note the honest consequence: the solo researcher will simply fail to reach C and will be told so, which is the correct behaviour.

techniques.name: Sufficient-sampling formulas: how many more reviewers to reach a target fraction of the asymptote
techniques.source: Chao, Colwell, Lin & Gotelli 2009, Ecology 90(4):1125-1133, eqs. 13-15 (https://www.uvm.edu/~ngotelli/manuscriptpdfs/ChaoEcology2009.pdf); building on Shen, Chao & Lin 2003, Ecology 84:798-804 (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/0012-9658%282003%29084%5B0798%3APTNONS%5D2.0.CO%3B2)
techniques.what_it_does: Given t sampling units with Q1 uniques and Q2 duplicates, computes the minimum number of ADDITIONAL units needed to reach any target fraction g of the estimated asymptotic richness. Their empirical result across seven published datasets: reaching 100% costs a median 2.23x the original effort (range 1.05x to 10.67x); reaching 90% costs a median 0.80x (range 0.33x to 1.10x).
techniques.assumption: Same as Chao2: closed population, near-homogeneous detection among rare items, correct repeat-identification. The authors show robustness to spatial non-independence, which is encouraging for the correlated-models case but is not a proof of robustness to it.
techniques.why: This converts the abstract stopping question into a budget question the founder can act on. I implemented eqs. 13-15 and verified against their published Table 2: my calculations reproduce every incidence-data figure exactly (Maudsley carabids m=20 vs published 20; Ellison ants m=62 vs 62 and 15.9 vs 16 and 6.2 vs 6; Butler seedlings m=270 vs 270). The implementation is correct and can be pointed at CDSFL's data the day overlap exists. The 90%-vs-100% asymmetry is the most actionable fact in this whole report: the last 10% of a finding population routinely costs more than everything before it. A convergence gate targeting exhaustiveness is targeting the wrong point on the curve.

techniques.name: The n log n extrapolation ceiling (smoothed Good-Toulmin and its optimality)
techniques.source: Good & Toulmin 1956, Biometrika 43:45-63; Efron & Thisted 1976, Biometrika 63:435-447 ('How many words did Shakespeare know?'); Orlitsky, Suresh & Wu 2016, PNAS 113(47):13283-13288 (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1607774113); incidence-data extension and the first principled prediction intervals: Eriksson 2026, 'The Unseen Species Problem Revisited', arXiv:2602.08769 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08769)
techniques.what_it_does: Predicts how many NEW items would appear in m additional samples. Classical Good-Toulmin is reliable only up to doubling (m <= n). Orlitsky et al. prove the smoothed estimator extends this to n log n samples AND that n log n is the largest possible estimation range for any estimator. Their phrase: the bird in the hand is worth log n in the bush.
techniques.assumption: i.i.d. sampling from a fixed distribution. Eriksson 2026 relaxes this to incidence/set-valued data with bounded set size and no within-set independence assumption, which is much closer to CDSFL's structure, and notes that prior incidence work assumed away precisely the dependence one is trying to capture.
techniques.why: This is the hard boundary on question 2's third deployment tier, and it is an impossibility result, not an engineering gap. Treating one reviewer-review as one sampling unit: a 5-model panel can extrapolate credibly to about 8 models (t ln t) or 12 (t log2 t), and a 20-model panel to about 60-86. There is no estimator, existing or future, that lets a five-seat panel predict what unlimited institutional access would find. Colwell et al. 2012 give the same practical warning from the applied side — extrapolation is reasonable to about double or triple the reference sample. The design consequence: do not build a feature that claims to tell an institution what its marginal 100th model buys; build one that reports the estimate's valid range and refuses outside it.

techniques.name: Partial identification / dependence-robust confidence sets
techniques.source: Sun, Van Baelen, Plettinckx & Crawford 2022, 'Dependence-robust confidence intervals for capture-recapture surveys', arXiv:2008.00127 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.00127)
techniques.what_it_does: Proves that without additional assumptions the population size is not point-identified, and constructs non-trivial confidence SETS from weak qualitative bounds on pairwise capture probabilities, via test-inversion bootstrap and profile-likelihood methods.
techniques.assumption: Only that you can state qualitative bounds on pairwise dependence — e.g. 'these two models are positively dependent but the pairwise capture probability is between a and b'. No independence assumption required.
techniques.why: This should be CDSFL's default output format. CDSFL cannot assert independence between reviewers: frontier models share pretraining corpora, share RLHF conventions, and are given identical prompts on identical artefacts. Their blind spots are correlated by construction. The authors' framing is exactly CDSFL's situation — real surveys use convenience samples where assumed dependence cannot be guaranteed and estimates under those assumptions lack empirical credibility. Reporting an interval under stated dependence bounds is both more honest and more defensible than a point estimate that quietly assumes something false. It also composes correctly with a Popperian harness: an interval is falsifiable in a way a point estimate is not.

techniques.name: Log-linear capture-recapture with interaction terms (k >= 3 sources)
techniques.source: Fienberg 1972, Biometrika 59:591-603; International Working Group for Disease Monitoring and Forecasting 1995, Am. J. Epidemiology; Hook & Regal, cautions in Am. J. Epidemiology 145(12):1138 (https://academic.oup.com/aje/article/145/12/1138/91636); applied to inspection data by Kamel & Sorenson, Proc. ISESE 2003, 213-222
techniques.what_it_does: With three or more sources, fits a log-linear model to the 2^k contingency table with the unobserved cell, including explicit pairwise (and higher) interaction terms that MODEL rather than assume away reviewer dependence.
techniques.assumption: That the highest-order interaction is absent (usually the k-way term), and that model selection is done well. Direction of bias is known: positive dependence between sources causes UNDERestimation of the population; negative dependence causes OVERestimation.
techniques.why: CDSFL's five seats across four vendors is exactly the k>=3 case where this becomes available, and it is the standard tool in epidemiology for precisely CDSFL's problem (heterogeneous, non-independent listing sources). But heed Hook & Regal's warning, which I would repeat verbatim to the founder: there is no proof or reassurance that a log-linear estimator on real data yields a valid estimate, or even one closer to truth than an alternative; and model selection may dominate the estimate. Use it as one member of an ensemble whose spread is itself the reported uncertainty, never as the single number.

techniques.name: Experience-based / subjective defect-content estimation (the technique that works with what CDSFL already records)
techniques.source: El Emam, Laitenberger & Harbich 2000, NRC/ERB-1060 (https://www.ehealthinformation.ca/web/default/files/wp-files/10601.pdf); Biffl 2000, IEEE Software 17(6):36-43; Wohlin, Petersson & Aurum 2001; Petersson & Wohlin 1999b; Padberg 2002; summarised in Petersson et al. 2004 sections 3.2-3.3
techniques.what_it_does: Estimates remaining defect content from each reviewer's HISTORICAL effectiveness (what fraction of known defects that reviewer typically finds) plus, optionally, the reviewer's own subjective minimum/most-likely/maximum estimate. Requires no overlap whatsoever.
techniques.assumption: That per-reviewer effectiveness is stable across artefacts and measurable from a calibration corpus. Reported performance with two reviewers: absolute bias and standard deviation both around 20%, less biased than any capture-recapture estimator at that panel size though not significantly so. El Emam et al. found professional inspectors' subjective estimates of their own effectiveness had median relative error of zero.
techniques.why: This is the one estimator in the whole literature that CDSFL can run TODAY, unchanged, on records that attribute each finding to exactly one model — and it is also the only one that degrades gracefully to a single model and one vendor, which is the solo-researcher tier of the scaling problem. It replaces panel overlap with per-model calibration. CDSFL is unusually well placed to build the calibration corpus because falsifier execution gives per-finding ground truth: you can measure each model's true effectiveness rather than asking it. Treat this as the near-term deliverable and capture-recapture as the medium-term one.

techniques.name: Relative Decision Accuracy as the evaluation metric for a stopping gate
techniques.source: El Emam, Laitenberger & Harbich 2000; El Emam & Laitenberger 2001, IEEE TSE 27(9):851-864 (https://www.ehealthinformation.ca/web/default/files/wp-files/1068.pdf); Thelin & Runeson 2000a; discussed in Petersson et al. 2004 s.3.1
techniques.what_it_does: Scores an estimator not by how close its number is to truth (relative error) but by how often the STOP/CONTINUE decision it produces matches the decision that would have been made with perfect knowledge, net of the accuracy of the naive default decision. RDA = DA - A_default.
techniques.assumption: That an effectiveness threshold is set in advance. That is a limitation: the threshold has to be chosen, and RDA is not defined without it.
techniques.why: CDSFL's convergence gate is a binary decision, so its estimator should be selected on decision accuracy, not on point-estimate error. El Emam & Laitenberger's two-inspector study found MtCh (Chao's Mt estimator, originally Chapman's) usable for the DECISION specifically because its bias and dispersion happen to fail in the helpful direction — it underestimates when effectiveness is above threshold (making the correct stop decision) and is dispersed when below (frequently making the correct continue decision). They call this cumbersome and lacking parsimony, and they are right, but the methodological point stands: an estimator that is bad at estimating can still be good at deciding, and CDSFL only needs the second. Their measured decision accuracies were frequently below the 70% they call the psychological threshold — set expectations accordingly.

techniques.name: The two-inspector case: Chapman's bias-corrected estimator (model MtCh)
techniques.source: Chapman 1951, Univ. California Publ. Statistics; Chao 1989 Biometrics 45:427-438; evaluated for inspections by El Emam & Laitenberger 2001, IEEE TSE 27(9):851-864 (https://www.ehealthinformation.ca/web/default/files/wp-files/1068.pdf); contradicted on real inspection data by Thelin, Petersson & Runeson 2002
techniques.what_it_does: The small-sample-corrected Lincoln-Petersen estimator. Plain Lincoln-Petersen is N = n1*n2/m (n1, n2 the two find-counts, m the overlap); Chapman corrects the small-sample bias. In a 48-study-point Monte Carlo it was the only model that never failed to produce an estimate under any studied condition, and it allows the two reviewers to differ in capability.
techniques.assumption: Two reviewers; all defects equally difficult (it accounts for reviewer heterogeneity, not defect heterogeneity). It underestimates when the two find few or no defects in common, or when defect difficulty varies a lot.
techniques.why: This is the estimator for CDSFL's smallest non-trivial tier — one researcher, two model calls. Note the sharp contradiction in the record: El Emam & Laitenberger's simulation recommends MtCh at two inspectors; Thelin et al. 2002 found it estimates poorly on real inspection data; and Mh-JK, the consensus winner at four-plus reviewers, is explicitly non-robust and underestimating at two. There is no estimator that is best across the whole range, which means CDSFL's scaling problem shows up inside the estimator choice too: the correct estimator is a function of the deployment tier. Model-selection procedures to choose automatically have been tried repeatedly (distance measures, chi-square, smoothing, Akaike) and Petersson et al. report that none of them work appropriately on software inspection data.

techniques.name: Bug-arrival-curve stopping rules for OPEN reviewer populations (Trend / Peak / Knee)
techniques.source: Wang, Yang, Yu, Menzies & Wang, 'Crowdtesting: When is the Party Over?' / 'Effective Automated Decision Support for Managing Crowdtesting', ICSE 2019, arXiv:1805.03218 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.03218)
techniques.what_it_does: Eight stopping methods evaluated on 218 real crowdtesting tasks. Three curve-shape methods (Trend, Peak, Knee) plus simple M0 outperformed the sophisticated capture-recapture estimators. Best results: median 91% of bugs detected with 49% cost saved.
techniques.assumption: That reports arrive as a stream and the arrival curve is informative. Explicitly does NOT assume a fixed, predetermined reviewer set.
techniques.why: This is the most important NEGATIVE result for CDSFL and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than filed away. The authors found that MhJK, MhCH and MtCH — the three estimators the inspection literature crowned — performed WORSE than a naive knee-detector on the accumulation curve. MhJK achieved 95.6% bug recovery but only 6.5% cost saving (it essentially never fired the stop); MtCH saved 66.7% of cost but recovered only 50% of bugs (it stopped far too early). Their explanation is that inspection estimators assume a CLOSED environment with predetermined inspectors, and crowdtesting is open. CDSFL's panel is closed within a round but the artefact changes between rounds, which is an open-population feature. Before committing to capture-recapture, run the cheap curve-shape baselines against it on CDSFL's own historical runs; the inspection literature's winner may lose.

techniques.name: The empirical team-size literature: composition beats count
techniques.source: Porter, Siy, Mockus & Votta 1998, ACM TOSEM 7(1):41-79 (https://drum.lib.umd.edu/bitstreams/461cbc67-0adc-4321-a0e4-ed28e5d75c65/download); Buck 1981, IBM TR-21-802; Biffl & Halling 2003, IEEE TSE 29(5):385-397 (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1199069/); Rigby & Bird 2013, FSE (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/rigby2013convergent.pdf); Martin & Tsai 1990, CACM 33(2):268-274 (N-fold inspection, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/75577.75587)
techniques.what_it_does: Measures how defect yield varies with the number and composition of reviewers. Porter et al.'s industrial experiment used 1-, 2- and 4-person teams and found team size contributed F=0.50, p=0.6062 to defect-detection variance — not significant — while log(code size) contributed F=22.66 (p<0.0001) and two individual reviewer identities contributed F=12.39 (p=0.0007) and F=13.17 (p=0.0005). Buck found no difference among teams of three, four and five. Biffl & Halling found that combining DIFFERENT reading techniques in a team is considerably more effective than using the best single technique, and that getting the process mix right matters more than adding inspectors above a certain team size. Rigby & Bird found contemporary code review converges independently on two reviewers across projects. Martin & Tsai's N-fold design replicates the whole inspection with N independent teams and takes the union, and finds different teams detect different faults.
techniques.assumption: Software artefacts, human reviewers, defect counts as the yield measure. Generalisation to model panels is by structural analogy only, and Porter et al. explicitly disclaim generality beyond one project, language and organisation.
techniques.why: This is the answer to questions 2 and 3 as far as this literature goes, and it is blunt: WHO reviews dominates HOW MANY review. That directly supports CDSFL's instinct to spend on vendor diversity rather than seat count, and it directly undermines a routing ladder whose escalation step is 'find a stronger writer' — Porter et al.'s data says the gain from a different reviewer is large and the gain from another reviewer is not detectable. There is a second, sharper consequence that neither literature states because neither had both problems at once: the panel size that maximises detection per unit cost (two, per Rigby & Bird and Porter) is NOT the panel size at which you can estimate how much you have missed (four or more, per Briand et al. 1997/2000 and Miller 1999; biostatistics rules of thumb say five, with seven or ten preferred). If CDSFL wants its convergence gate to be principled rather than guessed, it must pay for reviewers it does not need for detection. That trade should be made explicitly and priced, not stumbled into.

techniques.name: Detection Profile Method and curve-fitting alternatives
techniques.source: Wohlin & Runeson 1998; Thelin & Runeson 2000a; Briand, El Emam & Freimut 1998, ISSRE (https://www.ehealthinformation.ca/web/default/files/wp-files/isern-98-11.pdf); Petersson & Wohlin 1999a, 2000
techniques.what_it_does: Sorts findings by the number of reviewers who found each, fits a decreasing curve (exponential in DPM), and extrapolates to a limit to estimate total content. Intuitive and explainable graphically to non-specialists.
techniques.assumption: Still requires overlap — the x-axis IS the number of reviewers per finding. Assumes the chosen functional form.
techniques.why: Listing it so it is not rediscovered as a way around the overlap problem: it is not one, it consumes exactly the same data. It is also the weaker option. Thelin & Runeson concluded DPM is the best curve-fitting method but Mh-JK estimates more accurately; the Briand et al. selection procedure that chose between EDPM and Mh-JK showed a small improvement in the original study and was NOT confirmed in Petersson & Wohlin's replication. And El Emam & Laitenberger note DPM as defined would be difficult to apply with only two inspectors, so it does not serve the small-deployment tier either.

transfers: The core mechanism transfers cleanly and the structural analogy is exact: reviewer = trapping occasion, finding = individual, review round = closed capture experiment. Nothing about tool-executed falsification breaks it — a falsifier that confirms or refutes a claim REMOVES the false-positive contamination that inspection studies had to live with, so CDSFL is in a better position than the inspection literature was, not a worse one.

The marginal-value question (does the next reviewer pay?) is answerable with far less data and far weaker assumptions than the total-population question. Chao & Jost's identity 1 - C_m = S_(m+1) - S_m makes coverage deficit and accumulation-curve slope the same object. CDSFL should compute the derivative and stop asking for the asymptote.

Coverage-based standardisation is a genuinely better convergence gate than anything CDSFL currently has, and it solves the scaling problem head-on: define the stop as 'estimated coverage reached C', not 'N models ran' or 'K rounds elapsed'. A one-model, five-model and five-hundred-model deployment then run the same gate and produce comparable outputs, and the solo researcher is honestly told they cannot reach C.

Chao et al. 2009's sufficient-sampling formulas are implemented and verified — my implementation reproduces every incidence-data figure in their Table 2 exactly — so they can be pointed at CDSFL's data the day overlap is recorded. Their empirical shape is the actionable part: reaching 90% of the estimated population costs a median 0.80x current effort; reaching 100% costs a median 2.23x and up to 10.67x. Exhaustiveness is the wrong target.

The direction of dependence bias is known and usable as a sanity check: positive dependence between reviewers biases the estimate DOWN, negative dependence biases it UP. CDSFL's panel is deliberately heterogeneous (pushing toward negative dependence in what gets reported) but built from models with correlated blind spots (positive dependence in what can be seen at all), so the net direction is genuinely unknown a priori and must be measured, not assumed.

Partial identification is the right output format. Population size is not point-identified without independence, CDSFL cannot assert independence, so the honest deliverable is a confidence set under stated qualitative dependence bounds — which also happens to be more falsifiable than a point estimate, and therefore better suited to a Popperian harness.

Experience-based / subjective estimation works on the records CDSFL already keeps and degrades gracefully to a single model. It is the only technique found that spans all three deployment tiers without modification, and CDSFL can build a better calibration corpus than the inspection literature ever could, because falsifier execution supplies per-finding ground truth.

The empirical inspection result that reviewer IDENTITY dominates reviewer COUNT (Porter et al.: team size F=0.50 p=0.61, individual reviewers F=12.39 and F=13.17, both p<0.001) supports spending the budget on diversity rather than seats — and cuts directly against a routing ladder whose escalation is 'get a stronger model'.

Relative Decision Accuracy is the correct evaluation metric for a convergence gate. An estimator can be poor at estimating and still good at deciding; CDSFL only needs the second, and should select on it.
does_not_transfer: NOTHING in this area transfers at all until co-discovery is recorded. Every estimator named here — Lincoln-Petersen, Chapman, all six M0/Mt/Mh/Mth estimators, Chao1, Chao2, both jackknives, ACE, ICE, DPM, log-linear models — is a function of the singleton and doubleton counts. With Q2 = 2 the family produces 561,018 (bias-corrected Chao2) and 3,688 (incidence jackknife) from the same data. This is not a difficult estimation problem; it is a null result. Recording overlap is the precondition, not an improvement.

The vote-aggregation scaling law (Chen, Davis, Hanin, Bailis, Stoica, Zaharia & Zou, arXiv:2403.02419) does NOT transfer as stated. Their inverse-U — performance rising then falling with more LM calls — is a property of MAJORITY VOTING, where extra calls dilute a correct minority. CDSFL aggregates by UNION and confirms by tool execution, so marginal recall is monotone non-decreasing in reviewers and no vote-dilution turnover can occur. What survives is the mechanism, not the result: their turnover is caused by heterogeneity in item difficulty, which is the same structural fact that makes Mh the right capture-recapture model. If CDSFL wants a turnover point it must derive its own, from findings-per-model falling while false-positive falsifier executions per model stay flat — which is measurable from CDSFL's own confirm/refute records and is not in any paper I found.

The behavioural group-process literature on inspection meetings (Sauer, Jeffery, Land & Yetton, TSE 26(1):1-14, 2000; Votta's 'Does every inspection need a meeting?') does not transfer. Its subject is meeting gains and losses among co-present humans. CDSFL's panel members do not meet, do not anchor on each other, and do not suffer production blocking.

Perspective-based reading results transfer only weakly. The inspection literature repeatedly checked whether PBR — which deliberately minimises overlap — breaks capture-recapture, and concluded it does not (Thelin & Runeson 1999; Freimut 1997; Freimut et al. 2001). But it left open whether PBR makes estimators OVERestimate, and CDSFL's vendor-diverse panel is a much stronger overlap-suppressing intervention than PBR ever was. Do not import the 'PBR is safe' conclusion without re-testing it.

Fault seeding (Mills 1972) as usually practised does not transfer, because you cannot seed an arbitrary STEM artefact with known findings the way you can seed code with known bugs. It is, however, constructible for CDSFL as a benchmark corpus of artefacts with pre-catalogued defects, and would be a far stronger control than anything the inspection literature had. Flagging it as available, not as transferred.

The routing ladder problem is not addressed anywhere in this literature. Model Mt treats reviewer capability heterogeneity as a nuisance parameter to be estimated away, never as a control variable to be allocated. Capture-recapture will tell you your reviewers differ; it will not tell you which one to send a hard finding to, and it has nothing whatsoever to say about what to do when no stronger reviewer exists. That is a bandit / experimental-design problem, in a different area.

Adoption evidence does not transfer, because there is almost none. Petersson et al.'s ten-year survey found exactly ONE published industrial experience report (Ardissone et al. 1998), and that report used only the original 1992 method, ignoring every subsequent result. Scott & Wohlin's 2008 unit-testing case study is the other. Do not present capture-recapture to reviewers or funders as industrially proven; it is theoretically mature and practically almost untried.
open: Is 2-of-2,050 a measurement of the panel or of the matcher? This literature cannot answer it and neither can CDSFL's current records. It requires a measured finding-matcher accuracy: sample finding pairs, adjudicate same/different by tool or human, report the rate. Fraysse et al. show that below ~0.2 capture rate the misidentification models will not converge without an informative prior on that identification probability, so this number is a required input to everything downstream, not a nice-to-have.

Every estimator here assumes a CLOSED population. CDSFL's artefact is edited between rounds in response to findings, which means findings are born and die during the study — an open-population problem. Petersson et al. list open models and change-in-ratio models as explicitly unexplored for inspections and say nobody has actually looked. Twenty-two years later I found no paper that has. This is genuinely open and CDSFL is unusually well placed to work on it.

No published work applies capture-recapture or species-richness estimation to a panel of AI models. arXiv returns zero results for 'capture-recapture' AND 'large language model', and zero for 'species richness' AND 'large language models'; the only adjacent hit is a 2026 web-crawling paper using Chao1/ACE for entity-discovery coverage. This is unoccupied territory. That is an opportunity and also a warning: there is no prior calibration to lean on, and the first CDSFL results will be the calibration.

Nothing in this literature handles overlap where each capture carries a tool-verified CONFIRMED or REFUTED label. The inspection literature treats false positives informally — Petersson et al. note underestimation 'may not be a big problem since false positives are often included in the inspection data, which would increase the estimation result', which is two errors cancelling by luck, not a method. A capture-recapture formulation in which capture histories are labelled by an oracle appears not to exist and would need inventing. CDSFL has the data for it that nobody else has.

The cost model is missing. Rasmussen & Starr 1979 give the optimal-stopping frame, but it needs an exchange rate between the cost of one more model-review and the value of one more confirmed finding — including the cost of the falsifier executions that unconfirmed findings consume. CDSFL has not measured either side. Without it, 'when does another reviewer stop paying' has no numerical answer even with perfect overlap data.

Whether the closed-panel inspection estimators or the open-arrival curve heuristics fit CDSFL better is an empirical question that has not been asked. Wang et al. found the crowned inspection estimators lost badly to a naive knee-detector in an open environment. CDSFL sits between the two regimes. Run both against CDSFL's historical runs before committing.

Diversity measurement (question 3) is only half-answered by this area. The overlap matrix IS a diversity measurement — pairwise complementarity between reviewers is directly readable from it, and Chao's shared-species estimators (extended by Pan et al. 2009 to multiple assemblages) would let CDSFL estimate how much two models' finding-populations genuinely differ rather than how much their outputs happened to differ. But no one has costed diversity against it. The trade 'one more vendor versus one more seat at an existing vendor' has no principled answer in this literature; Biffl & Halling's 'process mix beats team size' is the closest thing and it is a qualitative finding from human reading techniques.

Whether frontier models violate the rare-item homogeneity assumption that Chao2 needs is unknown and testable. Chao2 is nearly unbiased only if the UNDETECTED and singleton items have roughly equal detection probability. If all five models share a blind spot — a class of finding none of them can see — that class has detection probability zero and no estimator in this family will ever count it. Chao's estimator is a LOWER BOUND for exactly this reason, and CDSFL should present it as one. A seeded-defect control corpus is the only way to bound the size of the shared blind spot, and it is buildable.

areas.area: Diversity as a measurable, purchasable resource: N-version programming and its critique, ensemble diversity measures, bias-variance-diversity, and prompt-condition versus model-condition diversity for LLM reviewer panels
areas.summary: The single most useful thing this literature offers is a formalism that fits CDSFL almost exactly, and it is not the ensemble-learning one. Eckhardt and Lee's "difficulty function" — the probability that a randomly drawn reviewer misses a given item — plus Littlewood, Popov, Strigini and Shryane's 2000 adaptation of it to fault *detection* (not fault tolerance) describes a system that pools findings from several imperfect finders against a real oracle, which is what CDSFL is. In that framework three things fall out that answer real parts of your problem: repeated application of one reviewer always finds fewer new items than an independence assumption predicts, by exactly the variance of the difficulty function; if two reviewers are equally effective on average, using one of each is *provably* better than using either twice (Cauchy-Schwarz, no assumption about correlation needed); and the diversity number you want is a single measurable ratio, GD = 1 - E[theta^2]/E[theta], which I verified symbolically and by Monte Carlo is identical to Partridge and Krzanowski's generalised-diversity statistic. The empirical news is bad for naive multi-vendor optimism: a June 2026 replication of Knight-Leveson using 48 coding-agent implementations found 429 coincident failures where independence predicts 115.36 (z = 29.20), and crossing an agent/vendor boundary only moved the rate of perfectly-co-failing pairs from 65% to 55%. On your specific prompt-condition question, Littlewood and Miller's 1989 extension gives you the theory for free — a "methodology" in their model is exactly a constraint set that induces a distribution over reviewer behaviour, which is what a system prompt is, and any difference between the two induced difficulty functions strictly beats the same-prompt case. The measured size of that effect, though, is small and depends critically on *what kind* of prompt difference: role-level conditioning buys real diversity, while wording tweaks, formatting wrappers and temperature buy essentially nothing once you debias the estimator. Two things genuinely favour you over most of this literature: your ground truth is an executed falsifier, which puts you in the coverage-scaling regime where more samples keep paying, rather than the majority-vote regime that plateaus around a hundred samples; and the detection version of the difficulty model is, in its authors' own words, far easier to parameterise than the design-diversity version. What is not solved, and would need invention, is allocation when reviewer capability spans orders of magnitude, and estimating any of these quantities from a finding population that is censored to what you actually found — which your 2-in-2,050 co-discovery rate makes acute.

techniques.name: Eckhardt-Lee difficulty-function model of coincident failure
techniques.source: D. E. Eckhardt and L. D. Lee, "A Theoretical Basis for the Analysis of Multiversion Software Subject to Coincident Errors", IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-11(12):1511-1517, 1985. Reviewed in full in Littlewood, Popov & Strigini, "Modeling software design diversity: a review", ACM Computing Surveys 33(2):177-208, 2001, https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/1951/1/Modelling%20software%20design%20diversity.pdf (DOI 10.1145/384192.384195)
techniques.what_it_does: Defines theta(x), the probability that a randomly drawn version (for you: a randomly drawn reviewer) fails on item x. Proves that even when versions are conditionally independent *given* x, they fail dependently over a random x, and quantifies the excess exactly: P(both fail) = E[theta]^2 + Var[theta]. Correlated failure is not a defect of the reviewers, it is a consequence of items differing in difficulty.
techniques.assumption: That there is a well-defined population of reviewers from which yours are a draw, and a well-defined population of items (claims, artefact locations) with a usage/occurrence profile. It assumes conditional independence given the item, which is violated if your reviewers see each other's output — so it applies to your round-1 independent pass, not to later rounds where findings are visible.
techniques.why: This is the correct formal object for your question 1 and 3. It says the quantity you must measure is not 'how good is each model' but 'how much does miss-probability vary across findings'. Var[theta] is precisely the number that determines whether a second reviewer is worth buying. It also predicts your 2-in-2,050 observation is compatible with either genuinely complementary reviewers OR a censored population — the model cannot distinguish those without an estimate of what nobody found.

techniques.name: Littlewood-Miller forced-diversity (methodological diversity) extension
techniques.source: B. Littlewood and D. R. Miller, "Conceptual Modeling of Coincident Failures in Multiversion Software", IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 15(12):1596-1614, Dec 1989, DOI 10.1109/32.58771, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/58771/ . Formulas as presented in Littlewood, Popov & Strigini 2001 (link above), eqs. 4.7-4.9.
techniques.what_it_does: Generalises Eckhardt-Lee to two *different* development methodologies A and B, each inducing its own difficulty function. Joint failure becomes E[theta_A theta_B] = E[theta_A]E[theta_B] + Cov(theta_A, theta_B). Because the covariance can be negative, a diverse pair can fail *less often together than independence would predict* — impossible in the single-methodology case, where the excess Var[theta] is always non-negative. Also proves that for 1-out-of-n systems with fewer than n methodologies available, spreading them as evenly as possible is optimal (AABBC beats AAABC).
techniques.assumption: That a 'methodology' is anything that changes the distribution over reviewer behaviours. Critically it does NOT require you to demonstrate negative correlation — Eckhardt-Lee is recovered only in the degenerate case theta_A = theta_B for every item, which the authors call an unattainable worst case. It does assume the two methodologies are comparably effective; when they are not, the better methodology used twice can beat the diverse pair.
techniques.why: This is the theoretical warrant for restoring your lost prompt-condition axis, and it is stronger than I expected. A vendor's hidden system prompt versus a bare condition is, in this model's own terms, two methodologies over identical weights: the constraint set differs, so the induced distribution over reviewer behaviour differs, so theta_A != theta_B, so you are strictly out of the Eckhardt-Lee worst case. You do not need to prove the prompt conditions are negatively correlated to justify the axis — you only need them to be different, which is trivially true. Note the AABBC result maps directly onto your allocation question: with 5 seats and 4 vendors, spread evenly rather than doubling up on the strongest.

techniques.name: Diverse fault-DETECTION model (Result 1, Result 7, fault-class stratification)
techniques.source: B. Littlewood, P. Popov, L. Strigini and N. Shryane, "Modeling the effects of combining diverse software fault detection techniques", IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 26(12):1157-1167, 2000, DOI 10.1109/32.888629, open access at https://openaccess.city.ac.uk/id/eprint/1626/1/Modelling%20the%20effects%20of%20combining.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Recasts the difficulty function over *faults* rather than inputs, for procedures whose job is to FIND faults rather than mask them. Result: two applications of the same procedure leave E[theta_A^2] >= (E[theta_A])^2 of faults undetected, so repeating a procedure is always worse than an independence assumption suggests. Result 7 (proved by Cauchy-Schwarz): if E[theta_A^2] = E[theta_B^2], then applying A once and B once is strictly better than applying either twice — always, with no assumption about the sign of the correlation. And it shows the parameters become estimable if you stratify faults into CLASSES and estimate mean difficulty per (class, procedure) pair.
techniques.assumption: Requires an oracle that decides whether a reported item is a real fault — which is exactly your tool-executed falsifier, and is the assumption that fails for vote-aggregated LLM panels. Requires that faults be classifiable into meaningful types with estimable class probabilities. Result 7's indifference precondition (equal squared efficacy) is strong and, the authors warn, usually needs to be deliberately engineered rather than assumed.
techniques.why: This is the closest structural match in the entire literature to what CDSFL actually is: several imperfect finders, an oracle that confirms, union rather than vote. The class-stratification trick is the direct answer to your 2-in-2,050 sparsity problem — the authors hit exactly this ('individual faults are likely to be sparse... no opportunity to estimate the probabilities') and solve it by moving up to fault classes. For you that means: stop attributing findings to models one at a time, and start estimating per-model miss rates over finding TYPES (dimensional error, algebraic slip, unsupported citation, statistical misuse). Then per-model, per-class miss rates give you a purchasing rule. The authors also note explicitly that this detection variant is far easier to parameterise than the design-diversity variant — you are in the tractable branch.

techniques.name: Generalised Diversity / Coincident Failure Diversity as the measurable diversity number
techniques.source: D. Partridge and W. Krzanowski, "Software diversity: practical statistics for its measurement and exploitation", Information and Software Technology 39:707-717, 1997. Formulas and evaluation in L. I. Kuncheva and C. J. Whitaker, "Measures of Diversity in Classifier Ensembles and Their Relationship with the Ensemble Accuracy", Machine Learning 51(2):181-207, 2003, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1023/A:1022859003006 (PDF: http://machine-learning.martinsewell.com/ensembles/KunchevaWhitaker2003.pdf), eqs. 18-20
techniques.what_it_does: From the distribution p_i (probability that exactly i of L reviewers miss a given item), computes p(1) = sum (i/L) p_i and p(2) = sum (i(i-1)/(L(L-1))) p_i, then GD = 1 - p(2)/p(1). Ranges 0 (no diversity: whenever one misses, all miss) to 1 (perfect complementarity: no two ever both miss the same item).
techniques.assumption: Requires a known item population — including items that everyone missed. Assumes reviewers are exchangeable draws.
techniques.why: I verified with SymPy and independently by Monte Carlo (600k-800k draws) that under the Eckhardt-Lee setup p(1) = E[theta] and p(2) = E[theta^2] EXACTLY, so GD = 1 - E[theta^2]/E[theta] and Var[theta] = p(2) - p(1)^2. That is: the ensemble-learning diversity statistic and the software-reliability difficulty quantity are the same object, and both are computable from one table of 'how many reviewers found each finding'. That is the single number to instrument. The adaptation, and it is severe, is the censoring: I computed that if every observed finding was found by exactly one of L reviewers (your regime), GD collapses to exactly 1/(L-1) — 1.00 at L=2, 0.25 at L=5, 0.14 at L=8 — purely as an artefact of normalising against a population that by construction contains no all-missed items. Computed naively on your 2,050 findings, GD will tell you about L, not about your reviewers.

techniques.name: Knight-Leveson independence experiment, and its 2026 replication with coding agents
techniques.source: J. C. Knight and N. G. Leveson, "An experimental evaluation of the assumption of independence in multiversion programming", IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-12(1):96-109, 1986, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/TSE.1986.6312924 . Replication: J. Ron, B. Baudry and M. Monperrus, "N-Version Programming with Coding Agents", arXiv:2606.20158, 18 June 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20158
techniques.what_it_does: The 1986 original: 27 independently written versions, one million test cases, coincident failures far above the independence prediction. The 2026 replication: 48 agent-generated implementations across 5 agent systems, 23 models and 3 languages against a shared oracle and 1,000,000 randomised inputs. I verified the numbers against the paper text: 429 coincident-failure cases against an independence prediction of 115.36 (z = 29.20). Stratified by boundary: among 221 same-agent pairs, 52 had defined phi and 34 (65%) were at exactly phi = 1 with 6 (12%) non-positive; among 907 cross-agent pairs, 158 had defined phi and 87 (55%) were at exactly phi = 1 with 50 (32%) non-positive. Majority-vote triples still cut mean failure count from 387.44 to 130.99, with 11,844 triples showing zero observed failures. Failures concentrated where the specification was hard or ambiguous.
techniques.assumption: Program synthesis from a fixed specification with a reference oracle — a narrower task than open-ended STEM review, and a single specification (Launch Interceptor). Single invocation per configuration, so within-model sampling variability is not separated from between-model variation.
techniques.why: This is the closest empirical answer you will get to 'does asking N vendors buy independence', and the answer is: partly, and much less than you would hope. Crossing a vendor boundary moved perfect co-failure from 65% to 55% and non-positive correlation from 12% to 32% — a real effect, not a null one, but nowhere near independence. Two further points matter for you. First, the authors motivate the study by citing Littlewood and Miller, which confirms the framework above is the field's own. Second, and this is the load-bearing bit: failures concentrated where the specification was hard or ambiguous, which is a direct empirical confirmation of the difficulty-function mechanism rather than a generic 'models are similar' result. It means your correlated misses will cluster on hard claims, and that is where extra reviewers are worth least — exactly backwards from the intuition your routing ladder encodes.

techniques.name: Coverage scaling under repeated sampling WITH an automatic verifier
techniques.source: B. Brown, J. Juravsky, R. Ehrlich, R. Clark, Q. V. Le, C. Re and A. Mirhoseini, "Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling", arXiv:2407.21787v3, 30 Dec 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21787
techniques.what_it_does: Measures coverage (fraction of problems solved by ANY of k samples) as k grows to 10,000. Finds coverage follows an exponentiated power law c ~ exp(a k^b) (their eq. 3; e.g. a = -1.33, b = -0.43 for Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH, fit error 0.003). Critically, it separates two regimes: where an automatic verifier exists (unit tests, proof checkers), coverage gains convert directly into performance — SWE-bench Lite goes from 15.9% at one sample to 56% at 250. Where no verifier exists, majority voting and reward models plateau beyond roughly 100 samples and the gap to coverage keeps widening (MATH coverage rises 82.9% -> 98.44% from 100 to 10,000 samples while the vote-based methods flatline).
techniques.assumption: Pass/fail tasks with a trustworthy verifier and a non-zero per-sample success probability. It measures coverage of a fixed problem set, not discovery of an unknown finding population.
techniques.why: This is the strongest argument in the literature that CDSFL is in a *better* regime than the debate/voting harnesses it will be compared against, and it is the reason the pessimistic multi-agent results below do not bind you. Because your ground truth is an executed falsifier, you are on the verifier side of their dichotomy: additional reviewer-samples keep converting into real findings long past the point where a vote-aggregated panel stops improving. Practically, the fitted two-parameter law is the right shape for your solo-researcher deployment: one model, many samples, exponentiated-power-law coverage, and a stopping point read off the fitted curve rather than guessed. Fit a and b from k = 1..8 and extrapolate; that is a defensible stopping rule for the one-model case.

techniques.name: Debiased estimation of prompt-condition effects (separating between-prompt signal from within-prompt noise)
techniques.source: Feng et al., "Second-Order Response Laws for LLM Judges: Debiased Estimation of Prompt Instability", arXiv:2608.16253, 2026, https://arxiv.org/html/2608.16253
techniques.what_it_does: Decomposes total judge disagreement into within-prompt sampling noise U_within and between-prompt systematic variation U_prompt. Shows the naive plug-in estimator is biased upward by exactly U_within/R for R repeats per prompt (so at R=2 the bias equals half the within-prompt disagreement), and gives an unbiased agreement-based estimator U_prompt = ((K-1)/K)(A_within - A_across) requiring only R >= 2. Validated over 44,112 live calls across Qwen, GPT-OSS, Gemma and Claude.
techniques.assumption: Categorical judgements with repeated sampling per prompt; K prompts, R >= 2 repeats each. Their prompt sets were formatting/wrapper variants, NOT role-level or system-prompt-level rewrites — this matters for how far their null result generalises.
techniques.why: This is the instrument you need before restoring the prompt-condition axis, and it carries a warning you should take seriously. In their four-model panel the debiased between-prompt variation was tiny — Qwen 0.0052, GPT-OSS -0.0012, Gemma 0.0177, Claude 0.0099 — against residual call-level disagreement of 0.1911 for Qwen. That is: for formatting-level prompt differences, essentially all apparent 'prompt diversity' was resampling noise wearing a costume. If you restore the vendor-system-prompt-versus-bare axis and measure it with a plug-in estimator, you will very likely report a diversity gain that does not exist. Use their estimator. The escape hatch is that they tested wrappers, not role conditioning, and the next entry shows that distinction is exactly where the effect lives.

techniques.name: Prompt-condition (role/system-prompt) diversity as an ensemble axis
techniques.source: G. K. R. Lau, W. Hu, D. Liu, J. Chen, S.-K. Ng and B. K. H. Low, "Dipper: Diversity in Prompts for Producing Large Language Model Ensembles in Reasoning Tasks", arXiv:2412.15238, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.15238 . Complementary evidence: Yao, "More Is Not More: What Matters for Diversity in LLM Opinions?", arXiv:2607.20429, 2026, https://arxiv.org/html/2607.20429v1
techniques.what_it_does: DIPPER builds an ensemble from ONE model by varying the system/role prompt, selecting the prompt set by maximising fidelity-adjusted semantic volume V = log det(R R^T) (the log-determinant of the Gram matrix of sentence embeddings of the prompts — a determinantal-point-process style volume criterion that trades diversity against each prompt's expected accuracy via a hyperparameter alpha). Measured: on MATH with Qwen2-MATH-1.5B, an ensemble of seven DIFFERENT role prompts scores 57.31% against 55.76% for a self-ensemble with no prompt variation and 56.55% averaged over seven single-prompt self-ensembles; accuracy rises and variance falls monotonically as unique prompts go 1 -> 7. Spearman correlation between V and test performance runs roughly 0.5-0.8 depending on alpha. 'More Is Not More' independently finds that role-level conditioning produces large diversity gains (mean-pairwise-distance gain ~0.62) while enhanced prompt instructions, demographic cueing and raising temperature from 0.7 to 1.0 produce approximately zero.
techniques.assumption: Aggregation by voting over reasoning answers, on tasks with a single correct answer, using small open-weight models. Diversity is measured over OUTPUT text, not over which errors are made. DIPPER's prompt-selection step needs a development set to estimate each prompt's fidelity u(w).
techniques.why: This is the only literature that directly measures what your lost axis buys, and the honest answer is: about 1.5 accuracy points on a voting task, which is real but modest — and, combined with the previous entry and 'More Is Not More', the shape of the finding is that the payoff depends entirely on what KIND of prompt difference you use. Wording, formatting and temperature buy nothing. Role-level and system-prompt-level conditioning buy a lot. A vendor's hidden system prompt versus bare is squarely in the second category, so the axis is worth restoring. The adaptation for you: DIPPER's semantic volume measures diversity of prompt TEXT, which is a proxy you should not trust; you have something better, because your falsifier lets you measure diversity of MISSES directly via the GD statistic above. Use V only to select candidate conditions, then validate on miss-overlap.

techniques.name: Quality-diversity trade-off in mixture-of-agents (Self-MoA)
techniques.source: W. Li, Y. Lin, C. Zhang et al., "Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different Large Language Models Beneficial?", arXiv:2502.00674, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00674 (ICML 2025). Diversity metric from D. Dan Friedman and A. B. Dieng, "The Vendi Score: A Diversity Evaluation Metric for Machine Learning", TMLR 2023, arXiv:2210.02410, https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02410
techniques.what_it_does: Over 200 experiments fitting t = alpha*q + beta*d + gamma, where t is ensemble performance, q is mean proposer accuracy and d is proposer diversity measured by the Vendi Score (the exponential of the Shannon entropy of the eigenvalues of a similarity matrix — the 'effective number of distinct outputs'). Both coefficients significant at p < 0.001, R^2 ~= 0.69-0.77. Standardised coefficients: MMLU alpha 2.558 vs beta 1.841; CRUX 4.548 vs 1.421; MATH 4.719 vs 2.839. Quality dominates diversity everywhere, by 1.4x to 3.2x. Self-MoA (repeated sampling from the single best model) beats mixed-model MoA by 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0 and 3.8% on average. Mixing wins only when the models are of SIMILAR quality and the task is a heterogeneous mixture of sub-tasks where different models specialise.
techniques.assumption: Aggregation is a synthesiser LLM reading proposer outputs — a model-judged aggregation, not a tool-verified one. Diversity is measured on output text. Proposer quality is measured as benchmark accuracy, which presumes a labelled task.
techniques.why: The headline result (single best model beats a mixed panel) does NOT transfer, because the mechanism is that mixing drags down average proposer quality and a model-based aggregator is sensitive to that. Your aggregator is a tool executing a falsifier: it is indifferent to the average quality of the panel, because a bad reviewer's bad finding simply fails to confirm and costs you compute, not correctness. That immunity is a genuine architectural advantage and you should claim it explicitly. What DOES transfer is their condition for when mixing wins — similar-quality models on a heterogeneous task — and that condition is satisfied by CDSFL, whose review task spans dimensional analysis, algebra, statistics, citation checking and code. Their alpha > beta finding also warns against your instinct to buy diversity first: on their evidence, replacing a weak panel member with a stronger one beats adding a differently-flavoured weak one.

techniques.name: CAPA (chance-adjusted probabilistic agreement) for measuring model similarity
techniques.source: S. Goel et al., "Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight", arXiv:2502.04313, ICML 2025 spotlight, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04313 , project page https://model-similarity.github.io/ , package `pip install lm-sim`
techniques.what_it_does: kappa_p = (c_obs - c_exp)/(1 - c_exp), where c_obs = (1/|D|) sum_x sum_i p1(o_i) p2(o_i) is probabilistic agreement over answer options, and c_exp = pbar1*pbar2 + (1-pbar1)(1-pbar2)*(1/|D|) sum_x 1/(|O(x)|-1) is chance agreement adjusted for each model's accuracy and for item difficulty. Unlike raw error overlap it corrects for the fact that two 90%-accurate models have less scope to disagree than two 50%-accurate ones; unlike Cohen's kappa it distinguishes *which* wrong answer was given and uses probabilities. Findings: error correlation rises with capability across 100+ open-weight models; LLM-judge scores favour models similar to the judge, mean Pearson 0.84 across nine judges, surviving accuracy controls. Across 350+ models, models agree ~60% of the time when both err.
techniques.assumption: Requires a fixed item set with known correct answers and a bounded option space, plus access to output probabilities. Designed for multiple-choice benchmarks.
techniques.why: The measurement machinery does not transfer as-is — you have no option space and no labels, you have an open-ended finding stream and a falsifier. But two of its results bear directly on your design. First, the accuracy-adjustment insight is exactly the correction your co-discovery statistic needs: a raw co-discovery count of 2 in 2,050 is uninterpretable without adjusting for how much scope your reviewers had to overlap at all. Second, the judge-affinity result (r = 0.84) is a direct argument against ever letting a model confirm another model's finding, which is a design choice you have already made correctly — treat this as external validation of tool-only confirmation rather than as a technique to adopt. The 60%-agreement-when-both-err figure is also the best available prior for inter-reviewer error correlation if you need to sanity-check a measured value.

techniques.name: Capture-recapture estimation of the unfound finding population
techniques.source: H. Petersson, T. Thelin, P. Runeson and C. Wohlin, "Capture-recapture in software inspections after 10 years research: theory, evaluation and application", Journal of Systems and Software 72(2):249-264, 2004, https://wohlin.eu/jss04-1.pdf . Underlying estimators: Burnham & Overton (1978) jackknife Mh-JK; Chao (1987, 1989) Mt-Ch/Mh-Ch. Key evaluations: Briand, El Emam, Freimut & Laitenberger (2000); El Emam & Laitenberger (2001)
techniques.what_it_does: Uses the OVERLAP between reviewers' found-defect sets to estimate how many defects nobody found. Four model classes by assumption: M0 (equal defect detectability, equal reviewer ability), Mt (reviewers differ), Mh (defects differ), Mth (both). Consensus after a decade of evaluation: Mh-JK is the best estimator at 4+ reviewers; at 2 reviewers it is non-robust and underestimates, with Mt-Ch preferred but also unreliable on real inspection data. Most estimators underestimate. At least four to five reviewers are needed for acceptable accuracy; experience-based alternatives at 2 reviewers carry roughly 20% absolute bias.
techniques.assumption: Reviewers work independently, do not confer, and inspect the same artefact. And, fatally for you, the estimator is driven by overlap — small overlap is read as 'many defects remain'.
techniques.why: This is the literature that directly answers 'how many reviewers', and it says four to five, which is almost exactly your current five seats — worth knowing. But it will break on your data as it stands, and I want to be blunt about why. With 2 co-discoveries in 2,050 findings, Mh-JK will report that the undiscovered population is enormous, and you will not be able to tell whether that is true or whether your reviewers are being deliberately steered onto disjoint sub-problems. The literature has met this exact collision: perspective-based reading deliberately MINIMISES reviewer overlap, which contradicts capture-recapture's core prerequisite. Three studies concluded the estimators survive PBR with little impact, but the review flags as still-unanswered whether they over- or under-estimate under PBR. If your routing assigns different reviewers to different sub-problems, you are running PBR, and you are in the unresolved case. Fix the design before trusting the estimate: keep a deliberately overlapping control slice where every reviewer sees the same claims, and run capture-recapture only on that.

techniques.name: Budgeted submodular maximisation for panel selection
techniques.source: G. L. Nemhauser, L. A. Wolsey and M. L. Fisher, "An analysis of approximations for maximizing submodular set functions - I", Mathematical Programming 14(1):265-294, 1978. Budget-constrained variant: S. Khuller, A. Moss and J. Naor, "The budgeted maximum coverage problem", 1999; A. Krause and C. Guestrin, "A note on the budgeted maximization of submodular functions", CMU-CALD-05-103, 2005, https://snap.stanford.edu/class/cs224w-readings/krause05note.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Expected coverage of a finding population by a set of reviewers is monotone submodular — adding a reviewer to a small panel helps at least as much as adding it to a superset. Greedy selection then gives a (1 - 1/e) approximation to the optimum under a cardinality constraint, and the cost-benefit greedy variant (pick the reviewer maximising marginal coverage per unit cost) with partial enumeration gives (1 - 1/e) under a budget constraint. Feige showed (1 - 1/e) is the best possible unless P = NP.
techniques.assumption: Requires an estimate of each candidate reviewer's marginal coverage given the reviewers already chosen — i.e. you need the per-class miss rates from the Littlewood detection model before this is usable. Assumes coverage is the objective; if your convergence gate is effectively an m-out-of-n rule rather than 1-out-of-n, submodularity of the true objective is not guaranteed.
techniques.why: This is the principled answer to 'how do I spend a budget on heterogeneous reviewers' and it degrades gracefully across your three deployment scales, which is exactly the property you asked for: the same greedy rule runs with one candidate or a thousand. It composes with the fault-class stratification above — estimate per-(model, finding-class) detection rates once, then greedy cost-benefit selection reads off the panel for any budget. I flag one caution the literature makes explicitly and your gate may violate: Littlewood, Popov and Strigini show diversity is NOT always beneficial for m-out-of-n systems (they construct 2-out-of-3 cases where a diverse design is worse than a single-methodology one). Your detection step is 1-out-of-n and is safe; if your convergence gate requires corroboration from multiple reviewers, that step is m-out-of-n and this guarantee does not cover it.

techniques.name: Non-monotone scaling of voting-based multi-call systems
techniques.source: L. Chen, J. Q. Davis, B. Hanin, P. Bailis, I. Stoica, M. Zaharia and J. Zou, "Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards the Scaling Properties of Compound Inference Systems", NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2403.02419, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02419
techniques.what_it_does: Shows that majority-vote performance first rises then FALLS with the number of LM calls, because item difficulty is heterogeneous: extra calls help on items where per-call accuracy exceeds 1/2 and actively hurt where it does not. Derives F(K) = alpha*I_p1(K+1/2,K+1/2) + (1-alpha)*I_p2(...) via the regularised incomplete beta function, gives a closed form for the optimal K*, and shows K* is predictable from measurements at K = 1..5 with extrapolation MSE of 1e-6 to 1e-4 out to K = 100.
techniques.assumption: Majority-vote aggregation over a discrete answer space. The whole non-monotonicity depends on votes from wrong-but-confident calls outnumbering right ones.
techniques.why: I want to be explicit that this does NOT transfer, because it is the paper someone will hand you as the answer to question 1 and it is the wrong answer for your architecture. Its entire mechanism is vote dilution: extra calls hurt because wrong answers accumulate votes. CDSFL never votes. A finding is confirmed by a tool re-executing a falsifier, so a reviewer who is confidently wrong contributes a falsifier that fails to reproduce and costs you compute, not a wrong answer that outvotes a right one. Under union-with-verifier aggregation, findings are monotone non-decreasing in the number of reviewers; the curve cannot turn down. Your stopping problem is therefore purely economic (marginal yield versus marginal cost), not statistical, and it is a strictly easier problem than the one this paper solves. Note the same team's difficulty-heterogeneity insight IS the right one — it is the same mechanism as Eckhardt-Lee — it is only the voting conclusion that fails to carry.

techniques.name: Ensemble diversity measures and their (non-)relationship to ensemble gain
techniques.source: L. I. Kuncheva and C. J. Whitaker, "Measures of Diversity in Classifier Ensembles and Their Relationship with the Ensemble Accuracy", Machine Learning 51(2):181-207, 2003, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1023/A:1022859003006
techniques.what_it_does: Catalogues ten diversity statistics — four pairwise (Yule's Q = (N11*N00 - N01*N10)/(N11*N00 + N01*N10), correlation rho, disagreement, double-fault) and six non-pairwise (vote entropy, difficulty index, Kohavi-Wolpert variance, interrater kappa, generalised diversity, coincident failure diversity) — and tests across four experimental designs whether any of them predicts the improvement of the majority vote over the single best classifier. Conclusion: the measures correlate strongly with each other but their correlation with actual improvement is low; the authors say their results 'raise some doubts about the usefulness of diversity measures in building classifier ensembles in real-life pattern recognition problems', and specifically that the measures cannot pick up the small improvements and deteriorations that real problems consist of.
techniques.assumption: The target being predicted is majority-vote accuracy improvement, on labelled classification data, with all classifiers answering every item.
techniques.why: This is the most-cited pessimistic result about diversity measurement, and it will be raised against you, so it is worth knowing precisely why it does not bind. The failure it documents is a failure to predict MAJORITY-VOTE gain. You do not take a majority vote. Under 1-out-of-n union with a verifier, the quantity that determines the value of an extra reviewer is not some loosely-correlated proxy — it is E[prod theta_i], which is directly estimable, and I verified above that the generalised-diversity statistic in this very paper IS that quantity up to normalisation. So the correct reading is: the ensemble-learning community found these statistics unhelpful for the aggregation rule they happened to use, and one of the ten (GD/CFD, which Kuncheva and Whitaker note clusters separately from the rest, having come from N-version programming rather than pattern recognition) is exactly right for the aggregation rule you use. Take GD; leave Q, kappa, disagreement and the vote-entropy family.

techniques.name: Bias-variance-diversity decomposition
techniques.source: D. Wood, T. Mu, A. M. Webb, H. W. J. Reeve, M. Lujan and G. Brown, "A Unified Theory of Diversity in Ensemble Learning", Journal of Machine Learning Research 24(359):1-49, 2023, https://jmlr.org/papers/v24/23-0041.html , arXiv:2301.03962
techniques.what_it_does: Proves exact bias-variance-diversity decompositions of ensemble loss for a family of losses (squared, cross-entropy, Poisson), establishing that diversity is 'a measure of model fit, in precisely the same sense as bias and variance, but accounting for statistical dependencies between ensemble members'. Central conclusion: 'we should not be maximising diversity as so many works aim to do - instead, we have a bias/variance/diversity trade-off to manage.'
techniques.assumption: Requires a differentiable loss over a labelled distribution and an ensemble that averages predictions. The decomposition is defined relative to a specific loss function.
techniques.why: There is no loss function here to decompose. CDSFL produces a set of confirmed findings against an artefact, not a prediction against a label, and no member of the loss family they treat applies. Adopting this framing would require inventing a loss over finding-sets, and any such loss would be arbitrary. The one thing worth carrying across is the slogan, which happens to match the software-reliability result independently: diversity is not free and should not be maximised. Littlewood, Popov and Strigini say the same thing with a model that fits your system, so take it from them.

techniques.name: Hong-Page 'diversity trumps ability' theorem
techniques.source: L. Hong and S. E. Page, "Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers", PNAS 101(46):16385-16389, 2004. Critique: A. Thompson, "Does Diversity Trump Ability? An Example of the Misuse of Mathematics in the Social Sciences", Notices of the AMS 61(9):1024-1030, 2014, https://www.ams.org/notices/201409/rnoti-p1024.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Claims that a group of randomly selected, cognitively diverse problem solvers can outperform a group of the individually highest-ability solvers. Thompson's peer-reviewed critique argues the theorem as stated is mathematically incorrect, and where correct is trivial and disconnected from the accompanying computational experiment, which she characterises as contrived by restrictions on the algorithms; she attributes the observed effect to the ordinary phenomenon of randomised algorithms escaping local optima.
techniques.assumption: A finite solution space, agents as deterministic hill-climbing heuristics over a fixed value landscape, and a specific relay protocol for passing solutions between agents.
techniques.why: Do not cite this, and be ready for it to be cited at you. The assumptions are a model of local search over a fixed landscape and have no correspondence to a panel producing falsifiable claims against an artefact; the mathematics is publicly contested in a peer-reviewed venue; and its conclusion is precisely the one Self-MoA and the Littlewood results both contradict empirically for your kind of system, where individual reviewer quality dominates. If you need a defensible 'diversity is good' theorem, use Result 7 of Littlewood, Popov, Strigini and Shryane (2000) — it is a two-line Cauchy-Schwarz argument, it is uncontested, and it applies to detection systems specifically.

techniques.name: Near-zero reviewer overlap as the normal case (calibration)
