techniques.source: A. Beygelzimer, Y. Dauphin, P. Liang and J. W. Vaughan, "Has the Machine Learning Review Process Become More Arbitrary as the Field Has Grown? The NeurIPS 2021 Consistency Experiment", arXiv:2306.03262, https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03262 ; blog summary https://blog.neurips.cc/2021/12/08/the-neurips-2021-consistency-experiment/ . Team-size evidence: A. A. Porter, L. G. Votta and V. R. Basili, "Comparing detection methods for software requirements inspections: a replicated experiment", IEEE TSE 21(6):563-575, 1995, https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/32.391380
techniques.what_it_does: NeurIPS 2021 routed 10% of submissions through two fully independent review committees. The committees disagreed on accept/reject for 23% of papers, and approximately half the accepted list would change on a rerun. Separately, the inspection literature finds four-person teams performing no better than two-person teams, attributed to process loss.
techniques.assumption: Human reviewers, a discrete accept/reject decision, and conference-scale workload. Not a finding-level overlap measurement.
techniques.why: I include this only as calibration for how you should read your own 2-in-2,050 number, because I think you may be treating it as a pathology when it is closer to a baseline. Independent expert reviewers of the same artefact reach substantially different conclusions as a matter of course; near-disjoint findings are what review looks like, not evidence that your harness is broken or that your reviewers are secretly redundant. What it does NOT license is the opposite inference — you cannot conclude your reviewers are complementary either, because both 'genuinely complementary' and 'each sampling shallowly from a huge unfound population' produce the same near-zero overlap. That ambiguity is only resolvable by deliberately measuring overlap on a controlled slice, which is the recommendation under capture-recapture above.

transfers: The Eckhardt-Lee/Littlewood difficulty function is the right formal object for your whole problem, and CDSFL sits in its EASIER branch. The 2000 fault-detection paper states explicitly that parameters are far more estimable for detection than for design diversity ('it is striking how much easier it is to obtain estimates of the key model parameters here'). You are not in the hard case.

One theorem answers question 3 outright. Littlewood, Popov, Strigini & Shryane (2000) Result 7: if two reviewers have equal squared efficacy E[theta_A^2] = E[theta_B^2], then A-once-plus-B-once strictly beats either twice. It follows from Cauchy-Schwarz and requires NO assumption about the sign of their correlation. Heterogeneity is provably worth buying when candidates are comparably good; the only hard part is establishing comparability.

There is one number to instrument, and it is cheap. GD = 1 - p(2)/p(1) computed from the distribution of how many reviewers found each finding. I verified with SymPy and independently by Monte Carlo (800k draws, max discrepancy 5.9e-4) that p(1) = E[theta] and p(2) = E[theta^2] exactly under conditional independence, so Var[theta] = p(2) - p(1)^2 and the ensemble-learning statistic and the software-reliability quantity are literally the same object.

The marginal value of the nth identical reviewer has an exact form, and it decays far faster than intuition suggests. Expected residual undetected fraction after n reviewers is E[theta^n]; marginal yield of reviewer n+1 is E[theta^n(1-theta)]. I verified this three ways (symbolic integration, closed-form Beta moment product, Monte Carlo). For Beta(2,3) difficulty (a reviewer finding 60% of findings on average), the naive independence model says 0.066% of findings remain unfound after 8 reviewers; the correct model says 1.8% - a 28x understatement. Marginal yield decays roughly as 1/n^2, not geometrically.

Prompt-condition diversity is theoretically warranted, and the argument is cleaner than you may expect. In Littlewood-Miller a 'methodology' is any constraint set inducing a distribution over behaviour - which is exactly what a system prompt is. Same weights plus different instruction condition gives theta_A != theta_B, which puts you strictly outside the Eckhardt-Lee worst case. You do not have to prove negative correlation; you only have to show the conditions differ.

But only ROLE-LEVEL prompt differences buy anything. Three independent sources agree: Feng et al. (2026) found debiased between-prompt variation of 0.005-0.018 for formatting wrappers against 0.19 residual call noise; 'More Is Not More' (2026) found ~0 effect for instruction tweaks, demographic cueing and temperature 0.7->1.0 but ~0.62 MPD gain for role conditioning; DIPPER found +1.55 points from seven distinct role prompts over a no-variation self-ensemble. A vendor's hidden system prompt versus bare is role-level. Restore it.

Your executable falsifier puts you in the good regime. Brown et al. (2024) separate verifier-present from verifier-absent: with a verifier, SWE-bench Lite goes 15.9% -> 56% from 1 to 250 samples; without one, majority voting and reward models plateau past ~100 samples while coverage keeps climbing (82.9% -> 98.44%). Coverage follows c ~ exp(a*k^b), two parameters fittable from k = 1..8. That is a defensible stopping rule for the solo-researcher deployment and an architectural advantage you should state explicitly.

Fault-class stratification is the direct fix for your co-discovery sparsity. Littlewood et al. (2000) hit exactly your problem ('individual faults are likely to be sparse') and solve it by estimating mean difficulty per (fault class, detection method) pair rather than per fault. Classify findings by TYPE, estimate per-model per-class miss rates, and both the diversity measure and the allocation rule become estimable from data you already have.

Question 2's mechanism, given those per-class rates, is standard: expected coverage is monotone submodular, so cost-benefit greedy gives (1-1/e) of optimal under any budget, and the same rule runs unchanged at one candidate or a thousand - which is precisely the scale-invariance you asked for.

Multi-vendor buys something, but far less than independence. Ron, Baudry & Monperrus (2026), verified against the source: crossing an agent boundary moved perfect co-failure (phi=1) from 65% to 55% and non-positive correlation from 12% to 32%. Real, measurable, and nowhere near the independence your routing ladder implicitly assumes.

Correlated misses concentrate on hard items, which inverts your routing ladder's premise. Both the theory (Var[theta] over the demand space) and the 2026 replication (failures traced to where the specification was hard or ambiguous) say co-failure clusters exactly where items are difficult. Escalating a hard finding to 'a stronger writer' is spending diversity budget where diversity is least available.
does_not_transfer: Kuncheva & Whitaker's pessimism about diversity measures. Their negative result is specifically that the ten statistics fail to predict MAJORITY-VOTE improvement. You do not vote. The one measure that came from the N-version world rather than pattern recognition (GD/CFD, which they note clusters separately from the other nine) is exactly the right one for union-with-verifier aggregation. Take GD, discard Q, kappa, disagreement, double-fault and the vote-entropy family.

The compound-AI non-monotone scaling law (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2024). Its entire mechanism is vote dilution - extra calls hurt because confidently-wrong answers accumulate votes. With tool confirmation, a wrong reviewer produces a falsifier that fails to reproduce; it costs compute, not correctness. Your finding count is monotone non-decreasing in reviewers and the curve cannot turn down. Your stopping problem is economic, not statistical, and is strictly easier than the one that paper solves.

Self-MoA's headline conclusion that a single best model beats a mixed panel. The mechanism is that mixing lowers mean proposer quality and their aggregator is an LLM sensitive to that. Your aggregator is a tool and is indifferent to panel mean quality. Their alpha > beta coefficients still transfer as a warning about buying diversity before quality, and their stated condition for when mixing DOES win - similar-quality models on a heterogeneous task - is satisfied by CDSFL.

Bias-variance-diversity decompositions (Wood et al., JMLR 2023). There is no loss function here to decompose. CDSFL emits a set of confirmed findings against an artefact, not a prediction against a label, and no member of their loss family applies. Adopting it would require inventing an arbitrary loss over finding-sets.

Hong-Page 'diversity trumps ability'. Peer-reviewed critique in the Notices of the AMS says the theorem as stated is mathematically incorrect and the supporting simulation is contrived. Its assumptions - finite solution space, deterministic hill-climbing agents, fixed value landscape - have no correspondence to falsifiable claims against an artefact. Do not cite it; be ready for it to be cited at you, and answer with Result 7 instead.

Capture-recapture AS CURRENTLY APPLICABLE to your data. Mh-JK needs 4-5 reviewers (you have 5, fine) but it is driven by overlap, and at 2 co-discoveries in 2,050 it will report an enormous unfound population without being able to distinguish 'genuinely complementary reviewers' from 'shallow sampling of a huge population'. Worse, if your routing assigns reviewers to different sub-problems you are effectively running perspective-based reading, whose explicit goal is to MINIMISE overlap - a prerequisite collision the inspection literature has met and left unresolved (whether estimators over- or under-estimate under PBR is still an open question in the 2004 review).

CAPA's measurement machinery as-is. It needs a fixed item set, known correct answers, a bounded option space and output probabilities. You have an open-ended finding stream and a falsifier. Its accuracy-adjustment INSIGHT transfers (raw co-discovery counts are uninterpretable without adjusting for scope to overlap); the metric does not.

Vendi Score and DIPPER's semantic volume as your primary diversity measure. Both measure diversity of output TEXT. Text diversity is a proxy for error diversity, and your falsifier lets you measure error diversity directly. Use semantic volume to SELECT candidate conditions; validate on miss-overlap.

Anything that assumes the panel can confirm its own findings. Goel et al. measured judge-affinity at mean Pearson 0.84 across nine judges, surviving accuracy controls - LLM judges systematically favour models similar to themselves. This validates your tool-only confirmation rule; it does not offer a technique to adopt.
open: Nobody has measured whether prompt-condition variation decorrelates ERRORS, as opposed to changing accuracy or output diversity. Every study I found measures one of: task accuracy (DIPPER, +1.55 points), lexical/semantic spread of outputs (Vendi, MPD, cluster count), or judgement instability (Feng et al.). None reports the joint miss-probability of two prompt conditions on the same item set - which is the quantity Littlewood-Miller says determines whether the axis is worth anything. Your harness can produce that number and the literature cannot. This is a publishable gap, not just a hole in your design.

There is no principled stopping rule for union-with-verifier aggregation. Every stopping result I found assumes either voting (Chen et al.'s K*), a fixed problem set (Brown et al.'s coverage curve), or a closed defect population (capture-recapture). A rule for 'stop when the marginal confirmed-finding yield per unit cost falls below threshold' with an open, growing finding population and heterogeneous reviewer costs does not exist in this literature. The Beta-moment marginal-yield formula I verified gives the shape; estimating it from censored data does not.

Estimating any of these quantities from a censored finding population is unsolved and is your binding constraint. I computed that if every observed finding was found by exactly one of L reviewers, GD collapses to exactly 1/(L-1) - 1.00 at L=2, 0.25 at L=5, 0.14 at L=8 - purely as an artefact of excluding items nobody found. Every diversity statistic in this literature assumes a known item population. Yours is defined by what you found. Nothing I read addresses this directly.

Allocation when reviewer capability spans orders of magnitude is genuinely open. The submodular machinery handles heterogeneous COST cleanly and FrugalGPT-style cascades (Chen, Zaharia & Zou 2023, arXiv:2305.05176; 98% cost reduction at GPT-4-matching quality) handle heterogeneous cost for routing. Neither handles the case your ladder actually breaks on: no stronger model exists. There is no literature on graceful degradation of an escalation ladder at its ceiling - what a solo researcher with one model should do when the routing rule says 'escalate' and there is nowhere to escalate to. Result 7 hints that repeated application under a DIFFERENT methodology (a different prompt condition) is the right substitute for a stronger model, but nobody has tested that substitution.

Whether your convergence gate is 1-out-of-n or m-out-of-n, and whether it is safe. Littlewood, Popov & Strigini construct explicit 2-out-of-3 examples where a methodologically diverse design is WORSE than a single-methodology one, and note this generalises to (n+1)-out-of-(2n+1). Your detection step is 1-out-of-n and is covered by the good results. If your gate requires corroboration across reviewers, that step is m-out-of-n and none of the diversity guarantees apply to it. I could not determine from the brief which it is; it is worth settling before you spend money on diversity.

The indifference precondition of Result 7 - equal squared efficacy between reviewers - is the practical blocker, and the authors say so. They suggest it may be possible to CONTRIVE indifference (e.g. by giving the weaker procedure more effort), which for you would mean equalising reviewers by sampling budget rather than picking the strongest. Nobody has tried this with LLM reviewers and it is the most directly testable idea in this whole area.

Whether same-weights-different-system-prompt is a genuinely distinct methodology or a wrapper around one. Ron et al. (2026) found that crossing agent and language boundaries left 55% of pairs at perfect co-failure - so nominal diversity axes can be mostly cosmetic. There is no reason to assume the prompt-condition axis is immune, and Feng et al.'s debiased result on formatting wrappers is a live warning that it might not be. Measure it with their estimator before committing to it.

areas.area: Area 3 — Allocating a fixed budget across uncertain options: bandits, optimal stopping, value of information, LLM cost control, and redundant execution — assessed for transfer to a falsification harness whose ground truth comes from executing a falsifier.
areas.summary: One structural fact decides almost every transfer question here, and it is not the one the brief leads with. CDSFL does not choose an answer; it accumulates a set. Findings are confirmed by a tool re-executing a falsifier, so the panel's output is the union of confirmed findings, filtered by a cheap automatic verifier. Nearly the entire LLM cost-control literature — FrugalGPT, RouteLLM, learning-to-defer, conformal cascades, majority-vote ensembles, best-arm identification, OCBA — solves the opposite problem: pick one output, from one model, and discard the rest. Those techniques transfer to the writer routing ladder (a genuine single-output task with a quality ordering) and do not transfer to the reviewer panel. The literature that does transfer to the panel is the discovery-process literature: species estimation and capture-recapture from software inspection and fuzzing (Eick 1992; Nielsen and Landauer 1993; Petersson et al. 2004; Böhme 2018; Lipp et al. 2023), which is the same problem shape — several imperfect detectors, an unknown population of defects, and overlap between detectors as the only signal of what remains unfound. That literature answers question 1 directly and it consumes exactly the statistic CDSFL is not recording: co-discovery. On the record as stated, 2 doubletons in 2050 findings, Chao1 estimates roughly 1.05 million undiscovered findings and Good–Turing estimates sample coverage at 0.2 percent (both cross-checked in Python and Wolfram). Those numbers are not a measurement, they are a diagnostic: either the panel members review disjoint sub-problems so co-discovery is structurally impossible, or deduplication is collapsing co-discoveries to a single attributed discoverer. That must be resolved before any stopping rule in this report can be fitted. For the escalation ladder, the correct object is Weitzman's reservation value (Pandora's box), because a box's index depends only on its own value distribution and its own cost, never on the other boxes — which is precisely the property that removes the hardcoded strength ordering and degrades gracefully to one model, where the rule becomes "keep sampling while expected gain exceeds cost". The rungs should be actions, not models — another sample, the failed falsifier fed back, more thinking budget, decomposition, a different vendor if one exists, a human — and the test-time-scaling literature (Brown et al. 2024; Snell et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2024; Muennighoff et al. 2025) shows sample-axis and sequential-axis rungs really do substitute for model-strength rungs when an automatic verifier is present, which is your case. For allocating heterogeneous reviewers at any scale, adaptive submodularity (Golovin and Krause 2011) with budgeted greedy (Krause and Guestrin 2005) is scale-free, needs no ladder, and dissolves question 3 entirely: you never measure diversity, you measure marginal yield per unit cost, and a reviewer correlated with one already used is automatically starved. That last point is important because measuring diversity directly is a known trap — Kuncheva and Whitaker (2003) and a 2026 capability-controlled audit both find diversity metrics are near-collinear with mean accuracy and predict almost nothing once capability is controlled.

techniques.source: I.J. Good (1953), Biometrika 40(3-4):237-264; operationalised for testing by M. Böhme, "STADS: Software Testing as Species Discovery", ACM TOSEM 27(2), 2018 — https://mboehme.github.io/paper/TOSEM18.pdf ; worked exposition at https://www.fuzzingbook.org/html/WhenToStopFuzzing.html
techniques.what_it_does: Estimates the probability that the next observation is a species never seen before, as p0 = f1/n where f1 is the number of species seen exactly once and n is the total number of observations. Böhme shows this is also an estimate of maximum residual risk — the chance an equally-resourced adversary finds something you did not. Sample coverage is 1 - p0.
techniques.assumption: Species are sampled from a stationary distribution; every discovery event is recorded once and attributed; singletons are informative about the unseen mass. Böhme's contribution is showing it survives adaptive sampling bias (AFL), which matters because a review panel is also adaptively biased.
techniques.why: This is the principled version of "the loop stops when a convergence gate fires". A finding is a species; a (model, round) dispatch is a sampling event; a confirmed finding is a capture. It is label-free, costs one division, and gives a stopping statement with an interpretation — 'the next dispatch has a 3% chance of surfacing a new confirmed finding'. The blocker is entirely instrumental: computed on your stated record (f1=2048, f2=2, n=2052) it returns p0 = 0.998, i.e. sample coverage 0.2%, which is not credible and is therefore a signal that the discovery record is not capturing repeat observations. Fix the record first; the estimator is then immediately usable. Note also that the project's own known 10.3% parser drop rate biases f1 upward and so inflates residual risk.

techniques.name: Capture–recapture defect content estimation (Chao1, Mh/Mth, jackknife, Lincoln–Petersen)
techniques.source: Eick, Loader, Long, Votta, Wiel (1992), applying ecological capture-recapture to design inspections; surveyed in H. Petersson, T. Thelin, P. Runeson, C. Wohlin, "Capture-recapture in software inspections after 10 years research — theory, evaluation and application", Journal of Systems and Software 72(3), 2004 — https://wohlin.eu/jss04-1.pdf ; Chao's estimators, https://www.uvm.edu/~ngotelli/manuscriptpdfs/ChaoEncyclopediaChapter.PDF ; Wohlin et al., ISSRE 2001 — https://wohlin.eu/issre01.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Uses the overlap between the defect sets found by independent reviewers to estimate total defect content, hence how many remain. Chao1 = S_obs + f1²/(2·f2). Model variants relax assumptions: Mt allows reviewers to differ in ability, Mh allows defects to differ in detectability, Mth both.
techniques.assumption: Closed population (the artefact does not change during the study), reviewers detect independently, and detection probabilities are estimable from overlap. Mh/Mth relax homogeneity but not independence. Estimators degrade badly at small reviewer counts and low overlap — exactly the regime you are in.
techniques.why: This is the closest existing literature to CDSFL's actual shape, and it is the reason your co-discovery statistic is load-bearing rather than incidental: overlap IS the estimator's only input. Two assumptions fail and both need handling. Independence fails — Kim et al. (2025) show LLM errors are substantially correlated across vendors and more correlated for stronger models, which biases capture-recapture toward under-estimating the remaining population. Closure fails across rounds, because a fix in round k changes the artefact; ecology's open-population models (Jolly–Seber) exist but their transfer here is untested. The adaptation is real work, not a config change. On the plus side, your ground truth is better than the inspection literature's: their 'defect' labels came from expensive human adjudication, yours come from executing a falsifier, so a confirmed finding is a genuinely labelled capture event and the estimator's input is cleaner than anything in that literature.

techniques.name: Pandora's box / Weitzman reservation values for the escalation ladder
techniques.source: M. Weitzman, "Optimal Search for the Best Alternative", Econometrica 47(3), 1979; modern survey: H. Beyhaghi and L. Cai, "Recent Developments in Pandora's Box Problem: Variants and Applications" — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.12242 ; LLM instantiation: Y. Kalayci, V. Raman, S. Dughmi, "Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N for Inference Time Optimization", 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01394 ; A. Belloni, Y. Chen, Y. Wei, "Online Pandora's Box for Contextual LLM Cascading", 2026 — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.07392
techniques.what_it_does: Each option is a locked box with a random payoff and an opening cost. Each box gets a reservation value ζ solving E[max(0, X - ζ)] = c. Open boxes in descending reservation value; stop when a realised payoff exceeds the best unopened reservation value. Kalayci et al. give a UCB-style Pandora that learns the reward distribution online and matches Best-of-N with 15–35% fewer generations; Belloni et al. give the contextual online version for LLM cascades.
techniques.assumption: Classical Weitzman assumes independent boxes, known value distributions, and a max-of-one-prize objective. The UCB and contextual variants drop the known-distribution assumption at the cost of regret bounds. All variants assume a scalar payoff and a reward model that can score a realisation.
techniques.why: This is the single best answer to your escalation-ladder question, and the reason is the specific structural property that a box's reservation value depends only on its own distribution and its own cost — never on the other boxes. That is exactly the property a hardcoded strength ordering lacks. Sort whatever models exist by their own reservation values and the ladder configures itself; with one model the rule degenerates without special-casing to 'keep opening boxes (drawing samples) while expected gain exceeds cost'. Two adaptations are required and neither is trivial. First, your payoff is a set union with diminishing returns, not the max of one prize; Pandora variants with combinatorial cost exist but I found no clean index policy for a submodular coverage payoff with correlated boxes. Second, your boxes are correlated (Kim et al. 2025), which classical Pandora forbids. Treat this as the right frame plus a genuine research increment, not a drop-in.

techniques.name: Adaptive submodular maximisation with budgeted greedy
techniques.source: D. Golovin and A. Krause, "Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization", JAIR 42:427-486, 2011 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.3967 ; budgeted (knapsack) case: A. Krause and C. Guestrin, "A Note on the Budgeted Maximization of Submodular Functions", 2005 — https://snap.stanford.edu/class/cs224w-readings/krause05note.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: For objectives with diminishing returns where each action's outcome is observed before the next choice, the adaptive greedy policy — pick the action with the highest expected marginal gain, or gain-per-unit-cost under a budget — is (1 - 1/e) competitive with the optimal adaptive policy under a cardinality constraint, and Krause–Guestrin's cost-benefit greedy recovers a constant-factor guarantee under a knapsack budget.
techniques.assumption: Adaptive monotonicity (an extra action never reduces expected value) and adaptive submodularity (the conditional expected marginal gain of an action never grows as more is observed). You need an estimate of the conditional expected marginal gain per action.
techniques.why: Finding-coverage over a set of reviewers is monotone and submodular almost by construction: each additional reviewer adds a shrinking set of not-yet-found findings. This answers question 2 and question 3 simultaneously and is the only technique here that is genuinely scale-free — the same rule runs with one reviewer or a thousand, with no ladder, no tiers, and no strength ordering. Critically, correlation between reviewers, which breaks capture-recapture, HELPS here: correlated reviewers have faster-diminishing marginal gains, so the submodularity assumption is safer for you than for a typical application. What it needs is an estimate of expected new confirmed findings per reviewer given what has already been found — estimable from your own logs once co-discovery is recorded. One caveat that must be stated: adaptive monotonicity holds for confirmed findings but not for HIL burden, so the true objective is coverage minus reviewer-attention cost, and your own record (parser drops, a dedup path that can delete a finding by repetition) shows the implemented pipeline is not monotone even where the idealised objective is.

techniques.name: Coverage scaling with repeated sampling under an automatic verifier
techniques.source: B. Brown, J. Juravsky, R. Ehrlich, R. Clark, Q.V. Le, C. Ré, A. Mirhoseini, "Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling", 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21787
techniques.what_it_does: Measures coverage — the fraction of problems solved by ANY of k samples — as a function of k. Coverage scales log-linearly over four orders of magnitude and is well fitted by an exponentiated power law. On SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-V2-Coder-Instruct goes from 15.9% at one sample to 56% at 250. The paper's central caveat is that coverage converts to performance only where answers can be automatically verified.
techniques.assumption: An automatic verifier exists that can identify a correct sample without a human; samples are drawn from the same model with non-zero temperature; the coverage curve extrapolates.
techniques.why: The verifier condition — which is the paper's own stated limit on when the result is useful — is satisfied by CDSFL by construction, because a falsifier re-executed by a tool is exactly the automatic verifier. This is the cleanest answer to the degenerate one-model case: with one vendor, the extra rungs on the ladder are extra samples, and the coverage law tells you the marginal return of the k+1th sample rather than leaving it to guess. It also reframes question 1: 'does another model pay' and 'does another sample pay' are the same question in different units, and the exchange rate between them is measurable on your own data.

techniques.name: Compute-optimal test-time allocation by problem difficulty
techniques.source: C. Snell, J. Lee, K. Xu, A. Kumar, "Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters", 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314 ; Y. Wu, Z. Sun, S. Li, S. Welleck, Y. Yang, "Inference Scaling Laws", 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00724 ; N. Muennighoff et al., "s1: Simple test-time scaling", EMNLP 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393
techniques.what_it_does: Shows the best way to spend inference compute depends on problem difficulty — sequential revision for easy items, more parallel sampling for hard ones — and that a compute-optimal per-prompt policy is >4x more efficient than fixed Best-of-N. Wu et al. show a 7B model plus tree search beating a 34B model at equal cost. s1 shows sequential 'budget forcing' on a single model scaling until it flattens at roughly six times the base.
techniques.assumption: A verifier or reward model to score candidates; a usable difficulty estimate per item; the model is capable enough that extra compute has something to work with (Snell finds gains concentrate where the base model already has non-trivial success rates).
techniques.why: This is the evidential basis for building a ladder whose rungs are ACTIONS rather than MODELS. Escalation along the model-strength axis is one axis among several, and it is the only one that fails when there is no stronger model. Sample count, sequential revision depth, feedback of the failed falsifier, and decomposition are all rungs that exist in every deployment including the solo-researcher case. The adaptation is that 'difficulty' for you is a property of a finding or a sub-problem, not of a prompt, and s1's flattening point (~6x) is a warning that the sequential axis saturates — it is not an unbounded substitute for a stronger reviewer.

techniques.name: Anytime-valid inference / e-processes for the convergence gate
techniques.source: A. Wald (1945), SPRT; Wald and Wolfowitz (1948) optimality; R. Johari, P. Koomen, L. Pekelis, D. Walsh, "Always Valid Inference: Continuous Monitoring of A/B Tests" — https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.04922 ; A. Ramdas, P. Grünwald, V. Vovk, G. Shafer, "Game-Theoretic Statistics and Safe Anytime-Valid Inference", Statistical Science 38(4), 2023 — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.01948
techniques.what_it_does: SPRT stops as soon as the log-likelihood ratio crosses a boundary and minimises expected sample size for fixed type-I and type-II error (Wald–Wolfowitz). Always-valid p-values and e-processes generalise this: they control type-I error at ANY data-dependent stopping time, so you may look after every round without inflating error, and e-values from successive rounds multiply.
techniques.assumption: SPRT proper needs two simple hypotheses and a likelihood model. E-processes need far less — a test supermartingale, which can be built non-parametrically for bounded statistics — but you must define the null ('the next dispatch yields no new confirmed finding at rate above r').
techniques.why: Your gate is evaluated after every round, which is textbook optional stopping. Any fixed-sample statistical claim made at that gate ('two rounds with no new findings, therefore converged') has an uncontrolled error rate under repeated peeking. An e-process fixes this at essentially no compute cost and converts the gate from a heuristic into a statement with a guarantee. I found no application of anytime-valid inference to a falsification or review harness — this looks like a cheap, defensible, and novel improvement rather than a solved problem you can cite your way out of.

techniques.name: Expected value of sample information (EVSI) and expected net benefit of sampling (ENBS)
techniques.source: H. Raiffa and R. Schlaifer, Applied Statistical Decision Theory (1961); R. Howard (1966), value of information; practical computation: the R `voi` package vignette — https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/voi/vignettes/voi.html ; overview — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_of_information
techniques.what_it_does: Computes the expected gain in decision quality from acquiring a specific additional sample, bounded above by EVPI, and subtracts its cost to give ENBS. Positive ENBS means run the extra study; negative means the existing evidence is sufficient. The EVSI curve rises fast then flattens toward the EVPI ceiling, which is where the optimal sample size comes from.
techniques.assumption: A specified decision, a utility function over outcomes, a prior over the unknown, and a sampling model for the new evidence. Without a stated decision that could change, EVSI is undefined — information with no decision attached has zero value by construction.
techniques.why: This is the correct formal frame for 'is another dispatch worth its cost' and I want to be blunt about why it is not yet usable: CDSFL has no utility function over findings. Until a finding's worth is quantified — even crudely, by severity class — EVSI cannot be computed, only gestured at. The tractable substitute is to make the utility 'expected number of new confirmed findings', at which point EVSI collapses into the adaptive-submodular marginal-gain rule above and you get the decision rule without the elicitation cost. If severity weights ever exist, upgrade to real EVSI. Recent LLM-side instantiations exist (BED-LLM, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21184 ; structured-uncertainty clarification via EVPI, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08798) but both are about asking the user a question, not about dispatching another reviewer.

techniques.name: FrugalGPT LLM cascade
techniques.source: L. Chen, M. Zaharia, J. Zou, "FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance", 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176
techniques.what_it_does: Queries a sequence of LLMs from cheap to expensive, scoring each response with a learned generation scorer and stopping when the score clears a learned threshold. Reports matching GPT-4 at up to 98% lower cost.
techniques.assumption: A fixed, known model pool with a fixed cost ordering; a labelled training set per task to fit the scorer and the thresholds; and critically, that the stronger model's answer REPLACES the weaker one — the cascade returns exactly one response.
techniques.why: The replacement assumption is a category error for a reviewer panel. In CDSFL a weak model's tool-confirmed finding is not superseded by a strong model's output; it is kept. Cascading therefore discards exactly the output you are trying to accumulate. It also assumes the fixed strength ordering you are trying to eliminate, and it needs per-task labelled data to fit the scorer. It does transfer to one specific place: the writer routing ladder, which genuinely is a single-output task with a quality ordering. Use it there and nowhere else.

techniques.name: RouteLLM preference-data routing
techniques.source: I. Ong, A. Almahairi, V. Wu, W.-L. Chiang, T. Wu, J.E. Gonzalez, M.W. Kadous, I. Stoica, "RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data", ICLR 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665 ; LMSYS writeup — https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm/
techniques.what_it_does: Trains a win-prediction model on Chatbot Arena human preference data to decide, per query, whether a strong or weak model should answer. Reports >2x cost reduction at maintained quality, with some transfer when the strong/weak pair changes.
techniques.assumption: A binary strong/weak pair, human preference labels as the training signal, and the assumption that response quality is a scalar the router can predict from the query alone.
techniques.why: Two hard failures. It is binary and pairwise, so it does not answer 'allocate N heterogeneous reviewers' at all; and its training signal is human preference over responses, which CDSFL does not have and could not cheaply generate — your labels attach to findings, not responses. The transfer claim in the paper (routers survive swapping the model pair) is about swapping two models, not about going from five to one or from five to fifty. Again, potentially usable for the writer ladder; not for the panel.

techniques.name: UniRoute — universal routing to previously unseen models
techniques.source: W. Jitkrittum, H. Narasimhan, A.S. Rawat, J. Juneja, Z. Wang, C.-Y. Lee, P. Shenoy, R. Panigrahy, A.K. Menon, S. Kumar, "Universal Model Routing for Efficient LLM Inference", ICLR 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08773
techniques.what_it_does: Represents every LLM as a K-dimensional feature vector of per-cluster error rates on K representative prompt clusters, then routes each prompt to the model with the lowest cost-adjusted error on its cluster. Handles models never seen at training time; evaluated over 30+ unseen LLMs.
techniques.assumption: You can measure each model's error rate on the representative clusters — so a small labelled probe set is needed per newly-arrived model — and that the objective is per-prompt selection of one model.
techniques.why: This is the only paper I found that directly attacks 'the allocation must adapt to the models actually present'. The transferable idea is not the routing rule but the model-representation object: profile every reviewer by its YIELD vector (confirmed findings per dollar, per sub-problem class) rather than by a scalar strength rank, and a new or unknown model slots in after a cheap probe. That representation is what makes the ladder resource-adaptive; it is also directly estimable from CDSFL logs because confirmation is automatic. The routing rule itself — pick one model per prompt — still does not transfer to the panel.

techniques.name: Learning to defer to multiple experts, and its budgeted variant
techniques.source: R. Verma, D. Barrejón, E. Nalisnick, "Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts: Consistent Surrogate Losses, Confidence Calibration, and Conformal Ensembles", AISTATS 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.16955 ; G. DeSalvo, C. Mohri, M. Mohri, Y. Zhong, "Budgeted Multiple-Expert Deferral", 2025 — https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26706
techniques.what_it_does: Learns jointly when to predict and when to defer to one of several experts, with consistent surrogate losses; the budgeted variant adds heterogeneous per-expert consultation costs and a hard budget, with guarantees on how deferral accuracy scales with budget and expert count.
techniques.assumption: Expert predictions available on training data; expert accuracies and costs known or estimable; and the deferred-to expert's answer becomes THE answer.
techniques.why: The budgeted multiple-expert framing looks tantalisingly close to yours — heterogeneous costs, choose whom to consult, fixed budget — but the replacement semantics defeat it, same as FrugalGPT. There is, though, one genuinely useful inversion worth noting: in CDSFL the infallible 'expert' is the falsifier execution, and the models are the classifiers deciding when consulting it is worthwhile. Read that way, L2D describes the model→tool dispatch decision rather than the reviewer-allocation decision, and the budgeted variant's cost model would apply to expensive falsifier executions. That is a different problem from the one in the brief, but it is a real fit if falsifier execution ever becomes the expensive step.

techniques.name: Conformal cascades and distribution-free threshold calibration
techniques.source: "Conformal Cascade: Distribution-Free Accuracy Guarantees for Multi-Tier LLM Inference", 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25018 ; A. Angelopoulos, S. Bates, A. Fisch, L. Lei, T. Schuster, "Conformal Risk Control" — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.02814 ; Learn Then Test for threshold families
techniques.what_it_does: Replaces miscalibrated confidence thresholds in a cascade with conformal prediction set size: accept when the calibrated set collapses to one answer, defer otherwise, yielding a finite-sample distribution-free accuracy bound of 1 - Kα by a per-tier union bound.
techniques.assumption: An exchangeable calibration set with ground-truth labels, and a well-defined answer set per query so that 'set size' is meaningful.
techniques.why: There is no answer set for 'review this artefact and report findings' — the output is an open-ended set of claims, not a candidate label set — so prediction-set size has no analogue. The observation the paper makes about LLM confidence being miscalibrated and thresholds needing per-pair, per-domain tuning is worth carrying forward as a warning against any confidence-threshold-based gate, but the machinery does not port. Conformal risk control might port to a narrower sub-decision, such as bounding the false-confirmation rate of the falsifier executor, if that ever needs a guarantee.

techniques.name: Best-arm identification, successive halving, Hyperband
techniques.source: K. Jamieson, A. Talwalkar, "Non-stochastic Best Arm Identification and Hyperparameter Optimization", AISTATS 2016 — http://proceedings.mlr.press/v51/jamieson16.pdf ; L. Li, K. Jamieson, G. DeSalvo, A. Rostamizadeh, A. Talwalkar, Hyperband, JMLR 2018; fixed-budget BAI survey — https://arxiv.org/html/2106.04763
techniques.what_it_does: Allocates a fixed budget across arms/configurations by repeatedly evaluating all survivors cheaply and eliminating the worst half, so exponentially more budget flows to promising candidates. Identifies the single best arm within a budget.
techniques.assumption: Stationary arms with i.i.d. draws, a single best arm worth identifying, and cheap low-fidelity evaluations that correlate with the high-fidelity outcome.
techniques.why: State this plainly: your objective is set-coverage, not identification of a maximiser, and your arms are not stationary — a reviewer's value DROPS after it has already contributed its findings, because findings are consumed. Successive halving over models per artefact would eliminate exactly the cheap, idiosyncratic reviewer whose value is in the two findings nobody else gets. There is one legitimate adaptation on a different axis: run Hyperband over SUB-PROBLEMS rather than reviewers — arms are regions of the artefact, budget is rounds, reward is discovery rate — halving out regions that have saturated. That is a defensible answer to part of question 2 and it does not suffer the consumption problem, because a saturated region genuinely is done.

techniques.name: Bandits with knapsacks / budget-constrained bandits
techniques.source: A. Badanidiyuru, R. Kleinberg, A. Slivkins, "Bandits with Knapsacks", JACM 65(3), 2018 (arXiv:1305.2545) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3164539 ; LLM instantiation: B. Zuo, Y. Zhu, "Strategic Scaling of Test-Time Compute: A Bandit Learning Approach", 2025 — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.12721
techniques.what_it_does: Extends bandits to settings where each pull consumes limited resources at heterogeneous per-arm cost, with sublinear regret against the best budget-feasible policy. Zuo and Zhu apply pure-exploration bandit ideas to allocating test-time compute across queries, reporting ~11% absolute gains at fixed budget on MATH-500 and AIME25.
techniques.assumption: Stationary reward distributions per arm, known per-pull costs, a hard resource budget. Zuo and Zhu additionally assume a verifier and that per-query difficulty is inferable through exploration.
techniques.why: The cost model is right — your reviewers genuinely have per-dispatch costs differing by more than an order of magnitude — and the Zuo–Zhu formulation is close to yours because it too assumes a verifier and allocates across items rather than selecting a model. The unfixed problem is stationarity: their arms are compute levels on a fresh query, yours are reviewers whose expected yield decays as the finding pool is consumed. That is a rested/decaying bandit, and the BwK regret guarantees do not survive it unmodified. Usable as the allocation layer ACROSS sub-problems (where each sub-problem is fresh) rather than across reviewers.

techniques.name: Hedged and tied requests (tail-at-scale redundancy)
techniques.source: J. Dean and L.A. Barroso, "The Tail at Scale", Communications of the ACM 56(2), 2013 — https://www.barroso.org/publications/TheTailAtScale.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Sends a duplicate request to a second replica once the first has exceeded roughly the p95 expected latency, takes the first response and cancels the rest; tied requests let duplicates cancel each other at dequeue. Adds ~5% load for large tail-latency reductions. Also gives the fan-out arithmetic: a per-backend p99 of 10ms yields an end-to-end p99 near 140ms at fan-out 100.
techniques.assumption: Requests are idempotent and replicas are interchangeable — any replica's response is as good as any other's. Requires a cancellation mechanism and a circuit breaker on the hedge rate.
techniques.why: The interchangeability assumption is false for reviewers, and that is the whole point of a panel — a second vendor's response is not a duplicate, it is the value. So do not hedge reviewer dispatches on quality grounds. Two narrower transfers are real. First, hedging is correct for the tool-execution stage, where replicas genuinely are interchangeable and a hung falsifier run should be duplicated after p95. Second, the fan-out arithmetic applies directly to a 5-vendor panel round: round latency is the max over vendors, so the slowest vendor sets the round time, and a per-vendor p99 stall becomes a per-round stall with probability roughly 1-(1-p)^5. Budget a per-vendor deadline with a graceful drop rather than letting one vendor hold the round — noting that a dropped vendor must be recorded as a non-observation, not silently, or it corrupts the co-discovery record the estimators depend on.

techniques.name: Diversity metrics for ensembles — and the case against measuring them
techniques.source: L.I. Kuncheva, C.J. Whitaker, "Measures of Diversity in Classifier Ensembles and Their Relationship with the Ensemble Accuracy", Machine Learning 51(2):181-207, 2003 — https://research.bangor.ac.uk/en/publications/measures-of-diversity-in-classifier-ensembles-and-their-relations/ ; D. Kim, "Are Diversity Metrics Measuring Diversity? A Capability-Controlled Audit of Majority-Vote Gain in LLM Ensembles", 2026 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20768 ; focal diversity: LLM-TOPLA — https://arxiv.org/html/2410.03953v1
techniques.what_it_does: Defines and tests diversity statistics (disagreement, Q-statistic, double-fault, Jaccard error-set similarity, focal diversity) as predictors of ensemble gain. Kuncheva and Whitaker find no prominent link between diversity and accuracy. The 2026 audit, over 31,900 subsets of 30 LLMs, finds strict diversity is near-collinear with one-minus-mean-accuracy (Spearman ρ = 0.991) and that most raw diversity–gain associations attenuate, reverse, or become specification-dependent once capability is controlled. The one survivor is pairwise co-failure, which retains a modest negative association with gain.
techniques.assumption: The audit's setting is majority-vote aggregation on multiple-choice benchmarks with a defined correct answer.
techniques.why: Question 3 asks how to measure diversity and trade it against cost. The honest answer from this literature is: don't build a diversity metric — twenty-three years of evidence says they are confounded with base capability and predict little. Two things do transfer. First, the one statistic that survives capability control is pairwise co-failure, whose direct analogue for you is pairwise CO-DISCOVERY on confirmed findings — the very quantity your record is missing, which closes the loop with the capture-recapture entry above. Second, the trade-off against cost does not need a diversity metric at all: adaptive-submodular marginal-gain-per-dollar starves a reviewer that duplicates an existing one automatically, because duplication shows up as low marginal yield. Note the audit's setting is majority vote, so its headline numbers (majority voting beats the strongest member in only 9.98% of size-3 subsets) do NOT describe your aggregation.

techniques.name: Correlated errors across LLM vendors
techniques.source: E. Kim, A. Garg, K. Peng, N. Garg, "Correlated Errors in Large Language Models", 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962
techniques.what_it_does: Empirically evaluates error covariance across 350+ models from different providers on leaderboard tasks and a resume-screening task. Finds substantial correlation — on one leaderboard dataset models agreed 60% of the time when both erred — and, importantly, that correlation is HIGHER between larger, more accurate models, even across distinct architectures and providers.
techniques.assumption: Benchmark tasks with defined correct answers; correlation measured on errors, not on discoveries.
techniques.why: This is the empirical fact that governs the marginal value of the Nth model and it cuts two ways. Against you: it breaks the independence assumption that capture-recapture needs, and it means a fifth frontier vendor buys less than naive independence would predict, with the effect getting WORSE as models improve. For you: correlated reviewers make marginal returns diminish faster, which is exactly the adaptive-submodularity condition, so the greedy allocation guarantee is on safe ground. The severe reading is that the institutional deployment with unlimited model access is worth less than it sounds — if the extra models are all frontier models, their errors are the most correlated of all, and the returns to breadth flatten faster than the returns to depth (more samples, more rounds) on the models you already have. That is a testable prediction and CDSFL can test it.

techniques.name: Non-monotone scaling of LLM calls under voting
techniques.source: L. Chen, J. Davis, B. Hanin, P. Bailis, I. Stoica, M. Zaharia, J. Zou, "Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards the Scaling Properties of Compound AI Systems", NeurIPS 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02419 ; contrast: J. Li et al., "More Agents Is All You Need", 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05120
techniques.what_it_does: Shows that for Vote and Filter-Vote systems, accuracy first rises then FALLS with more LM calls, because a task mixing easy and hard queries gets better on the easy ones and worse on the hard ones as votes accumulate. Provides an analytical scaling model that predicts the optimal call count from a small sample. Li et al. report the opposite-looking result — monotone gains up to ~15-20 agents — under different conditions.
techniques.assumption: Majority-vote or filter-then-vote aggregation over a shared answer space.
techniques.why: This is worth flagging explicitly as GOOD news you should not accidentally inherit. The famous 'more models can hurt' result is an artefact of voting: with a union-and-verify objective, an extra reviewer can never remove a confirmed finding, so coverage is monotone non-decreasing in reviewers. Do not import a vote-derived optimal-N. The caveat is real though: monotone in confirmed findings is not monotone in HIL burden, and your own record shows implementation paths (the parser drop, dedup collapsing repeats) that can make the realised pipeline non-monotone for mechanical reasons rather than statistical ones. The failure mode is the same shape; the cause is different, and so is the fix.

techniques.name: Adaptive-Consistency and early-stopping self-consistency
techniques.source: P. Aggarwal, A. Madaan, Y. Yang, Mausam, "Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs", EMNLP 2023 — https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.761/ (arXiv:2305.11860); early-stopping variant — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.10480
techniques.what_it_does: Draws samples one at a time and after each one evaluates a Dirichlet/beta-binomial posterior over the answer tallies, halting when the dominant answer's posterior mass clears a threshold. Reports up to 7.9x sample reduction with under 0.1% accuracy loss across 17 datasets and three LLMs.
techniques.assumption: A discrete answer space over which tallies can be formed, and agreement as the confidence signal.
techniques.why: The stopping statistic is agreement among samples, which is precisely the signal CDSFL deliberately does not use — findings are confirmed by tools, never by model agreement, and that is a stated design principle. Importing a posterior-over-tallies stopping rule would smuggle model voting back in through the stopping criterion. The transferable shape — a Bayesian posterior updated after each dispatch, with a threshold on it — is right; the sufficient statistic must be new-confirmed-findings, not answer agreement, which lands you back at Good–Turing and the e-process.

techniques.name: Secretary problem and its family
techniques.source: Classical optimal stopping; surveyed alongside Pandora variants in Beyhaghi and Cai — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.12242
techniques.what_it_does: Observe candidates sequentially, must accept or reject irrevocably with no recall, maximise probability of selecting the best; the 1/e rule.
techniques.assumption: No recall, one selection, no inspection cost, unknown values revealed only on arrival.
techniques.why: Both defining assumptions fail. You have full recall — every finding produced by every reviewer is retained — and you make no single selection. The brief lists the secretary family as a candidate; it should be dropped rather than adapted. Pandora's box is the member of the optimal-stopping family that fits, precisely because it has costly inspection and permits recall.

techniques.name: Optimal computing budget allocation (OCBA) and ranking-and-selection
techniques.source: C.-H. Chen and colleagues, mid-1990s onward — http://seor.vse.gmu.edu/~cchen9/ocba.html ; overview — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimal_computing_budget_allocation
techniques.what_it_does: Allocates a fixed simulation budget across design alternatives to maximise the probability of correctly selecting the best, giving proportionally more replications to alternatives that are pivotal to the comparison.
techniques.assumption: Noisy but repeatable evaluations of a scalar performance measure per alternative; a single best alternative worth identifying; normality assumptions in the standard derivation.
techniques.why: Same failure as best-arm identification: the objective is correct selection of one alternative, not coverage of a set. There is no 'best reviewer' to identify in CDSFL; there is a cheapest sufficient set. Listing it as related would be padding.

techniques.name: Saturation-based stopping with a predicted target class
techniques.source: S. Lipp, D. Elsner, S. Kacianka, A. Pretschner, M. Böhme, S. Banescu, "Green Fuzzing: A Saturation-Based Stopping Criterion using Vulnerability Prediction", ISSTA 2023 — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3597926.3598043 (PDF: https://mboehme.github.io/paper/ISSTA23-green.pdf)
techniques.what_it_does: Stops a campaign when coverage of PREDICTED-VULNERABLE functions saturates, rather than when crashes or overall coverage saturate. Evaluated over 30 C programs, 240 security bugs, 1,280 campaigns: terminates 24-hour campaigns 6-12 hours early while missing on average under 0.5 of 12.5 bugs.
techniques.assumption: A usable predictor of where the interesting defects live (they train a classifier on CVE history with static-analysis and software-metric features), and that saturation on the predicted subset implies saturation on the real one.
techniques.why: This is the most operationally mature stopping criterion in the transferring literature and its lesson is specific: measure saturation on the sub-population you care about, not on the whole. For CDSFL that means gating on saturation of HIGH-SEVERITY confirmed findings, not on total finding count — total count saturates late and is dominated by low-value findings, so a total-count gate spends budget after the valuable discovery has stopped. The adaptation is that their predictor is trained on CVE history; yours would be a severity classifier over findings, which your own confirmed-finding record can train.

transfers: The discovery-process family transfers wholesale and is the right home for question 1: Good–Turing residual risk as the convergence gate (Böhme, TOSEM 2018), capture–recapture defect estimation (Eick 1992; Petersson/Thelin/Runeson/Wohlin 2004), the Poisson 1-(1-p)^n evaluator curve (Nielsen and Landauer 1993), and saturation-on-the-target-class stopping (Lipp et al., ISSTA 2023). CDSFL is the same problem shape — imperfect detectors, unknown defect population, overlap as the only evidence of what remains — and it has a BETTER label source than any of them, because confirmation is a tool execution rather than human adjudication.

Co-discovery is not a nice-to-have statistic; it is the input every one of these estimators consumes. On the figures as stated (2,050 findings, 2 co-discovered), Chao1 returns 1,050,626 total findings and Good–Turing returns 0.2% sample coverage — verified independently in Python and Wolfram. Those are not estimates, they are a red flag: either panel members review disjoint sub-problems so co-discovery is structurally impossible, or deduplication collapses co-discoveries to a single attributed discoverer. Resolve which before fitting anything.

Weitzman reservation values (Pandora's box) give the escalation ladder the exact property it lacks. A box's index depends only on its own value distribution and its own cost, never on the other boxes — so the ladder becomes 'sort whatever reviewers exist by their own reservation values', with no global strength ranking, and it degenerates without special-casing to 'keep drawing while expected gain exceeds cost' when only one model is present. Kalayci, Raman and Dughmi (2025) give the UCB version that learns the distributions online; Belloni, Chen and Wei (2026) give the contextual online version for LLM cascades.

The ladder's rungs should be ACTIONS, not models — another sample, the failed falsifier fed back, more thinking budget, decomposition, a different vendor if one exists, a human as terminal rung. Brown et al. (2024) show coverage scales log-linearly with repeated sampling and converts to real performance precisely when an automatic verifier exists, which is your case by construction; Wu et al. (2024) show a 7B model with search beating a 34B model at equal cost; Muennighoff et al. (2025) show sequential budget-forcing on one model scaling until it flattens around 6x. Model strength is one axis among several, and it is the only one that disappears in the solo-researcher deployment.

Adaptive submodularity (Golovin and Krause, JAIR 2011) with budgeted greedy (Krause and Guestrin 2005) is the scale-free answer to question 2 and dissolves question 3. Pick the reviewer with the highest expected new-confirmed-findings per unit cost given what has already been found; (1-1/e) competitive under a cardinality constraint, constant-factor under a knapsack budget. It needs no ladder, no tiers, no strength ordering, and it runs identically with one reviewer or a thousand. Correlation between reviewers — which breaks capture-recapture — makes this assumption SAFER, since it accelerates the diminishing returns the guarantee depends on.

You should never build a diversity metric. Kuncheva and Whitaker (2003) found no prominent link between diversity and ensemble accuracy; the 2026 capability-controlled audit finds strict diversity is 0.991-collinear with one-minus-mean-accuracy and that most diversity–gain associations reverse or vanish under control. The only survivor is pairwise co-failure — whose analogue for you is pairwise co-discovery, the statistic you are already missing. Trade diversity against cost implicitly via marginal yield per dollar; a reviewer that duplicates an existing one is starved automatically without anyone naming diversity.

Anytime-valid inference (Johari et al.; Ramdas, Grünwald, Vovk and Shafer, Statistical Science 2023) should govern the convergence gate. The gate is peeked at every round, which is textbook optional stopping, so any fixed-sample claim made there has an uncontrolled error rate. An e-process fixes this for near-zero compute and converts 'two quiet rounds therefore converged' into a statement with a guarantee. I found no prior application of this to a review or falsification harness.

The famous 'more calls can hurt' result (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2024) does NOT apply to you and you should not inherit its optimal-N. That non-monotonicity is an artefact of majority voting over mixed-difficulty tasks; a union-and-verify objective is monotone non-decreasing in reviewers, because an extra reviewer can never remove a tool-confirmed finding. Your only costs of another reviewer are money, HIL attention, and known pipeline defects.

Tail-at-scale hedging (Dean and Barroso, 2013) transfers as engineering, not epistemics. Hedge the falsifier EXECUTION, where replicas genuinely are interchangeable; never hedge a reviewer dispatch, since a second vendor's differing answer is the value, not a duplicate. The fan-out arithmetic is directly relevant to a 5-vendor round: round latency is the max over vendors, so a per-vendor p99 stall becomes a per-round stall with probability about 1-(1-p)^5. Give each vendor a deadline with a graceful drop — and record the drop as an explicit non-observation, or it silently corrupts the co-discovery record.
does_not_transfer: FrugalGPT, RouteLLM, learning-to-defer (including the budgeted multiple-expert variant), and conformal cascades all assume the escalated-to model's answer REPLACES the earlier one, returning exactly one output per query. CDSFL keeps a weak model's tool-confirmed finding regardless of what a strong model says. Cascading a reviewer panel would discard exactly what you are accumulating. All four are legitimate for the WRITER routing ladder, which genuinely is a single-output task with a quality ordering — that split is the useful result, not a rejection of the literature.

Best-arm identification, successive halving and Hyperband over MODELS do not transfer. Two independent failures: the objective is set-coverage, not identification of a maximiser, so the cheap idiosyncratic reviewer whose value is two findings nobody else gets is exactly what halving eliminates; and the arms are non-stationary in a specific way, because a reviewer's expected yield DROPS once it has contributed its findings — findings are consumed. That is a rested/decaying bandit, not a stochastic one. Hyperband over SUB-PROBLEMS (arms are artefact regions, budget is rounds, reward is discovery rate) does transfer and is a reasonable partial answer to question 2.

OCBA and ranking-and-selection do not transfer, for the same reason as best-arm identification: they maximise the probability of correctly selecting the best alternative. There is no best reviewer to identify; there is a cheapest sufficient set.

The secretary problem family should be dropped rather than adapted. It assumes no recall and one irrevocable selection; you have full recall and select nothing. Pandora's box is the member of the optimal-stopping family that fits, because it has costly inspection and permits recall.

Adaptive-Consistency and early-stopping self-consistency do not transfer despite looking close. Their stopping statistic is agreement among samples — the exact signal CDSFL refuses on principle. Importing them would smuggle model voting back in through the stopping criterion. The shape (Bayesian posterior updated per dispatch, threshold on it) is right; the sufficient statistic must be new confirmed findings.

Diversity metrics as an optimisation target do not transfer, and this is a positive finding rather than a gap. Twenty-three years of evidence says they are confounded with base capability and predict little once that is controlled.

EVSI is the right frame for 'is another dispatch worth its cost' but is NOT currently computable for you, because CDSFL has no utility function over findings — information with no decision attached has zero value by construction. Substituting 'expected new confirmed findings' as the utility collapses EVSI into the adaptive-submodular marginal-gain rule, which is the practical move; upgrade to real EVSI only if severity weights ever exist.
Hedging reviewer dispatches on quality grounds does not transfer. Hedging assumes replica interchangeability; the whole premise of a panel is that reviewers are not interchangeable.
open: Pandora's box with a SET-UNION (submodular coverage) payoff and CORRELATED boxes. The reservation-value index result rests on the max-of-one-prize objective with independent boxes. Variants exist for combinatorial cost and order constraints, but I found no clean index policy for a submodular coverage payoff over correlated boxes — which is exactly the object a resource-adaptive CDSFL ladder needs. Combining adaptive submodularity with reservation values looks tractable, but it is an invention, not a citation.

Capture–recapture with detectors that are known to be correlated AND round-adaptive AND filtered by a verifier that removes false positives. Böhme handles adaptive sampling bias for a single fuzzer; the inspection literature handles heterogeneous detection (Mh/Mth); Kim et al. document the correlation. Nobody has put all three together, and the correlation direction (stronger models correlate MORE) means the bias grows as your panel improves.

The closed-population assumption fails across CDSFL rounds, because a fix in round k changes the artefact and so changes the defect population. Ecology's open-population models (Jolly–Seber) exist but their transfer to a review loop where the population is edited between captures is, as far as I can find, untested.

The exchange rate between 'one more sample from model A' and 'one sample from model B' for a falsification task with an executable verifier. Brown et al. give the within-model coverage law; Kim et al. give the cross-model error correlation; nobody has measured the trade directly. This is a cheap, clean, publishable experiment that CDSFL is unusually well placed to run — and the co-discovery instrumentation is its prerequisite, which makes fixing that instrumentation a research asset rather than only a repair.

Whether the institutional deployment (effectively unlimited model access) is worth what it appears to be. Kim et al. imply the marginal value of breadth flattens fastest exactly among frontier models, so depth (more samples, more rounds on the models you already have) may dominate breadth at the high end. That is a falsifiable prediction and it inverts the naive reading of the three-scale requirement.

A stopping rule and an allocation rule that are the SAME rule at N=1, N=5 and N=unbounded. UniRoute is the only work I found that adapts to the models actually present, and it still assumes per-prompt selection of one model. The assembly proposed here — action-rungs indexed by reservation value, allocated by adaptive-submodular marginal yield, gated by a Good–Turing e-process on high-severity confirmed findings — is constructible from existing parts, but no one has built or evaluated it. Treat it as a design to be falsified, not a solved problem to be adopted.

Anytime-valid inference applied to a falsification or review harness. The statistics are mature and the fit is exact; the application appears to be absent from the literature. That is an opportunity, but it also means there is no prior art to tell you which test supermartingale behaves well when the discovery process is adaptively biased.

areas.area: Combining fallible judges, and knowing when to stop asking (crowdsourcing label aggregation, adaptive/budget-aware allocation, item response theory, wisdom-of-crowds and its failure modes) — assessed for transfer to a harness whose ground truth is a tool re-executing a falsifier.
areas.summary: The crowdsourcing-aggregation literature (Dawid–Skene and everything downstream of it) exists to solve a problem CDSFL does not have: recovering an unobservable truth from a pattern of agreement. CDSFL observes the truth directly, because a tool executes the falsifier. That single fact deletes about two-thirds of this literature outright, and it changes what remains from an unsupervised latent-variable problem into an ordinary supervised one — per-model ability and per-finding difficulty can be fitted by regression against verifier outcomes, with no EM, no latent label, and no vote anywhere in the pipeline. The parts that do survive are the parts that were never about truth: allocation (where to spend the next dispatch), stopping (when the next dispatch stops paying), and diversity pricing. For those, the literature that genuinely transfers is not crowdsourcing at all — it is species-discovery estimation from ecology as imported into fuzzing by Böhme, the N-version-programming theory of correlated failure (where truth has always come from execution against an oracle), and algorithm-portfolio scheduling. The stopping question in particular is close to solved in principle: Good–Turing gives the probability that the next dispatch yields a finding you have not already got, and you stop when that falls below the price of a dispatch. The blocker is not theory, it is instrumentation. CDSFL's "2 of 2,050 co-discoveries" is the exact sufficient statistic these estimators consume, and taken at face value it implies Chao1 ≈ 1,050,626 latent findings and a sampled coverage of roughly 0.2% — a number so extreme that the far likelier reading is that co-discovery is unmeasurable by construction rather than genuinely absent. Nothing can be decided about the marginal value of the Nth model until that is fixed, and no published work applies this estimation machinery to a tool-verified multi-model review panel, so the last mile is invention.

techniques.name: Dawid–Skene latent-class aggregation (EM over confusion matrices)
techniques.source: A. P. Dawid & A. M. Skene, "Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Observer Error-Rates Using the EM Algorithm", Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C (Applied Statistics) 28(1):20–28, 1979. https://academic.oup.com/jrsssc/article/28/1/20/6953573 and https://www.jstor.org/stable/2346806
techniques.what_it_does: Given only unlabelled items and multiple observers' categorical judgements, jointly estimates each item's latent true class and each observer's full confusion matrix, by EM. Reliable observers are up-weighted; the up-weighting is derived entirely from who agrees with whom.
techniques.assumption: (1) A latent true label exists and is the only common cause of judgements. (2) Observers are conditionally independent given that label. (3) Each observer has a stationary confusion matrix across items. (4) Enough items are judged by overlapping sets of observers for the confusion matrices to be identifiable — i.e. co-judgement is dense.
techniques.why: Every one of the four assumptions fails or is irrelevant here. Assumption 1 is the exact inversion of CDSFL's founding principle: truth is the falsifier's exit status, not a latent variable behind opinions. Assumption 2 is empirically false for LLM panels (see Kim et al. 2025 and Kohli 2026). Assumption 4 is unmet by construction — with 2 co-discoveries in 2,050 findings there is essentially no overlap structure to fit a confusion matrix to. And the one output that would be useful, per-model reliability, is available far more cheaply and far more honestly by counting each model's verified-finding rate against the tool. Importing Dawid–Skene would be smuggling voting back in as a truth criterion while also being statistically unidentifiable.

techniques.name: The Dawid–Skene extensions: GLAD, Raykar et al., and spectral-EM
techniques.source: J. Whitehill, T.-f. Wu, J. Bergsma, J. Movellan, P. Ruvolo, "Whose Vote Should Count More: Optimal Integration of Labels from Labelers of Unknown Expertise", NIPS 2009. https://papers.nips.cc/paper/3644-whose-vote-should-count-more-optimal-integration-of-labels-from-labelers-of-unknown-expertise · V. Raykar, S. Yu, L. Zhao, G. Valadez, C. Florin, L. Bogoni, L. Moy, "Learning From Crowds", JMLR 11:1297–1322, 2010. http://www.umiacs.umd.edu/labs/cvl/pirl/vikas/publications/raykar_JMLR_2010_crowds.pdf · Y. Zhang, X. Chen, D. Zhou, M. I. Jordan, "Spectral Methods Meet EM: A Provably Optimal Algorithm for Crowdsourcing", NIPS 2014. https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3824
techniques.what_it_does: GLAD adds a per-item difficulty parameter so that log-odds of correctness is bilinear in (labeler expertise, item difficulty). Raykar et al. fold annotator sensitivity/specificity into a jointly-trained logistic classifier. Zhang et al. give a spectral initialiser that makes the non-convex Dawid–Skene likelihood provably converge at the minimax-optimal rate.
techniques.assumption: All inherit Dawid–Skene's conditional independence and latent-truth assumptions. Zhang et al. additionally need enough items per worker and per worker-group for the moment/spectral estimates to concentrate.
techniques.why: Same fatal objection as Dawid–Skene, plus a specific one: Zhang et al.'s optimality is optimality at recovering the latent label. That is a guarantee about a quantity CDSFL deliberately refuses to define. The one genuinely valuable idea in this cluster is GLAD's *parameterisation* — that difficulty is a property of the item, not just noise in the judge. Keep the parameterisation, throw away the estimation method; see the IRT entry, which gets the same parameters from observed verifier outcomes instead of inferring them from agreement.

techniques.name: Item response theory (2PL/3PL) fitted against verifier outcomes
techniques.source: F. Lord & M. Novick, Statistical Theories of Mental Test Scores, 1968 (classical source). Applied to NLP/ML: J. Lalor, H. Wu, H. Yu, "Building an Evaluation Scale using Item Response Theory", EMNLP 2016. https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.08889 · F. Martínez-Plumed et al., "Making Sense of Item Response Theory in Machine Learning", ECAI 2016 · Tutorial: "Item Response Theory for Natural Language Processing", EACL 2024. https://aclanthology.org/2024.eacl-tutorials.2.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Models P(judge j succeeds on item i) as a function of a scalar judge ability θ_j and item parameters (difficulty b_i, discrimination a_i, guessing c_i). Yields a common scale on which judges and items are directly comparable, and an item information function saying which items best discriminate at a given ability level.
techniques.assumption: Unidimensional ability (one latent competence explains performance across items); local independence given ability; monotone item characteristic curves; and — critically for the standard estimators — a large, roughly balanced response matrix.
techniques.why: This is the single most useful import in the entire named brief, precisely because the verifier removes the hard part. In crowdsourcing, IRT parameters are latent and must be inferred from agreement. In CDSFL, the response is *scored*: model j proposed a falsifier for finding i, and the tool either confirmed or refuted it. That makes it plain supervised IRT with an answer key — a logistic fit, not a latent-variable model. This directly repairs the routing ladder: 'escalate to a stronger writer' becomes 'escalate to a model whose fitted θ exceeds this finding's fitted b', and when no such model exists the ladder *knows* it and can escalate along a different axis instead of failing. The adaptation needed: unidimensionality is almost certainly wrong for a panel (a model strong at numerical falsification may be weak at logical ones), so use multidimensional IRT or per-domain θ; and CDSFL's response matrix is currently far too sparse to fit anything, which is the same instrumentation blocker as everywhere else.

techniques.name: Good–Turing discovery probability and the Chao1/Chao2 richness lower bounds
techniques.source: I. J. Good, "The population frequencies of species and the estimation of population parameters", Biometrika 40:237–264, 1953 · A. Chao, "Nonparametric estimation of the number of classes in a population", Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 11:265–270, 1984 · C.-H. Chiu, Y.-T. Wang, B. Walther, A. Chao, "An improved nonparametric lower bound of species richness via a modified Good–Turing frequency formula", Biometrics 70(3):671–682, 2014. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/biom.12200
techniques.what_it_does: From the counts of singletons (f1: findings seen exactly once) and doubletons (f2: findings seen exactly twice), estimates (a) the probability that the next observation is of a species not yet seen — the Good–Turing discovery probability, f1/n — and (b) a nonparametric lower bound on total richness, Chao1 = S_obs + f1²/(2·f2).
techniques.assumption: Individuals are sampled independently (or at least exchangeably) from a fixed community; species identity is observed without error; the community is closed during sampling. Chao1 is only a *lower* bound, and is severely unstable when f2 is tiny.
techniques.why: This is the principled stopping rule the brief asks for, and CDSFL's records already hold the sufficient statistics. Stop dispatching when the estimated probability that the next dispatch surfaces a *new* verified finding falls below (cost of a dispatch ÷ value of a finding). No agreement is consulted anywhere — f1 and f2 are counts of tool-confirmed findings, so the truth criterion is untouched. But run the numbers on the figure in the brief and the result is a diagnostic, not an answer: with f1=2048, f2=2, n=2052 observations, Chao1 = 1,050,626 (bias-corrected 700,759) and estimated sample coverage Ĉ = 1 − f1/n = 0.195%, i.e. the estimator says CDSFL has seen roughly one five-hundredth of the finding space and the next dispatch is ~99.8% likely to be productive. That is not a credible reading of a mature harness. The credible reading is that f2 is an artefact of attributing each finding to exactly one model. Chao1's variance blows up as f2→0 precisely so you notice this. Treat the number as an alarm on the instrumentation, not as a measurement of the world.

techniques.name: STADS: software testing as species discovery, and residual-risk estimation for adaptive samplers
techniques.source: M. Böhme, "STADS: Software Testing as Species Discovery", ACM TOSEM 27(2), 2018. https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02130 · M. Böhme, D. Liyanage, V. Wüstholz, "Estimating Residual Risk in Greybox Fuzzing", ESEC/FSE 2021. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3468264.3468570 and https://mboehme.github.io/paper/FSE21.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Maps a testing campaign onto an ecological sample: a generated input is an individual, a covered branch (or discovered bug) is a species. Then imports thirty years of biostatistics to answer 'how much is left', 'how much more effort for 10% more coverage', and 'what is the residual risk that a bug exists given none was found'. The 2021 paper shows residual risk cannot be estimated directly for a greybox campaign, argues that the discovery probability is a sound upper bound on it, and — the key contribution for CDSFL — diagnoses that Good–Turing's i.i.d. assumption is violated by adaptive samplers and supplies a correction.
