techniques.assumption: That 'the same species' is mechanically decidable (a branch ID, a coverage bitmap). That the sampler's adaptivity can be characterised well enough to correct for the induced bias. That the program under test is fixed during the campaign.
techniques.why: This is the closest structural match to CDSFL in the entire literature, and it is a match on exactly the axis that matters: ground truth is execution, not agreement. A fuzzer's crash is confirmed by running the input; CDSFL's finding is confirmed by running the falsifier. Both then face the identical question — when has the campaign paid out? Two consequences transfer immediately. First, CDSFL's rounds are adaptive (round k conditions on round k−1's findings), so the naive Good–Turing estimate is biased in exactly the way Böhme et al. 2021 characterise, and their correction is the right starting point rather than a fresh derivation. Second, and less comfortably: STADS works because 'species' is mechanically defined. CDSFL's 'same finding' is a semantic judgement, and that is where the whole approach either lands or fails — see the open questions.

techniques.name: Capture–recapture estimation of remaining defects in software inspection
techniques.source: S. G. Eick, C. R. Loader, M. D. Long, L. G. Votta, S. Vander Wiel, "Estimating software fault content before coding", ICSE 1992 (first application) · H. Petersson, T. Thelin, P. Runeson, C. Wohlin, "Capture–recapture in software inspections after 10 years research — theory, evaluation and application", Journal of Systems and Software 72(2):249–264, 2004. https://wohlin.eu/jss04-1.pdf · L. Briand, K. El Emam, B. Freimut, O. Laitenberger, "A comprehensive evaluation of capture-recapture models for estimating software defect content", IEEE TSE 26(6), 2000. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/852741/
techniques.what_it_does: Treats independent inspectors as trapping occasions and defects as animals; the overlap between inspectors' defect lists estimates how many defects neither found. Models M0/Mt/Mh/Mth vary in whether they allow occasion effects (inspector effectiveness) and heterogeneity (defect detectability).
techniques.assumption: Inspectors search independently; every defect has a nonzero detection probability; defects are matched reliably across inspectors' lists; and — the practical killer — enough inspectors and enough overlap for the estimator to be stable.
techniques.why: The setup maps onto CDSFL almost line for line: N reviewers, one artefact, overlapping finding lists, estimate what is left. But the decade of evaluation work is a warning, not an endorsement. Briand et al. and Petersson et al. found these estimators substantially biased and highly unstable with few inspectors and small defect counts — which is precisely CDSFL's moderate-scale regime of ~5 seats. Two further mismatches: independence between reviewers is exactly what LLM panels violate (see the N-version entries), and heterogeneity in finding 'detectability' is severe, which pushes you to model Mh and inflates variance further. Usable as a rough bound with explicit confidence intervals; not usable as a gate trigger on its own.

techniques.name: Deduplication as the load-bearing failure mode
techniques.source: G. Klees, A. Ruef, B. Cooper, S. Wei, M. Hicks, "Evaluating Fuzz Testing", ACM CCS 2018. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3243734.3243804 and https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~dstefan/cse227-spring20/papers/klees:evaluating.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Surveys 32 fuzzing papers and finds methodological problems in every evaluation, then demonstrates experimentally that those problems produce wrong conclusions. Central finding for us: crash count, the field's most-used metric, is inaccurate because deduplication heuristics (stack hashes, coverage profiles) both merge distinct bugs and split single bugs.
techniques.assumption: None that matter — this is a negative empirical result about measurement practice.
techniques.why: Everything in the species-discovery family consumes f1 and f2, and f1/f2 is *entirely* a function of your deduplication rule. Klees et al. is the demonstration that getting that rule wrong silently corrupts the headline number in a whole subfield. CDSFL's '2 of 2,050' is the same statistic and therefore carries the same exposure. Worse: the obvious way to decide whether two findings are 'the same' is to ask a model — which would reintroduce model agreement as a truth-adjacent criterion through the back door of the dedup step. That is a real architectural hazard and it should be named explicitly in the design, not left to a helper function.

techniques.name: N-version programming: the independence assumption and its refutation
techniques.source: J. C. Knight & N. G. Leveson, "An experimental evaluation of the assumption of independence in multiversion programming", IEEE TSE SE-12(1):96–109, 1986. https://www.csc.kth.se/utbildning/kth/kurser/DA2210/vettig13/Seminarier/KnightLeveson.pdf · D. E. Eckhardt & L. D. Lee, "A theoretical basis for the analysis of multiversion software subject to coincident errors", IEEE TSE SE-11(12), 1985. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/TSE.1985.231895 · B. Littlewood & D. Miller, "Conceptual modeling of coincident failures in multiversion software", IEEE TSE 15(12), 1989. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/32.58771
techniques.what_it_does: Knight & Leveson built 27 independently-written versions of one program at two universities and ran a million test cases: coincident failures were far more frequent than independence predicts. Eckhardt & Lee supply the mechanism — inputs vary in intrinsic difficulty, so even independently-developed versions fail together on the hard ones. Littlewood & Miller extend it: forcing versions to use *different methodologies* can produce better-than-independent failure behaviour.
techniques.assumption: Correctness is decided by executing versions against a test oracle. Versions are developed from a common specification.
techniques.why: This is the right theory for CDSFL's diversity question and it comes from a field where truth has always meant execution. Three consequences. (1) 'Ask N models and union the findings' cannot be priced by assuming independence — Knight & Leveson is the canonical demonstration that the assumption is unsafe even under strong independence protocols. (2) Eckhardt & Lee's variable-difficulty model explains *why* the panel will look diverse on easy findings and correlated on hard ones, which is exactly the regime where an extra model is supposed to earn its keep. (3) Littlewood & Miller give the actionable design principle and it is not 'add vendors': force methodological diversity — different falsification strategies, different decompositions, different roles — because that is the axis with theory saying it can beat independence, whereas vendor diversity has no such guarantee.

techniques.name: N-version programming replicated with LLM coding agents
techniques.source: J. Ron, B. Baudry, M. Monperrus, "N-Version Programming with Coding Agents", arXiv:2606.20158, June 2026. https://arxiv.org/html/2606.20158
techniques.what_it_does: Direct replication of Knight & Leveson using LLMs: 48 admitted implementations from 5 coding agents, 23 models and 3 languages, each run against 1 million randomised test cases with correctness decided by differential testing against a validated reference oracle.
techniques.assumption: Correctness by executed differential test against an oracle — the same truth criterion CDSFL uses.
techniques.why: This is the empirical answer to 'does asking a different vendor buy you independent coverage', measured under CDSFL's own truth criterion. It does not. Observed coincident failures 429 against 115.36 predicted under independence (z = 29.20, p ≈ 1.8e−187), independence rejected in all three languages separately, and 87 of 158 cross-agent pairs showed *perfect* co-failure (φ = 1). Crossing a vendor boundary does not eliminate correlated failure profiles. For CDSFL this is severe in both directions: it undercuts any pricing of the Nth model that assumes vendor diversity buys independence, and it makes the '2 of 2,050' figure even harder to believe on its face, because the best available evidence says frontier models fail *together* far more than chance — which should produce co-discovery, not its absence.

techniques.name: Correlated errors across LLMs, and effective sample size for judge panels
techniques.source: E. Kim, A. Garg, K. Peng, N. Garg, "Correlated Errors in Large Language Models", ICML 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962 · G. Kohli (Apple), "Nine Judges, Two Effective Votes: Correlated Errors Undermine LLM Evaluation Panels", arXiv:2605.29800, May 2026. https://arxiv.org/html/2605.29800v1
techniques.what_it_does: Kim et al. measure error correlation across 350+ models on leaderboard and resume-screening tasks. Kohli quantifies how much independent information a judge panel actually carries, using the Kish effective sample size n_eff = k / (1 + (k−1)·φ̄) where φ̄ is mean pairwise phi correlation of errors, cross-validated with an eigenvalue measure n_eff = k/λ_max.
techniques.assumption: Kim et al.: none beyond having a correctness key. Kohli: that the panel's output is combined by *vote* — n_eff is defined relative to a Condorcet-style independence baseline.
techniques.why: Two findings transfer and one conclusion does not. Transfers: (a) Kim et al. find larger and more accurate models have *more* correlated errors, even across distinct architectures and providers — which means a routing ladder that always escalates to the strongest available model is actively destroying the diversity it depends on, a real and counter-intuitive design consequence; (b) Kohli's mean-pairwise-φ on error vectors is a cheap, computable diversity metric CDSFL can adopt today, and the empirical scale is sobering — 9 frontier judges from 7 families yielded n_eff ≈ 2.18, asymptoting near 2.6. Does not transfer: Kohli's conclusion that 'aggregation cannot compensate' (Dawid–Skene closing ≤11% of the Condorcet gap) is a statement about voting, and CDSFL does not vote. Under union-with-a-verifier the correct figure of merit is not n_eff but expected marginal *coverage*, and the two can diverge sharply — a model that is redundant for voting can still be the only one that finds a particular defect.

techniques.name: Diversity measures for ensembles, and the negative result about them
techniques.source: L. Kuncheva & C. Whitaker, "Measures of Diversity in Classifier Ensembles and Their Relationship with the Ensemble Accuracy", Machine Learning 51(2):181–207, 2003. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1023/A:1022859003006 · D. Partridge & W. Krzanowski, "Software diversity: practical statistics for its measurement and exploitation", Information and Software Technology 39(10), 1997. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0950584997000232
techniques.what_it_does: Kuncheva & Whitaker evaluate ten diversity statistics (Q, correlation, disagreement, double-fault, entropy, difficulty index, Kohavi–Wolpert variance, interrater agreement, generalised diversity, coincident failure diversity) against ensemble accuracy. Partridge & Krzanowski introduce distinct-failure diversity — what matters is not whether versions fail on the same input but whether they fail the *same way*.
techniques.assumption: Kuncheva & Whitaker's evaluation assumes a voting or weighted-voting combiner.
techniques.why: Kuncheva & Whitaker's headline is negative — diversity measures did not reliably predict ensemble accuracy, and they explicitly doubt their usefulness for building ensembles. Do not import that pessimism uncritically, because it is conditioned on a *vote*: under voting, diversity must help the majority, and it often doesn't. Under CDSFL's union-with-a-verifier, every true finding from any member is kept and every false one is discarded by the tool, so marginal coverage is monotone in the double-fault/coincident-failure structure in a way it simply is not for voting. The theoretically right metric for CDSFL is therefore the double-fault rate or Partridge & Krzanowski's coincident-failure diversity, evaluated against union coverage — and the fact that nobody has validated diversity metrics against a union-with-verifier combiner is a cheap experiment CDSFL is unusually well placed to run.

techniques.name: Repeated sampling with an automatic verifier
techniques.source: B. Brown, J. Juravsky, R. Ehrlich, R. Clark, Q. V. Le, C. Ré, A. Mirhoseini, "Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling", arXiv:2407.21787, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21787
techniques.what_it_does: Measures coverage — the fraction of problems solved by at least one of k samples — as k varies over four orders of magnitude. Coverage grows log-linearly and is well fitted by an exponentiated power law. With a verifier (code tests, formal proofs) coverage converts directly into solved problems: SWE-bench Lite goes from 15.9% at one sample to 56% at 250. Without a verifier, reward-model or majority-vote selection plateaus after a few hundred samples.
techniques.assumption: An automatic verifier exists and is sound. Samples are drawn from the same model at nonzero temperature.
techniques.why: This is the cleanest existing evidence for CDSFL's central architectural bet, and it also supplies a usable functional form. Three transfers. (1) The verifier is what makes repeated dispatch pay — that is measured, not asserted, and it validates the founding principle empirically rather than philosophically. (2) The exponentiated power law is the curve to fit to CDSFL's own coverage-versus-dispatches data, giving extrapolation ('how many more dispatches for 10% more findings') without needing Chao's assumptions. (3) The ceiling is the *selector*, not the sampler — which reframes the routing ladder's failure. When there is no stronger model, more samples from the model you have still buys coverage, provided the tool is doing the selecting. That is the solo-researcher answer, and it is a positive one.

techniques.name: Voting-based scaling of LLM calls, and its non-monotonicity
techniques.source: L. Chen, J. Q. Davis, B. Hanin, P. Bailis, I. Stoica, M. Zaharia, J. Zou, "Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards Scaling Laws of Compound Inference Systems", NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2403.02419. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02419
techniques.what_it_does: Analyses Vote and Filter-Vote systems and shows performance first rises then *falls* with the number of LLM calls, because a task mixes easy and hard queries: more calls help on easy queries and hurt on hard ones. Gives a method to compute the optimal call count from a small sample.
techniques.assumption: Majority-vote aggregation over calls.
techniques.why: Useful as a warning and as a mechanism, not as a method. The warning: any CDSFL component that resolves anything by counting models — including, quietly, a deduplication or confidence heuristic — inherits non-monotone scaling, so 'more models' can make it worse and the harness would have no way to tell. The mechanism is worth noting because it is the same one Eckhardt & Lee identified forty years earlier: heterogeneous item difficulty is what makes naive aggregation break. The optimal-call-count calculation itself does not transfer, because it optimises vote accuracy, which CDSFL does not compute.

techniques.name: Budget-optimal task allocation for unreliable workers
techniques.source: D. R. Karger, S. Oh, D. Shah, "Budget-Optimal Task Allocation for Reliable Crowdsourcing Systems", Operations Research 62(1):1–24, 2014 (arXiv:1110.3564, 2011). https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.3564
techniques.what_it_does: Poses the allocation problem as: minimise total assignments needed to reach a target reliability. Gives a random-regular bipartite assignment plus an iterative message-passing inference algorithm, and proves order-optimality. Notably shows the minimum price to reach a target reliability scales the same way for adaptive and non-adaptive schemes.
techniques.assumption: Workers are transient and cannot be reused or profiled over time; a single latent binary answer per task; reliability is the objective.
techniques.why: The inference half is unusable (latent answer again). The allocation half is worth having, and one result is directly useful as a discipline: adaptivity buys only constant factors here, which is an argument against building an elaborate adaptive dispatcher before a simple round-robin has been measured. The assumption that workers are transient and unprofilable is exactly inverted for CDSFL — models are persistent, re-queryable and cheaply profiled against the verifier — so the resulting allocation should be *better* than their bounds, not worse. Restate the objective as expected new verified findings per unit cost and the machinery is reusable.

techniques.name: Decision-theoretic control of when to ask again (TurKontrol / POMDP workflow control)
techniques.source: P. Dai, Mausam, D. S. Weld, "Decision-Theoretic Control of Crowd-Sourced Workflows", AAAI 2010. https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~weld/papers/dai-aaai10.pdf · P. Dai, C. H. Lin, Mausam, D. S. Weld, "POMDP-based control of workflows for crowdsourcing", Artificial Intelligence 202:52–85, 2013. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000437021300057X
techniques.what_it_does: Formulates 'should I buy one more judgement, or ship what I have?' as a POMDP over a belief about artefact quality, trading marginal quality against marginal cost. Applied to three cases including controlling how many votes to solicit and when to switch workflows.
techniques.assumption: A calibrated model of how much a worker's contribution improves artefact quality, and a utility function converting quality into money. In their voting case, quality is again inferred from agreement.
techniques.why: The *frame* is right and is the correct formal home for CDSFL's stopping decision: a belief-state controller choosing between 'dispatch again', 'dispatch to a different model', and 'stop'. What has to change is the observation model. Theirs is a noisy vote; CDSFL's is a tool verdict, which is far higher quality and lower variance — so the belief state is sharper and the POMDP is easier, not harder. The genuine cost is that CDSFL must name a value for a verified finding and a cost for a dispatch. That is a policy decision the founder has to make, not something the literature supplies, and no stopping rule of any kind can be principled until it is made.

techniques.name: Value of information / expected value of sample information
techniques.source: R. A. Howard, "Information Value Theory", IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics 2(1):22–26, 1966. https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1966.300074 · H. Raiffa & R. Schlaifer, Applied Statistical Decision Theory, 1961
techniques.what_it_does: Defines the value of an observation as the difference in expected payoff between deciding with it and deciding without it, giving a maximum price a rational decision-maker should pay for it. EVSI extends this to the value of a sample of a given size.
techniques.assumption: A specified decision, a payoff function, and a prior over outcomes. Value is *instrumental* — information that cannot change any decision is worth exactly zero, however true it is.
techniques.why: This is the honest general answer to question 1, and it reframes it usefully. 'When does asking another model stop paying?' is not a statistical question, it is a decision-theoretic one: the Nth dispatch is worth buying only while its expected marginal payoff exceeds its price. The zero-value clause is the sharp edge — a dispatch that would surface a finding nobody will act on is worth nothing regardless of how novel it is, which suggests weighting findings by severity in the stopping rule rather than counting them. The catch is that EVI needs a prior over what the next dispatch will find, and that prior is exactly what species-discovery estimation would supply. The two techniques compose: Good–Turing gives P(next dispatch is productive), VOI turns it into a stop/continue decision.

techniques.name: Adaptive submodularity and the greedy coverage policy
techniques.source: D. Golovin & A. Krause, "Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization", JAIR 42:427–486, 2011. https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/10731 (arXiv:1003.3967)
techniques.what_it_does: Generalises submodularity to adaptive policies that observe outcomes as they go, and proves that simple adaptive greedy is near-optimal (1−1/e competitive with the optimal policy) for adaptive monotone submodular objectives, with extensions to matroid and independence-system constraints.
techniques.assumption: The objective is adaptive monotone submodular; the distribution over item states is known or estimable; outcomes of chosen actions are observed.
techniques.why: There is a real structural fit here that is worth stating precisely: the union of tool-verified findings is a monotone submodular set function of the set of dispatches — adding a dispatch never removes a verified finding, and its marginal contribution shrinks as the union grows. That is the formal reason 'diminishing returns' is not just an intuition here, and it means greedy allocation (next dispatch to whichever model/sub-problem has highest expected marginal new-finding yield) carries a (1−1/e) guarantee rather than being a heuristic. This is the best-founded answer to question 2 available. The adaptation cost is the prior: you need estimates of expected marginal yield per (model, sub-problem) pair, which is again the measurement precondition. Note that submodularity holds for the *union* precisely because the verifier discards false positives — under voting it would not.

techniques.name: Algorithm portfolios and per-instance algorithm selection
techniques.source: J. R. Rice, "The Algorithm Selection Problem", Advances in Computers 15:65–118, 1976. https://docs.lib.purdue.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1098&context=cstech · B. Huberman, R. Lukose, T. Hogg, "An economics approach to hard computational problems", Science 275:51–54, 1997 · C. Gomes & B. Selman, "Algorithm portfolios", Artificial Intelligence 126(1–2):43–62, 2001 · L. Xu, F. Hutter, H. Hoos, K. Leyton-Brown, "SATzilla: Portfolio-based Algorithm Selection for SAT", JAIR 32:565–606, 2008. https://jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/10556
techniques.what_it_does: Rice formalises picking an algorithm per instance from measurable instance features. Huberman et al. and Gomes & Selman show that running a diverse set of heavy-tailed solvers in parallel, with a chosen time split, dominates any single solver in expectation. SATzilla learns empirical hardness models to select per instance, and won repeatedly at SAT competitions.
techniques.assumption: A pool of solvers with measurable per-instance performance, and instance features predictive of that performance. Crucially, solver *output is verifiable* — a SAT assignment is checked, not voted on.
techniques.why: This is the right family for question 2, and it is the only family in this whole survey where the combination rule is already 'take whichever answer verifies' — the same rule CDSFL uses. Two things transfer. First, portfolio construction is explicitly about *complementarity* rather than individual strength: SATzilla's pool deliberately includes solvers that are individually mediocre but cover instances the strong ones miss, which is the direct rebuttal to a routing ladder that only ever escalates upward. Second, per-instance selection from features is precisely 'allocate heterogeneous reviewers to sub-problems'. The adaptation: SATzilla trains on large labelled instance sets that CDSFL does not have, so start with the portfolio insight (build for complementarity, verified selection) and defer the learned selector.

techniques.name: Universal restart scheduling under an unknown runtime distribution
techniques.source: M. Luby, A. Sinclair, D. Zuckerman, "Optimal speedup of Las Vegas algorithms", Information Processing Letters 47(4):173–180, 1993. https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~diz/pubs/speedup.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: For a randomised algorithm with unknown runtime distribution, gives a universal restart schedule — the sequence 1,1,2,1,1,2,4,1,1,2,4,8,… — whose expected time is within O(log) of the optimal fixed-cutoff strategy for *any* such algorithm, with no knowledge of the distribution required.
techniques.assumption: Runs are independent given a restart; success is verifiable when it occurs (Las Vegas, not Monte Carlo); restarting is cheap relative to a run.
techniques.why: This is the concrete answer for the solo researcher with one model and one vendor, and it is the only technique in this report that is genuinely scale-free by construction. With one model, the portfolio is over *restarts* — different seeds, temperatures, decompositions, roles — and a stochastic LLM dispatch under a tool verifier is exactly a Las Vegas algorithm: variable time to success, success recognisable when it happens. Luby's schedule then gives a defensible allocation policy that needs no calibration data, no per-model profile, and no second vendor, and degrades gracefully because it is the *same* policy at every scale — the institution runs the same schedule across more parallel arms. It also supplies the missing rung when the routing ladder has no stronger model: restart the model you have on the same finding with a fresh decomposition, on a principled schedule, rather than failing.

techniques.name: Anytime-valid inference: confidence sequences and e-values
techniques.source: S. Howard, A. Ramdas, J. McAuliffe, J. Sekhon, "Time-uniform Chernoff bounds via nonnegative supermartingales" (2020) and "Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences", Annals of Statistics 49(2), 2021 · A. Ramdas, P. Grünwald, V. Vovk, G. Shafer, "Game-theoretic statistics and safe anytime-valid inference", Statistical Science, arXiv:2210.01948. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.01948
techniques.what_it_does: Constructs estimates and tests whose error guarantee holds uniformly over all sample sizes and all data-dependent stopping times, built from nonnegative martingales. You may look at the data after every observation and stop whenever you like without inflating error.
techniques.assumption: The martingale construction must match the data-generating process; guarantees are typically conservative relative to a fixed-n test.
techniques.why: This is a small, cheap, and I think currently-missing correctness fix for the convergence gate. A gate that is evaluated after every round is, statistically, continuous peeking — and any fixed-sample threshold checked repeatedly has an error rate far above its nominal level. That means a gate can fire spuriously simply because it was checked often enough, which is a silent failure that would look exactly like convergence. Replacing the gate's underlying estimate with a confidence sequence (or an e-value threshold) makes 'stop the moment the criterion is met' formally legitimate. It requires no change to the truth criterion, no model agreement, and modest implementation effort.

techniques.name: Bayesian Truth Serum and the surprisingly-popular algorithm
techniques.source: D. Prelec, "A Bayesian Truth Serum for Subjective Data", Science 306:462–466, 2004. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1102081 · D. Prelec, H. S. Seung, J. McCoy, "A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem", Nature 541:532–535, 2017. https://www.nature.com/articles/nature21054 · Negative evidence: P. Schoenegger & S. Verheyen, "Taking a Closer Look at the Bayesian Truth Serum: A Registered Report", Experimental Psychology 69(4), 2022. https://econtent.hogrefe.com/doi/abs/10.1027/1618-3169/a000558
techniques.what_it_does: Asks each respondent both for an answer and for a prediction of the distribution of others' answers, then scores answers by how much more common they are than collectively predicted. The 2017 version selects the answer that is surprisingly popular, and is provably optimal under a Bayesian common-prior model even when the truth is a minority view.
techniques.assumption: Respondents are Bayesian agents with a common prior who have private signals, are strategically responsive to the score, and produce honest meta-predictions. The 2017 optimality proof rests on that generative model.
techniques.why: Refuse this one on three independent grounds, any one of which is sufficient. First and decisively: it is a truth criterion derived from the structure of agreement, which is exactly what CDSFL exists not to do — however clever the mechanism, the output is 'this is probably true because of how opinions are distributed', not 'a tool executed this and it held'. Second, the mechanism's power comes from incentive compatibility, and LLMs are not score-maximising strategic agents; there is no reason a model's meta-prediction reflects a private signal rather than the same pretraining prior that produced its answer, and shared pretraining is precisely the common-cause the model assumes away. Third, the empirical record is weak even in its home domain — Schoenegger & Verheyen's registered report failed to find significant differences in response behaviour between BTS-incentivised participants and simply-paid ones. CDSFL already has something strictly better than a clever proxy for truth: actual truth, from execution.

techniques.name: Repeated labelling: when does another judgement pay?
techniques.source: V. Sheng, F. Provost, P. Ipeirotis, "Get Another Label? Improving Data Quality and Data Mining Using Multiple, Noisy Labelers", KDD 2008. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1401890.1401965 · P. Ipeirotis, F. Provost, V. Sheng, J. Wang, "Repeated labeling using multiple noisy labelers", Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 28:402–441, 2014. https://ipeirotis.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/dmkd-2013-repeated-labeling.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Derives analytically the conditions under which buying repeated labels for existing items beats buying labels for new items, as a function of labeller noise, and shows the answer depends on where you are on the learning curve.
techniques.assumption: Labels are noisy observations of a latent truth; the downstream objective is model quality; the marginal value of a label is mediated by a learner.
techniques.why: Only the question shape transfers, and it transfers well: 'spend the next unit of budget deepening an existing item, or broadening to a new one?' is CDSFL's dispatch dilemma exactly. Their analytic answer does not transfer, because it is parameterised by label noise and downstream learner accuracy, neither of which exists here. Substituting the right quantities — deepen when the marginal probability of an unfound finding on this artefact exceeds the marginal probability on the next one, both estimated from discovery curves — turns it into a usable rule. Cite it for the framing, re-derive the content.

techniques.name: Empirical saturation in human inspection at roughly two reviewers
techniques.source: A. Porter, H. Siy, A. Mockus, L. Votta, "Understanding the sources of variation in software inspections", ACM TOSEM 7(1):41–79, 1998 · C. Sauer, D. R. Jeffery, L. Land, P. Yetton, "The Effectiveness of Software Development Technical Reviews: A Behaviorally Motivated Program of Research", IEEE TSE 26(1):1–14, 2000 · P. C. Rigby & C. Bird, "Convergent contemporary software peer review practices", ESEC/FSE 2013, pp. 202–212. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/rigby2013convergent.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Porter et al. found two reviewers discovered as many defects as four; Buck found no difference between teams of three, four and five; Sauer et al. summarise the consensus that two inspectors find an optimal number of defects. Rigby & Bird then show six industrial and OSS projects (Android, Chrome, AMD, Bing, Office, SQL) independently converged on a median of two active reviewers, with only minimal increase in review comments when more reviewers participated.
techniques.assumption: Human reviewers reading the same artefact, defects confirmed by discussion and author agreement rather than by a tool. Artefacts are code changes of bounded size.
techniques.why: This is the strongest empirical prior available on question 1, and it is worth taking seriously precisely because six organisations converged on it independently rather than deriving it. But it is also a falsification target, and CDSFL is the instrument that can test it. Human saturation at two is plausibly an attention artefact — humans reading the same artefact look at the same things — and there is no reason to assume LLMs saturate at the same point. Note the collision this creates: this literature predicts heavy overlap and fast saturation, while CDSFL's 2-in-2,050 records report essentially zero overlap. Both cannot be right. Either LLM panels are radically more complementary than human inspectors (a genuinely interesting empirical claim, and publishable), or the co-discovery statistic is broken. Resolving that is worth more than any technique in this report.

techniques.name: Intrinsic self-correction fails, but tool-grounded retry is a different regime
techniques.source: J. Huang, X. Chen, S. Mishra, H. S. Zheng, A. W. Yu, X. Song, D. Zhou, "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet", ICLR 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798
techniques.what_it_does: Shows that when a model is asked to revise its own reasoning using only its own capabilities, with no external feedback, performance does not improve and often degrades.
techniques.assumption: The defining condition is *intrinsic* self-correction — no external signal enters the revision loop.
techniques.why: This resolves the routing ladder's dead end, and in CDSFL's favour. The naive fix when no stronger model exists — re-ask the same model to try harder — is exactly the intrinsic setting this paper shows does not work, so the ladder is right to refuse it. But CDSFL is never in the intrinsic setting: the tool's verdict on the previous falsifier is external feedback by construction. So a retry that feeds back the falsifier's actual output is a categorically different operation from 'try again', and the negative result does not bind it. The design consequence: the ladder should escalate along evidence and method before it escalates along model strength — feed back tool output, then change decomposition, then change methodology or role (per Littlewood & Miller), then draw more samples (per Brown et al.), and only then reach for a stronger model. Only that last rung can be unavailable, so the ladder never has to fail.

techniques.name: Best-arm identification and successive halving
techniques.source: J.-Y. Audibert & S. Bubeck, "Best arm identification in multi-armed bandits", COLT 2010 · Z. Karnin, T. Koren, O. Somekh, "Almost Optimal Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits", ICML 2013
techniques.what_it_does: Under a fixed budget of pulls, identifies the arm with highest expected reward by progressively eliminating (Successive Rejects) or halving (Sequential Halving) the candidate set.
techniques.assumption: The objective is to identify a single best arm; rewards are i.i.d. per arm; the value of the answer is in the identity of the winner.
techniques.why: Wrong objective, and importing it would quietly re-create the routing ladder's original bug. CDSFL does not want the best model, it wants the largest union of verified findings — and the model with the lowest mean yield may be the only one that finds a particular class of defect, exactly as in a SAT portfolio. Successive halving would eliminate that model early, in a way that looks like efficient allocation while destroying coverage. If you want a bandit formulation, the right one is a coverage/submodular-maximisation objective (Golovin & Krause), not pure exploration for a maximum.

techniques.name: Reviewer assignment with coverage and load constraints
techniques.source: L. Charlin & R. Zemel, "The Toronto Paper Matching System: An automated paper-reviewer assignment system", ICML workshop 2013. https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~lcharlin/papers/tpms.pdf · I. Stelmakh, N. Shah, A. Singh, "PeerReview4All: Fair and Accurate Reviewer Assignment in Peer Review", JMLR 22, 2021. https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume22/20-190/20-190.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Solves the assignment of reviewers to submissions as a constrained matching/flow problem maximising total expertise subject to load bounds per reviewer, coverage counts per item, and conflict constraints. PeerReview4All adds a max-min fairness objective so no single item gets a uniformly poor assignment.
techniques.assumption: Coverage counts are fixed exogenously (every paper gets k reviews); expertise scores are available; the goal is a one-shot static assignment.
techniques.why: The constraint structure is the right vocabulary for question 2 — load, coverage, conflict — and PeerReview4All's max-min objective is a good fit for a harness that must not let any sub-problem go unexamined just because it is unglamorous. Two adaptations are needed and both are substantial. The fixed coverage count k is exactly the parameter CDSFL wants to *derive* rather than assume, so coverage must become a decision variable driven by the discovery estimate. And the assignment must be sequential rather than one-shot, because each round's verified findings change the expertise estimates for the next. That combination — adaptive coverage counts under a verifier — is not in this literature.

transfers: The verifier converts an unsupervised problem into a supervised one, and that is the single most important consequence in this whole area. Per-model ability and per-finding difficulty do not need Dawid–Skene, GLAD or spectral EM — they can be fitted by ordinary supervised regression against tool verdicts. Keep GLAD's ability-by-difficulty parameterisation; discard the entire latent-variable estimation apparatus built around it.

Good–Turing discovery probability is a drop-in stopping rule that consults no agreement whatsoever: stop when P(next dispatch yields a new verified finding) falls below cost-per-dispatch divided by value-per-finding. CDSFL already logs the sufficient statistics. This is the closest thing in the report to 'your problem is solved', and the blocker is instrumentation rather than theory.

Böhme's STADS and the residual-risk work are the closest structural match anywhere in the literature, because fuzzing shares CDSFL's exact truth criterion — a crash is confirmed by execution, not by consensus. Their diagnosis that adaptive sampling breaks Good–Turing's i.i.d. assumption applies verbatim to CDSFL's round structure, and their correction is the right starting point rather than a fresh derivation.

N-version programming is the right theory for reviewer diversity, and it too comes from a field where truth is execution against an oracle. Knight & Leveson refute failure independence, Eckhardt & Lee explain the mechanism (input difficulty varies, so versions fail together on the hard cases), and Littlewood & Miller give the actionable lever: forced methodological diversity can beat independence, whereas vendor diversity carries no such guarantee.

Ron, Baudry & Monperrus (2026) replicate Knight & Leveson with 23 LLMs under executed differential testing and reject independence decisively — 429 coincident failures against 115.36 predicted, and 87 of 158 cross-agent pairs at perfect co-failure. Any pricing of the Nth model that assumes cross-vendor independence is unsupported by the best available evidence.

The union of tool-verified findings is a monotone submodular function of the dispatch set — adding a dispatch never removes a verified finding, and marginal yield shrinks as the union grows. That makes diminishing returns a theorem rather than an intuition here, and it means greedy allocation carries a (1−1/e) guarantee via Golovin & Krause rather than being a heuristic. Note this holds because the verifier discards false positives; under voting it would not.

Luby, Sinclair & Zuckerman's universal restart schedule is the scale-free policy the harness needs. A stochastic dispatch under a tool verifier is a Las Vegas algorithm, so the schedule 1,1,2,1,1,2,4,… is within O(log) of optimal with zero knowledge of the runtime distribution — which means the same policy serves the one-model solo researcher and the unlimited-access institution, and gives the routing ladder a principled rung that does not require a stronger model to exist.

Brown et al.'s repeated-sampling result is direct empirical support for CDSFL's founding bet: with a verifier, coverage keeps scaling log-linearly over four orders of magnitude; without one, selection plateaus after a few hundred samples. The ceiling is the selector, not the sampler. Their exponentiated power law is also the right functional form to fit to CDSFL's own coverage curve for extrapolation.

Portfolio construction from SAT (Rice, Gomes & Selman, SATzilla) is the only mature allocation literature whose combination rule is already 'take whichever answer verifies'. Its central lesson contradicts the current routing ladder: portfolios are built for complementarity, deliberately retaining individually-mediocre solvers that cover instances the strong ones miss.

Kim et al. (ICML 2025) find that larger and more accurate models have MORE correlated errors, even across providers. A ladder that always escalates to the strongest available model is therefore actively spending down the diversity it depends on — an argument for escalating along methodology before capability.

Anytime-valid confidence sequences and e-values make a repeatedly-evaluated convergence gate statistically legitimate. A gate checked every round is continuous peeking, and a fixed-sample threshold checked that way will fire spuriously at a rate far above its nominal level — a silent failure indistinguishable from real convergence. Cheap to fix, and it touches nothing about the truth criterion.

Howard's value-of-information gives the honest general frame: the Nth dispatch is worth buying only while expected marginal payoff exceeds price, and information that cannot change a decision is worth zero however true it is. This composes with Good–Turing, which supplies the required prior. It also forces a decision the literature cannot make for you: what a verified finding is worth relative to a dispatch.
does_not_transfer: Dawid–Skene, GLAD, Raykar et al. and Zhang et al.'s spectral-EM as TRUTH CRITERIA. All four infer an unobservable label from the structure of agreement. CDSFL observes the label. Importing any of them would reintroduce voting as truth under a more sophisticated name, and would additionally be unidentifiable — with 2 co-discoveries in 2,050 findings there is no overlap structure from which to fit a confusion matrix.

Prelec's Bayesian Truth Serum and the surprisingly-popular algorithm. Refuse on three independent grounds: (1) it derives truth from the shape of the agreement distribution, which is the thing CDSFL exists not to do; (2) its power comes from incentive compatibility over Bayesian agents with private signals and a common prior, and LLMs are not score-maximising strategic agents — shared pretraining is exactly the common cause the model assumes away, so a meta-prediction is not evidence of a private signal; (3) Schoenegger & Verheyen's registered report found no significant behavioural difference between BTS-incentivised and simply-paid respondents even in its home domain.

Majority voting and self-consistency in any form, including as a hidden component. Chen et al. show vote-based scaling is non-monotone — performance rises then falls with call count — so a harness that resolves anything by counting models can get worse as it grows and have no way to detect it. This applies to quiet uses too: a deduplication or confidence heuristic that asks models whether two findings are 'the same' is voting.

Kohli's conclusion that aggregation cannot compensate for correlated judges. The finding is real but vote-specific: n_eff is defined against a Condorcet independence baseline. Under union-with-a-verifier the correct figure of merit is expected marginal coverage, not effective vote count, and the two diverge — a judge that is redundant for voting can still be the sole discoverer of a defect. Take Kohli's mean-pairwise-φ metric; leave the conclusion.

Kuncheva & Whitaker's pessimism about diversity measures. Their negative result is conditioned on a voting combiner, where diversity must help the majority and frequently doesn't. Under union-with-a-verifier, coverage is monotone in the coincident-failure structure by construction. Do not import the conclusion; do import double-fault and coincident-failure diversity as candidate metrics, and note that nobody has validated them against a union-with-verifier combiner.

Best-arm identification and successive halving. The objective is to find the single best arm, which is the wrong target — CDSFL wants maximum union coverage, and successive halving would eliminate exactly the low-mean, high-complementarity models that a portfolio exists to retain. Importing it would re-create the routing ladder's original bug while looking like efficient allocation.

Karger–Oh–Shah's message-passing inference (the allocation half is usable; the inference half is not), and their assumption that workers are transient and unprofilable — which is inverted here, since models are persistent, re-queryable and cheaply profiled against the verifier.

The specific analytic thresholds in Sheng/Provost/Ipeirotis and the optimal-call-count calculation in Chen et al. Both are parameterised by quantities CDSFL does not compute — label noise, downstream learner accuracy, vote accuracy. Cite them for the question shape; re-derive the content against verified-finding yield.

Capture–recapture as a gate trigger. Ten years of evaluation (Briand et al. 2000, Petersson et al. 2004) found these estimators substantially biased and unstable with few inspectors and small defect counts, which is precisely the 5-seat regime. Usable as a bound with explicit intervals; not as a decision rule on its own.

The 'two reviewers is optimal' result should not be imported as a setting. It is a robust human finding (Porter et al., Sauer et al., six projects in Rigby & Bird) but it is plausibly an attention artefact of humans reading the same artefact, and it flatly contradicts CDSFL's own near-zero observed overlap. Treat it as a falsification target, not a default.
open: What is a 'finding', for counting purposes? Every technique that answers question 1 — Good–Turing, Chao, STADS, capture–recapture — consumes f1 (found once) and f2 (found twice), and both are entirely determined by the rule that decides when two findings are the same. STADS works because 'species' is mechanically defined (a branch ID). CDSFL's sameness is semantic. And the obvious implementation — ask a model whether two findings match — would smuggle model agreement back into the pipeline through the deduplication step, defeating the founding principle at exactly the point nobody would look. This is the crux, it is genuinely open, and it needs invention rather than import. A defensible route is to canonicalise on the FALSIFIER rather than the finding text: two findings are the same when their falsifiers exercise the same code path or assert the same predicate — mechanical, tool-decidable, and consistent with the truth criterion. That idea is not in any literature I found.

Is the 2-of-2,050 co-discovery figure a measurement or an artefact? Taken at face value it yields Chao1 = 1,050,626 latent findings and sampled coverage of 0.195%, and it contradicts the two best-evidenced priors available: human inspection saturates at ~2 reviewers, and LLM failures are strongly correlated (429 vs 115.36 coincident failures in the Knight–Leveson replication). Three explanations must be separated before any allocation question can be answered, and CDSFL's own logs can separate them: (a) dispatch topology — if models are asked DIFFERENT sub-questions, co-discovery is structurally impossible and the statistic is meaningless by design; (b) attribution policy — if the schema records exactly one model per finding, co-discovery is unrepresentable rather than absent; (c) deduplication — if near-identical findings are stored as distinct rows, every co-discovery is silently converted into two singletons. Check (a) first; it is the cheapest and it changes everything downstream.

Does Böhme's adaptive-sampling correction survive the jump from a fuzzer to a panel? CDSFL's rounds are adaptive in the same way greybox fuzzing is — round k conditions on round k−1 — so the i.i.d. assumption behind Good–Turing is violated identically. But a fuzzer's adaptation is a characterisable seed-scheduling policy, whereas a panel's adaptation is mediated by natural-language context. Whether the correction transfers, and how to even parameterise the bias, is unstudied.

Nobody has published species-discovery or capture–recapture estimation applied to a multi-model, tool-verified review panel. Searching for the combination turns up the components in isolation and nothing joining them. The mapping is the novel contribution and it is unclaimed — which is an opportunity, but also means there is no prior art to borrow validation from.

How should reviewers be allocated when capability spans orders of magnitude and the objective is union coverage under a verifier? Portfolio work assumes a fixed solver set with measurable runtimes; peer-review assignment assumes exogenously fixed coverage counts; adaptive submodularity assumes an estimable item-state distribution. None of them handles a single policy that must run identically at N=1 and N=unbounded with coverage counts derived rather than assumed. Luby's schedule is the best partial answer found and it addresses scheduling, not heterogeneous assignment.

Do diversity metrics predict union coverage under a verifier? Theory says they should, because coverage is monotone in coincident-failure structure once false positives are discarded — but Kuncheva & Whitaker showed they fail to predict VOTING accuracy, and nobody has run the union-with-verifier equivalent. This is a cheap, well-scoped, publishable experiment that CDSFL is unusually well placed to run, and it would settle question 3 empirically rather than by argument.

What is a verified finding worth, and what does a dispatch cost? Every principled stopping rule in this report — value of information, the POMDP formulation, the Good–Turing threshold — bottoms out in that ratio, and no literature can supply it. Until it is named (probably severity-weighted, since VOI says a finding nobody will act on is worth zero regardless of truth), every stopping rule remains a threshold picked by guess wearing a formula.

Is the closest published prior art actually weaker than CDSFL? 'Refute-or-Promote' (arXiv:2604.19049, April 2026) is an adversarial stage-gated multi-agent defect-discovery methodology — the nearest neighbour I could find — and it advances findings through inter-agent debate rather than independent execution. That suggests CDSFL's tool-verified criterion is a genuine differentiator rather than a reinvention, but the comparison deserves a careful read of the paper rather than reliance on my extraction of it, which came from a compressed PDF and should be treated as provisional.

areas.area: Area 5: dividing one review problem across a varying number of workers — classical scaling theory (Amdahl, Gustafson, Brent/span, work-stealing, MapReduce/BSP), parallel search (portfolio vs divide-and-conquer), and the empirical evidence on replicate-versus-partition for defect detection
areas.summary: Before any technique applies, one thing has to be said: the co-discovery figure of 2 in 2,050 is almost certainly a defect in how CDSFL decides two findings are the same, not a fact about model diversity. Human experts reviewing the same artefact overlap at 5–65% (typically ~40%), and a simulation of five reviewers with wildly heterogeneous and very low detection probabilities still produces ~19% co-discovery; to produce 0.098% you would need each model to detect about 0.05% of a latent pool of roughly 841,000 findings, a figure two independent methods (Chao's multi-list estimator and numerical inversion of the binomial co-discovery identity) agree on exactly. This matters enormously because every principled stopping rule in this literature — capture-recapture, Good-Turing, Chao richness, submodular coverage, scalability-law calibration — takes overlap as its primary input, so none of them can currently be run on CDSFL's records. On the substantive questions, the classical scaling laws transfer as bounds on latency but not on recall, and confusing the two is the most likely modelling error here: Brent's work-span bound says the useful number of reviewers is capped by parallelism (total work divided by round depth), and Rigby and Bird's industrial data confirms that adding reviewers did not reduce the number of review rounds. The strongest transferable result comes from fuzzing, the one mature field whose ground truth is also an executed oracle: Böhme and Falk show that finding the same bugs faster costs linearly more machines but finding linearly more bugs costs exponentially more machines, and that sharing findings between workers matters far more than worker count. The software-inspection literature converges, across thirty years and multiple independent studies, on two reviewers as the point where undifferentiated replication stops paying, which means the current five-seat panel is already past the knee. The one positive partition result — Porter, Votta and Basili's defect-based reading — partitions the question while replicating the artefact, not the other way round; partitioning by stakeholder perspective was refuted by a later replication and a meta-analysis. The genuinely new part, which no literature covers, is a coverage-objective switching rule between replication and partition, and deployment-invariant overdecomposition for review; those need invention.

techniques.name: Work–span analysis and the greedy-scheduling theorem (Brent's theorem)
techniques.source: R. P. Brent 1974 (JACM) and R. L. Graham 1966/1969, as stated and proved in R. D. Blumofe and C. E. Leiserson, "Scheduling Multithreaded Computations by Work Stealing", Journal of the ACM 46(5), 1999. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/324133.324234 (full text: https://www.csd.uwo.ca/~mmorenom/CS433-CS9624/Resources/Scheduling_multithreaded_computations_by_work_stealing.pdf)
techniques.what_it_does: Bounds parallel execution time as T_P <= T_1/P + T_infinity, where T_1 is total work and T_infinity is the critical path (span). The paper states the operative corollary explicitly: linear speedup holds only while the parallelism T_1/T_infinity is Omega(P). Beyond that, extra workers idle.
techniques.assumption: The computation is a fixed dependency DAG: the total work is known and does not grow when you add workers, and the dependency structure is what limits concurrency.
techniques.why: It gives CDSFL a computable ceiling on panel width that it can measure from data it already has: span is the number of rounds to convergence (findings in round k depend on round k-1 disclosure), work is total review effort. Beyond p* = work/span, extra models buy nothing in latency. Rigby and Bird's industrial data independently confirms the mechanism — more reviewers produced "no increase in the number of change sets submitted (i.e., the same number of rounds of reviewing)". The adaptation is severe though: CDSFL's work is NOT fixed, because more models generate more findings which generate more falsifier executions and more adjudication. So this bounds latency, not recall.

techniques.name: Amdahl's law / strong scaling
techniques.source: G. M. Amdahl, "Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities", AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, 1967. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1465482.1465560 (PDF: https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~rezaul/Spring-2012/CSE613/reading/Amdahl-1967.pdf). Empirically validated for LLM teams by E. Mieczkowski, K. M. Collins, I. Sucholutsky, N. Vélez, T. L. Griffiths, "Language Model Teams as Distributed Systems", arXiv:2603.12229, March 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12229
techniques.what_it_does: Speedup = 1/((1-p) + p/s). The serial fraction caps speedup regardless of worker count. Mieczkowski et al. tested this directly on LLM teams doing collaborative coding and found Amdahl provides a clear empirical bound (Kruskal-Wallis H=61.4, p<0.001 across parallelisability conditions), with observed speedup falling significantly BELOW the bound even in the highly-parallel condition (median 2.19x, Wilcoxon p<0.001).
techniques.assumption: Fixed total workload; the serial fraction is identifiable and constant; the metric of interest is time-to-completion.
techniques.why: The serial fraction in CDSFL is falsifier execution, gate evaluation and HIL adjudication. If adjudication is serialised on one human, that caps the whole system no matter how many models you buy — worth measuring before buying seats. But the adaptation is the same trap as above: Amdahl is a statement about time for fixed work, and CDSFL's real question is coverage for unknown work. The 2026 LLM-teams result validates it for wall-clock on coding tasks; it does not license any claim about how many findings a wider panel will produce.

techniques.name: Gustafson's law / weak scaling
techniques.source: J. L. Gustafson, "Reevaluating Amdahl's Law", Communications of the ACM 31(5):532–533, 1988. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/42411.42415 (open version: https://cacm.acm.org/research/reevaluating-amdahls-law/)
techniques.what_it_does: Reframes scaling: with more workers you should not run the same fixed problem faster, you should run a proportionally larger problem in the same time. Speedup is then linear in worker count because the parallel fraction grows with the problem.
techniques.assumption: The problem has a scalable dimension along which more work is genuinely wanted, and enlarging it is scientifically meaningful rather than padding.
techniques.why: This is the honest answer to the institution-with-unlimited-access case, and it is the one piece of classical theory that transfers without distortion. An institution should not run the same review 500 models wide — the species-accumulation curve makes that nearly worthless. It should weak-scale the scope: more artefacts, more defect classes per artefact, deeper falsifier construction, more independent falsifier re-executions. The design consequence is that the resource-scaling axis should be problem size, not panel width, and the harness should expose scope as a first-class dial.

techniques.name: Universal Scalability Law (Amdahl plus a coherency term)
techniques.source: N. J. Gunther, Guerrilla Capacity Planning / "How to Quantify Scalability", Performance Dynamics. https://www.perfdynamics.com/Manifesto/USLscalability.html (formal treatment and fitting procedure: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/usl/vignettes/usl.pdf)
techniques.what_it_does: Speedup(n) = n / (1 + alpha(n-1) + beta*n(n-1)). The contention term alpha grows linearly and the coherency term beta grows quadratically, so beyond some n throughput goes RETROGRADE — adding workers makes the system slower in absolute terms. Reduces to Amdahl when beta = 0.
techniques.assumption: Reconciliation cost between workers is genuinely pairwise, i.e. O(n^2).
techniques.why: CDSFL has a concrete quadratic term: reconciling N models' finding sets against each other is pairwise matching, which is exactly the coherency mechanism. So the harness has a predicted retrograde region, and it is falsifiable from run data by fitting alpha and beta. The adaptation is that the quadratic is a design choice rather than a law — keying every finding to its executed falsifier gives a canonical index and drops reconciliation to O(N). Corroborating evidence: Mieczkowski et al. measured O(n^2) message growth in decentralised LLM teams versus O(n) with a coordinator, and their self-coordinating teams achieved median speedup 0.88x — slower than a single agent — versus 1.36x for pre-assigned teams, with median 19 failed tests versus 4.

techniques.name: Work-stealing with overdecomposition
techniques.source: R. D. Blumofe and C. E. Leiserson, "Scheduling Multithreaded Computations by Work Stealing", JACM 46(5), 1999 (Cilk). https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/324133.324234
techniques.what_it_does: Decompose the problem into far more units than there are workers, then let idle workers steal units from busy ones. Achieves T_1/P + O(T_infinity) expected time without knowing unit costs in advance, and is existentially optimal to within a constant factor.
techniques.assumption: Units are independently executable, cheap to migrate, and the dependency structure is strict (a unit's results are needed only by its parent).
techniques.why: This is the mechanism that answers the varying-deployment question, and it is the reason to prefer it over static assignment. If review is decomposed into a fixed, deployment-independent set of review-units, the same protocol runs on one model (units executed sequentially) and on five hundred (units executed concurrently), with the artefact of record identical and comparable across both. The adaptation: review units are not fully independent — a finding in one unit changes what counts as a finding in another — so the strictness assumption is violated and cross-unit disclosure has to be handled explicitly at round boundaries.

techniques.name: Cube-and-conquer: overdecomposition with a cost-balancing cutoff heuristic
techniques.source: M. J. H. Heule, O. Kullmann, S. Wieringa, A. Biere, "Cube and Conquer: Guiding CDCL SAT Solvers by Lookaheads", HVC 2011. https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~marijn/publications/cube.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Partitions a problem into thousands to millions of subproblems (583 to 493,870 cubes in their benchmark table, run on at most 12 cores), then solves them independently. The cutoff heuristic is chosen so that (1) subproblem costs are comparable and (2) the sum of subproblem costs does not exceed the cost of solving the whole problem. In one case a partition gave maximal per-job time of 5 seconds, "enabling trivial optimal parallelization with more than 2000 processors".
techniques.assumption: A partition axis exists along which subproblems are genuinely separable, and the partitioning step itself is cheap relative to solving.
techniques.why: Two things transfer cleanly. First, the number of partitions is decoupled from the number of workers by orders of magnitude — this is precisely the structural answer to deployments varying by orders of magnitude, and it is more useful than any rule for choosing N. Second, condition (2) is a falsifiable acceptance test for any proposed partition axis of a STEM artefact: if the total review effort across partitions exceeds the effort of reviewing the whole, that axis is illegitimate and should be rejected. CDSFL can run that test directly. Note the paper also documents retrograde behaviour: one instance solved in 2,632 seconds on ONE core, roughly half the 12-core wall time.

techniques.name: Portfolio versus divide-and-conquer: the objective determines which one scales
techniques.source: Heule et al. 2011 (above); I. P. Gent et al., "A Review of Literature on Parallel Constraint Solving", arXiv:1803.10981, 2018. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.10981 — which also reports Caniou et al. 2015 (near-linear multi-walk scaling to 8,192 cores), Lai and Sahni 1984 (parallel branch-and-bound anomalies including absolute slowdown), and McCreesh and Prosser 2015.
techniques.what_it_does: Portfolio = every worker attacks the whole problem (replication); the system finishes when the FASTEST finishes. Heule et al. state plainly that portfolios "mostly exploit the lack of robustness of SAT solvers" — they monetise variance, not aggregation, and therefore hit diminishing returns quickly. Divide-and-conquer partitions the search space and scales to thousands of cores. Crucially, Gent et al. report that pure replication (multi-walk) gave almost linear improvement up to 8,192 cores — but for time-to-first-solution.
techniques.assumption: For portfolios: worker runtimes are high-variance and heavy-tailed, and the objective is a MINIMUM over workers. For divide-and-conquer: the space admits balanced partition.
techniques.why: This is the crispest principled switching rule available, and it is about the OBJECTIVE rather than about N. If the objective is a minimum statistic (time to find any counterexample, first falsification of a specific claim), replication with diversity scales beautifully and far. If the objective is a union/coverage statistic (find all defects, satisfy a convergence gate over the finding set), replication follows the species-accumulation curve and partition is the only thing that scales. CDSFL's convergence gate is a coverage objective, which places it on the partition side — but nobody has published the crossover for a coverage objective, so the rule transfers as a diagnosis, not as a formula. Gent et al. also report that the interaction between search order and work splitting matters more than load balance, i.e. the choice of partition axis dominates effort balancing.

techniques.name: Defect-based (scenario) reading: partition the QUESTION, replicate the ARTEFACT
techniques.source: A. A. Porter, L. G. Votta, V. R. Basili, "Comparing Detection Methods for Software Requirements Inspections: A Replicated Experiment", IEEE TSE 21(6):563–575, 1995. https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/32.391380 ; summarised with the reading-family taxonomy in V. Basili, G. Caldiera, F. Lanubile, F. Shull, "Studies on Reading Techniques", UMD. https://www.cs.umd.edu/users/basili/publications/technical/T114.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Each reviewer reads the whole document but is given a distinct procedural scenario targeting one defect class (data-type inconsistency, incorrect function, ambiguity/omission). Results across two replications with 48 graduate subjects: defect-based readers performed significantly better than ad hoc and checklist readers; they focused on their assigned fault classes but "were no less effective at detecting other faults"; checklist reading was no more effective than ad hoc; and collection meetings produced no net improvement in fault detection rate.
techniques.assumption: Defect classes are enumerable in advance, are roughly disjoint, and a per-class procedure can be written that actually changes what the reviewer attends to.
techniques.why: This is the only positive partition-beats-undifferentiated-replication result I found for defect detection, and its SHAPE is the important part: the artefact is replicated (everyone sees all of it) while the analysis is partitioned. That preserves detection of cross-cutting defects, which partitioning by module or file would destroy. For CDSFL this maps to assigning each model a distinct falsifier class rather than a distinct region of the artefact. Two adaptations needed: the class taxonomy has to be built for STEM artefacts rather than requirements documents, and the finding that focused readers lost nothing on other classes is a single experiment family and should be re-tested, not assumed.

techniques.name: Perspective-based reading (partition by stakeholder role)
techniques.source: B. Regnell, P. Runeson, T. Thelin, "Are the Perspectives Really Different? Further Experimentation on Scenario-Based Reading of Requirements", Empirical Software Engineering 5(4), 2000. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1009848320066 ; M. Ciolkowski, "What do we know about perspective-based reading? An approach for quantitative aggregation in software engineering", ESEM 2009. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/ESEM.2009.5316026 ; original positive results in Basili et al. (above)
techniques.what_it_does: Assigns reviewers distinct stakeholder perspectives (designer, tester, user) on the assumption that different perspectives find different defects and their union covers more.
techniques.assumption: The perspectives genuinely induce different defect profiles.
techniques.why: The founding assumption was tested and did not hold. Regnell, Runeson and Thelin found no significant difference in the defect coverage of the three perspectives, and reported a simulation showing 30 subjects would have sufficed to detect such a difference had it existed — so this is a reasonably powered null, not an underpowered one. Ciolkowski's quantitative meta-aggregation found PBR no better than ad hoc for requirements documents and LESS effective than checklists as a way of structuring inspections. Assigning CDSFL models different 'roles' or personas is the direct analogue and should be expected to fail for the same reason: a role label does not change what the reviewer can actually see. Partition on the defect/falsifier class, which has evidence, not on the persona, which does not.

techniques.name: Controlled team-size experiments: the empirical knee is at two reviewers
techniques.source: A. Porter, H. Siy, A. Mockus, L. Votta, "Understanding the Sources of Variation in Software Inspections", ACM TOSEM 7(1):41–79, 1998. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/268411.268421 ; P. C. Rigby and C. Bird, "Convergent Contemporary Software Peer Review Practices", ESEC/FSE 2013. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/rigby2013convergent.pdf ; C. Sauer, D. R. Jeffery, L. Land, P. Yetton, "The Effectiveness of Software Development Technical Reviews: A Behaviorally Motivated Program of Research", IEEE TSE 26(1), 2000. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/32.825763
techniques.what_it_does: Porter et al. varied team size and the number and sequencing of sessions in a controlled industrial experiment: the changes did not significantly influence defect detection rate, but some combinations dramatically increased inspection interval. Rigby and Bird measured Google (Android, Chrome), Microsoft (Bing, Office, SQL), AMD and six OSS projects: median number of active reviewers is two everywhere despite three or four being invited; "two reviewers discovered as many defects as four"; Buck found no difference between teams of three, four and five; and there was "only a minimal increase in the number of comments" with more active reviewers and no increase in the number of rounds. Sauer et al. conclude individual task expertise is the primary driver of review performance.
techniques.assumption: Reviewers are drawn from a comparable competence pool and the artefact is of a scale one reviewer can hold.
techniques.why: This is a convergent multi-decade result across controlled experiments and large-scale industrial telemetry, and it points squarely against the instinct to widen the panel. It sets an informative prior: the five-seat setup is already past the knee for undifferentiated replication, and the marginal seat should be spent on the RIGHT reviewer for the sub-problem, not on another reviewer. Sauer's expertise-dominance finding is also the correct diagnosis of the routing-ladder failure: the escalation axis should be per-defect-class competence, not a single 'stronger model' chain, which has no support in this literature and which by construction has a top.

techniques.name: N-fold inspection (replication with N independent teams) and its cost-optimal-N model
techniques.source: J. Martin and W. T. Tsai, "N-Fold Inspection: A Requirements Analysis Technique", Communications of the ACM 33(2), 1990. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/75577.75587 ; performance model in "The performance of the N-fold requirement inspection method", Requirements Engineering journal. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02802773
techniques.what_it_does: Nine independent teams inspect the same requirements document. Different teams detect different faults, so the union achieves a higher fault detection ratio than any team. The follow-up paper gives a simple probabilistic model predicting fault detection ratio as a function of inspector expertise and number of teams, and derives from it the most cost-effective number of teams.
techniques.assumption: Teams are genuinely independent, and fault detection ratio against a known ground-truth fault list is measurable.
techniques.why: This is the closest published precedent for what CDSFL does now — deliberate replication across independent reviewers of one artefact — and the cost-optimal-N model is the shape of answer Question 1 wants. But the model is parameterised by expertise and team count fitted to observed overlap, so it cannot be instantiated for CDSFL until finding-identity is fixed. Note also that CDSFL deliberately violates the independence assumption: cross-disclosure between rounds is a design feature, so any N-fold-style estimate must be computed on round-1 output only, before models see each other's findings.

techniques.name: Capture-recapture defect content estimation (Mh-JK) as an operational continue/stop rule
techniques.source: S. G. Eick, C. R. Loader, M. D. Long, L. G. Votta, S. Vander Wiel, "Estimating Software Fault Content Before Coding", ICSE 1992; comprehensively reviewed in H. Petersson, T. Thelin, P. Runeson, C. Wohlin, "Capture-Recapture in Software Inspections after 10 Years Research: Theory, Evaluation and Application", Journal of Systems and Software, 2004. https://wohlin.eu/jss04-1.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Uses the overlap between reviewers' fault sets to estimate remaining fault content, then drives an explicit decision: A1 send the artefact back as not ready, A2 hold a meeting, A3 assign additional reviewers, A4 continue without a meeting. The review's consolidated findings: most estimators underestimate; Mh-JK is the best estimator for software inspections; Mh-JK is appropriate for four reviewers or more and is non-robust with two; DPM is the best curve-fitting alternative. The core intuition is stated directly — "if the overlap is large, few faults are left to be detected; if the overlap is small, many faults are undetected".
techniques.assumption: Three conditions the paper names explicitly: reviewers have equal detection ability (relaxed by Mt), reviewers work independently, and faults are equally difficult to discover (relaxed by Mh; the recommended fix for heterogeneity is to stratify faults into groups and estimate each group separately).
techniques.why: This is the most operationally complete answer to Question 1 in the literature — it is not just an estimator, it is a decision procedure with 'assign additional reviewers' as an explicit branch. Three adaptations are mandatory. First, it cannot run at all until finding-identity is fixed; the paper itself flags this, recommending re-estimation after the meeting with false positives removed and "an improved perception of which faults noted by the reviewers should be viewed as being identical". Second, independence is violated by design in CDSFL's round structure, so estimate on pre-disclosure output only. Third, stratify by falsifier class, which is the paper's own recommended remedy for heterogeneous detectability and which CDSFL is unusually well placed to do.

techniques.name: Species-discovery estimators with an executable oracle: Good-Turing and Chao1 (STADS)
techniques.source: M. Böhme, "STADS: Software Testing as Species Discovery", ACM TOSEM 27(2), Article 7, 2018. https://doi.org/10.1145/3210309 ; underlying estimators from Good 1953 and Chao 1984/1987.
techniques.what_it_does: Treats each discovered behaviour as a species. Good-Turing gives the discovery probability U(n) = f1/n — the probability the next sample yields something new, where f1 is the number of singletons. Chao1 estimates total richness as S_obs + f1^2/(2*f2) using singletons and doubletons, and coverage as S_obs/S_hat. Böhme wires these into AFL's status screen as a live residual-risk readout.
techniques.assumption: Species relative abundances do not change substantially during the campaign, and samples are exchangeable draws from one distribution.
techniques.why: This is the best-fitting stopping rule available AND it comes from the only mature field whose ground truth, like CDSFL's, is an executed oracle rather than a label — that is exactly the property that makes it worth adapting rather than the label-based alternatives. The stopping rule is directly implementable: stop asking when U(n) falls below the cost threshold. Two adaptations. First, exchangeability fails for heterogeneous models — each model is a different sampling distribution — so the correct form is multi-list capture-recapture (Mh/Mth), not single-list Good-Turing. Second, running the estimators on CDSFL's current numbers is itself the diagnostic that exposes the matching defect: with f1=2048 and f2=2, Chao1 returns roughly 1.05 million latent findings and Good-Turing returns a ~99.8% chance the next report is new, which is not a credible description of a STEM artefact.

techniques.name: The exponential-cost law for discovery under an executable oracle
techniques.source: M. Böhme and B. Falk, "Fuzzing: On the Exponential Cost of Vulnerability Discovery", ESEC/FSE 2020. https://mboehme.github.io/paper/FSE20.EmpiricalLaw.pdf (DOI https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3368089.3409729 ; data at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.11911287)
techniques.what_it_does: From over four CPU-years across nearly three hundred open-source programs: finding the SAME bugs linearly faster requires linearly more machines, but finding linearly MORE bugs in the same time requires exponentially more machines (R^2 = 97.26% on the reported fit). The mechanism is the species-accumulation curve S(n) = sum_i [1 - (1-p_i)^n] under a power-law abundance distribution: individual exponential discovery curves sum to an approximately linear aggregate. Section 6.1 reports separately that running 32 greybox fuzzers in parallel WITHOUT a shared global queue "does not scale much better than running 32 blackbox fuzzers in parallel".
techniques.assumption: Stated explicitly and unusually honestly by the authors: the law is contingent on species probabilities following roughly a power law. It does NOT hold if all species are equally likely, or if only one species remains undiscovered.
techniques.why: This is the sharpest available answer to Question 1 and its transfer condition is testable on CDSFL's own data rather than assumed — fit the finding-detectability distribution and check for power-law shape. If it holds, the marginal-value question has a quantitative answer: each additional finding costs roughly a doubling of panel resource, which makes wide replication indefensible and forces the partition or weak-scaling route. The sharing result is arguably more actionable still: it says cross-disclosure between models dominates panel width, which validates CDSFL's round structure as the load-bearing mechanism and suggests spending marginal effort on disclosure quality rather than seats. Their methodological prescription also transfers directly: compare configurations by time to find the SAME findings, not by findings found in a fixed budget, because a small increase in the latter hides an exponential cost.

techniques.name: The evaluator effect and the variability of the matching process
techniques.source: M. Hertzum and N. E.
