Jacobsen, "The Evaluator Effect: A Chilling Fact About Usability Evaluation Methods", International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction 15(1), 2003. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1207/S15327590IJHC1501_14 ; M. Hertzum et al., "Revisiting the Evaluator Effect in Usability Tests", Behaviour & Information Technology, 2014. https://mortenhertzum.dk/publ/BIT2014.pdf ; K. Hornbæk and E. Frøkjær, "Comparison of techniques for matching of usability problem descriptions", Interacting with Computers 20(6):505–514, 2008. https://academic.oup.com/iwc/article-abstract/20/6/505/667956
techniques.what_it_does: Defines any-two agreement — problems found by both of a pair divided by problems found by either, averaged over pairs — as the standard overlap metric, precisely because raw detection rate inflates agreement when there are few evaluators. Reported values across the literature: 42% (four evaluators), 42% (50 evaluators), 53%, 61%, 64%, 64%, 69%, 81%; the 2003 review spans 5% to 65%. Hornbæk and Frøkjær had 52 evaluators match the same set of problem descriptions and found that a substantial share of apparent disagreement came from the MATCHING process itself, concluding it "may be as variable as the evaluator effect itself".
techniques.assumption: Problem descriptions are natural-language and matched by human judgement — which is exactly the condition CDSFL does not have to accept.
techniques.why: This is the diagnostic instrument for the 2/2050 problem and it should be adopted immediately. First, any-two agreement is the right metric and CDSFL should report it rather than a raw co-discovery count, because the raw count is not comparable across panel sizes. Second, it supplies the literature baseline — 5% to 65%, typically ~40% — against which 0.098% is roughly two to three orders of magnitude low, which is the quantitative basis for treating it as a measurement artefact. Third, Hornbæk and Frøkjær identify the exact failure mode. And CDSFL has an escape the HCI field does not: two findings can be declared identical iff the same executed falsifier discriminates them, converting a subjective matching problem into a mechanical one. That is a genuine methodological advantage worth exploiting and worth writing up.

techniques.name: Constructive diversity plus finding-sharing (ensemble fuzzing)
techniques.source: Y. Chen, Y. Jiang, F. Ma, J. Liang, M. Wang, C. Zhou, X. Jiao, Z. Su, "EnFuzz: Ensemble Fuzzing with Seed Synchronization among Diverse Fuzzers", USENIX Security 2019. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity19/presentation/chen-yuanliang (preprint https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.00182)
techniques.what_it_does: Defines base-worker diversity by three CONSTRUCTIVE heuristics — diversity of coverage-information granularity, of input generation strategy, and of seed selection and mutation strategy — then selects maximally diverse workers on those axes and couples them with a globally-asynchronous locally-synchronous shared seed pool. Against six base fuzzers it found 66.7% to 140% more unique bugs. It explicitly frames a conventional parallel mode as ensemble fuzzing with identical workers, which "lack diversity when using the same fuzzing strategy".
techniques.assumption: The mechanistic axes chosen actually induce different search behaviour, and workers can share intermediate artefacts cheaply.
techniques.why: It is the closest working system to what CDSFL is: heterogeneous workers, executable ground truth, shared intermediate findings. The transferable lesson for Question 3 is deflationary but important — in the one place this is made to work in production, diversity is ASSERTED BY CONSTRUCTION on named mechanistic axes, not measured by a statistic. For CDSFL the analogous axes would be training lineage, tool access, and falsifier-construction strategy. It does not answer how to trade diversity against cost quantitatively; nobody in this line does.

techniques.name: Effective-channel bound on multi-agent scaling
techniques.source: Y. Yang, C. Qu, M. Wen, L. Shi, Y. Wen, W. Zhang, S. Gu, "Understanding Agent Scaling in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems via Diversity", arXiv:2602.03794, February 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03794
techniques.what_it_does: Shows empirically that homogeneous agent scaling saturates quickly while heterogeneous scaling (different models, prompts, tools) keeps paying, then formalises why: system performance is bounded by intrinsic task uncertainty, I_MAS(n) <= H(Y|X), and residual uncertainty decays as (1-alpha)^K <= e^{-alpha*K} in the number of EFFECTIVE CHANNELS K, not the number of agents. Homogeneous agents saturate because K stops growing.
techniques.assumption: A well-defined target Y with finite conditional entropy H(Y|X), and evidence that can be treated as information channels about that target.
techniques.why: The conceptual reframe is right and useful for Question 3 — count effective independent channels, not seats, and treat the complementarity rate alpha as the quantity worth measuring. But the transfer is weaker than it first appears and should not be oversold: their bound is on INFERRING a target with bounded entropy from a label, whereas CDSFL's target is an open-ended defect set whose entropy is unknown and whose ground truth comes from execution rather than inference. They also give no estimator for K or alpha in practice, so this supplies vocabulary and a saturation argument, not a usable rule.

techniques.name: MapReduce and BSP (bulk-synchronous parallel)
techniques.source: L. G. Valiant, "A Bridging Model for Parallel Computation", CACM 33(8):103–111, 1990, DOI 10.1145/79173.79181, https://dblp.org/rec/journals/cacm/Valiant90.html ; J. Dean and S. Ghemawat, "MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters", OSDI 2004, https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi-04/mapreduce-simplified-data-processing-large-clusters
techniques.what_it_does: BSP structures computation as supersteps separated by global barriers; MapReduce assigns work by a static key-to-worker map with a shuffle between phases.
techniques.assumption: The decomposition is known before execution (the key function is static), work per key is roughly predictable, and a global barrier per superstep is affordable.
techniques.why: Both assumptions fail at the point that matters. CDSFL's decomposition is data-dependent — you cannot know which part of an artefact hides the hard finding until a model has looked — so there is no static key function to write, and this is precisely the irregular case that motivated amorphous data-parallelism (Pingali et al., PLDI 2011, https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~pingali/CS377P/2024fa/papers/tao.pdf). The barrier is worse than useless here: it makes the slowest model set every round's duration, which is the straggler problem with no remedy on offer beyond speculative re-execution. Work-stealing over an overdecomposed unit set is the correct primitive instead. Adopting a MapReduce shape would hard-code the very assumption — that you can partition before you look — that makes review hard.

techniques.name: Redundancy for label aggregation: sampling-and-voting, majority vote, Dawid-Skene-style crowdsourcing
techniques.source: J. Li, Q. Zhang, Y. Yu, Q. Fu, D. Ye, "More Agents Is All You Need", arXiv:2402.05120, 2024. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.05120 (reports optimal ensemble sizes of roughly 10–40 with marginal returns diminishing beyond); multi-agent debate results converging on plateaus at 2–3 rounds and 2–4 agents
techniques.what_it_does: Queries N workers on the same question and aggregates by voting to raise accuracy above any individual worker's.
techniques.assumption: THE critical one: there is no oracle. Ground truth must be manufactured from noisy worker outputs, so redundancy buys accuracy.
techniques.why: Stating this plainly because it is the largest and most superficially attractive body of work in reach, and importing its N-selection formulas would be a category error. CDSFL's ground truth comes from a tool re-executing a supplied falsifier. A finding is confirmed or it is not, and a second model agreeing adds nothing to that determination — CDSFL has already codified this as findings never being confirmed by model vote. Consequently redundancy in CDSFL buys RECALL ONLY, never accuracy, and every 'optimal number of voters' result in this literature is optimising a quantity CDSFL does not need to buy. The correct family for a recall-only objective is the species/coverage family above, not the voting family.

techniques.name: Ensemble diversity measures
techniques.source: L. I. Kuncheva and C. J. Whitaker, "Measures of Diversity in Classifier Ensembles and Their Relationship with the Ensemble Accuracy", Machine Learning 51(2):181–207, 2003. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1023/A:1022859003006
techniques.what_it_does: Systematically evaluates ten diversity statistics over binary classifier outputs — four averaged pairwise (Q statistic, correlation, disagreement, double-fault) and six non-pairwise (vote entropy, difficulty index, Kohavi-Wolpert variance, interrater agreement, generalised diversity, coincident failure diversity) — against ensemble accuracy.
techniques.assumption: Workers emit comparable outputs on a common labelled instance set, so pairwise agreement is computable.
techniques.why: Worth naming precisely because it looks like the answer to Question 3 and is not. The paper's own conclusion is that large diversity may not correspond to better ensemble results and that it raises doubts about the usefulness of diversity measures for actually building ensembles. Beyond that, every one of the ten statistics needs a common instance set with per-instance agreement — which CDSFL does not have, because reviewers emit open-ended findings rather than labels on shared instances, and because the identity relation between findings is the very thing that is broken. Adopting any of these measures now would produce a number with no defensible meaning.

transfers: The diagnosis of the 2/2050 figure, which is the highest-value item here and blocks everything else. Any-two agreement between human experts on the same artefact runs 5–65% (typically ~40%); a simulation of five reviewers with mean per-finding detection probability as low as 0.0025 still yields ~19% co-discovery. Two independent methods agree that 0.098% co-discovery implies a latent pool of ~841,000 findings with each model detecting ~0.049% of it: Chao's multi-list estimator gives 840,911 and numerical inversion of the binomial co-discovery identity gives 841,328 (per-model p = 4.878e-4, matching to six significant figures; verified in SciPy and independently in Wolfram Language). That is not a credible description of a STEM artefact, so the finding-identity/matching function is the defect. Hornbæk and Frøkjær measured exactly this failure mode in 52 evaluators and concluded the matching process is as variable as the effect it purports to measure.

The consequence of that diagnosis: capture-recapture, Good-Turing, Chao1, submodular coverage and USL calibration ALL take overlap as their primary input, so none can be run on the current records. Fixing finding-identity is a prerequisite, not an improvement — and CDSFL has an escape the HCI and inspection literatures do not, because two findings can be declared identical iff the same executed falsifier discriminates them, converting a subjective matching problem into a mechanical one.

Work-span analysis as the ceiling on panel width: useful reviewer count is capped by parallelism (total work / round depth), and Rigby and Bird's industrial telemetry independently confirms the mechanism by showing that more reviewers produced no reduction in the number of review rounds.

Gustafson's weak-scaling reframe as the answer to the institutional case: with effectively unlimited models, scale the SCOPE (more artefacts, more defect classes, deeper falsifiers, more independent re-executions) rather than the panel width. This is the only classical scaling law that transfers without distortion.

Overdecomposition as the answer to deployments varying by orders of magnitude: decouple the number of review units from the number of models, exactly as cube-and-conquer generates hundreds of thousands of cubes for twelve cores. The same protocol then runs on one model sequentially and five hundred concurrently, producing comparable artefacts of record. This is more useful than any rule for choosing N.

Cube-and-conquer's cutoff condition (2) as a falsifiable acceptance test for any proposed partition axis: if the summed review effort across partitions exceeds the effort of reviewing the whole artefact, the axis is illegitimate. CDSFL can run this test directly.

The objective-based switching rule: replication scales far for MINIMUM statistics (time to first counterexample — near-linear to 8,192 workers in the multi-walk case) and poorly for UNION/COVERAGE statistics, where it follows the species-accumulation curve. CDSFL's convergence gate is a coverage objective, which places it on the partition side.

Partition the QUESTION, replicate the ARTEFACT — the shape of the one positive partition result (defect-based reading). Assign each model a distinct falsifier class while every model still sees the whole artefact, so cross-cutting findings survive. Partitioning by module or file would destroy them.

Böhme and Falk's sharing result: 32 greybox fuzzers without a shared queue scaled no better than 32 blackbox fuzzers. Cross-disclosure between workers dominates worker count, which validates CDSFL's round structure as the load-bearing mechanism and argues for spending marginal effort on disclosure quality rather than seats.

Böhme and Falk's methodological prescription: compare configurations by time to find the SAME findings, not by findings found within a fixed budget, because a small increase in the latter conceals an exponential cost. This should govern how CDSFL benchmarks panel configurations.

Sauer et al.'s expertise-dominance finding as the correct diagnosis of the routing-ladder failure: escalate on per-defect-class competence, not on a single 'stronger model' chain. A total order over models is not a thing the literature supports, and by construction it has a top — which is exactly the failure being observed.
Any-two agreement as the metric to report instead of a raw co-discovery count, since raw counts are not comparable across panel sizes — the reason the HCI field adopted it in the first place.

The prior that two reviewers is the empirical knee for undifferentiated replication, convergent across a controlled TOSEM experiment, Google/Microsoft/AMD/OSS telemetry, and Buck's three-versus-four-versus-five comparison. The current five-seat panel is already past it.
does_not_transfer: Redundancy-for-accuracy in all its forms — sampling-and-voting, majority vote, multi-agent debate agent counts, Dawid-Skene-style crowdsourcing inference. These exist to MANUFACTURE ground truth from noisy labels. CDSFL has an oracle, so redundancy buys recall only and never accuracy, and every 'optimal number of voters' result in that literature optimises a quantity CDSFL does not need to buy. This is the largest and most superficially attractive body of work in reach and it should be refused explicitly.

MapReduce and BSP. Both assume the decomposition is known before execution; CDSFL's is data-dependent, so there is no static key function to write. The bulk-synchronous barrier additionally makes the slowest model set every round's duration with no remedy on offer. Adopting this shape would hard-code the assumption that makes review hard.

Amdahl, Gustafson and Brent as models of RECALL. They are statements about time for fixed work. CDSFL's question is coverage for unknown, growing work. Using speedup curves to reason about how many findings a wider panel will produce is the single most likely modelling error available in this area, and the 2026 LLM-teams paper does not license it — that paper measured wall-clock on coding tasks with pre-specified subtask dependencies, not defect recall on an artefact.

Perspective-based / role-based partitioning. The founding assumption was tested by Regnell, Runeson and Thelin and did not hold — no significant difference in defect coverage between perspectives, with a simulation confirming the study had power to detect one — and Ciolkowski's meta-aggregation found PBR no better than ad hoc and worse than checklists. Giving CDSFL models different personas is the direct analogue and should be expected to fail for the same reason: a role label does not change what a reviewer can see.

Ensemble diversity statistics (Q statistic, disagreement, double-fault, Kohavi-Wolpert variance and the rest). Kuncheva and Whitaker's own conclusion doubts their usefulness for building ensembles, and every one of them requires a common labelled instance set with per-instance agreement — which CDSFL does not have, and cannot have until the finding-identity problem is fixed.

Partitioning the artefact by region, module or file. Nothing in the inspection literature supports it, and the one positive partition result works the other way round (replicate the artefact, partition the analysis). Region-partitioning would forfeit cross-cutting findings, which are disproportionately the valuable ones in a STEM artefact.

Portfolio-style scaling as a route to more findings. Heule et al. state plainly that portfolios monetise the LACK OF ROBUSTNESS of individual workers — they exploit variance in time-to-solution. That mechanism produces a minimum statistic, not a larger union, so it does not deliver coverage however many workers are added.
open: The central question is genuinely open and needs invention: there is no empirical study of replicate-versus-partition for defect finding where ground truth is an EXECUTED falsifier. The inspection literature has human judges scored against a seeded or consensus defect list; the fuzzing literature has an executable oracle but homogeneous workers partitioning an input space rather than heterogeneous reviewers partitioning an artefact. CDSFL sits precisely in the gap and could produce the first evidence.

No principled rule exists for switching from replication to partition as a function of worker count for a COVERAGE objective. The parallel-search literature gives the crossover for minimum objectives; the species literature gives the marginal-value curve for replication; nobody has joined them. This is a real gap and a publishable one.

Whether partitioning costs cross-cutting findings has never been measured for review. Cube-and-conquer's condition (2) — that summed sub-problem cost must not exceed whole-problem cost — is the right test and has a direct review analogue, but no one has run it. CDSFL could, cheaply, and the answer would determine whether partition is viable at all.

Deployment-invariant review protocols — one protocol producing comparable artefacts of record on one model and on five hundred — appear nowhere in the literature. Overdecomposition is the right primitive but has not been applied to review.

How to measure diversity and trade it against cost (Question 3) is the weakest-supported of the three questions and needs invention. The ensemble-diversity literature's own verdict on its measures is negative; EnFuzz asserts diversity by construction rather than measuring it; Yang et al. supply the right abstraction (effective channels K and complementarity rate alpha) but no estimator for either. Nothing available produces a defensible diversity number for a heterogeneous model panel.

The 'which reviewer for which sub-problem' half of Question 2 is unsolved. Sauer et al. establish that task expertise dominates review performance, but no one has a per-defect-class competence matrix for language models, and building one requires exactly the co-discovery data the matching defect is currently destroying. The scheduling half (work-stealing over overdecomposed units) is comparatively well covered.

Whether CDSFL's finding-detectability distribution actually follows a power law is unknown and determines whether Böhme and Falk's exponential-cost law applies at all — the authors are explicit that the law fails under equal detectability. This is testable on existing data once matching is fixed, and it should be tested rather than assumed, because it decides whether the marginal-value question has a quantitative answer or not.

Capture-recapture estimators assume reviewer independence, which CDSFL violates deliberately through cross-round disclosure. Estimating on round-1 pre-disclosure output only is the obvious workaround, but nobody has validated capture-recapture for a panel that is independent in round 1 and deliberately coupled thereafter; the estimator's behaviour under that regime is unstudied.

areas.area: Area 6: stopping rules for a defect search whose target population size is unknown — software reliability growth models, mutation adequacy, error seeding / plant-capture estimation, capture-recapture on reviewer overlap, and species-richness (unseen species) estimation from ecology.
areas.summary: There is a large, mature literature on exactly this question, and most of it is NOT the software reliability growth literature you might expect — it is capture-recapture statistics, which was imported into software inspection in 1992 and into fuzzing in 2018. The single most important result for CDSFL is that your seeding experiment and your co-discovery record are the same statistical instrument viewed from two sides, and both are currently unusable, for different reasons. Five seeds, all found, is a degenerate input: the Mills/Petersen estimator returns "zero defects remaining" as an exact point estimate, and the honest 95% bound derived from 5-for-5 is that your panel might be catching as little as 55% of that defect class. Simulation shows that if the plants are even slightly easier to find than real defects — the failure your first catalogue had — the estimator does not merely lose precision, it confidently reports zero remaining with a 95% interval of [0, 0]; there is no amount of statistical machinery that recovers from a non-representative plant, which is why the ecology literature names plant/target exchangeability its single fundamental assumption. On the other side, a co-discovery rate of 2 in 2,050 is not a weak signal but a broken one: fed to Chao2 it implies over a million undiscovered findings and a sample coverage of 0.2%, which is not a credible measurement but a symptom, and the two candidate causes (a finding-matcher that fails to recognise the same defect reported twice, versus a round protocol that shows round-k findings to round-k+1 reviewers and thereby suppresses re-discovery by construction) bias the answer in opposite directions and must be separated by measurement before any estimator is applied. The genuinely good news is that plant-capture is a single-occasion method, so it is the only technique here that works with one model and one vendor — it is the natural backbone for your smallest deployment — and Böhme's STADS framework plus the Bron et al. technology-assisted-review work give you tested, off-the-shelf machinery for the residual-risk and stopping-rule half. The genuinely bad news is that your ground truth coming from executing a falsifier does not rescue you here: it makes each individual finding sound, but every estimator in this literature needs a reliable answer to "are these two findings the same finding", and nothing published handles estimator behaviour when that species-identity function is itself noisy.

techniques.name: Mills error seeding, formalised as plant-capture
techniques.source: H.D. Mills, "On the Statistical Validation of Computer Programs", IBM Federal Systems Division report FSC-72-6015, 1972; J.W. Duran & J.J. Wiorkowski, "Capture-Recapture Sampling for Estimating Software Error Content", IEEE TSE SE-7(1):147-148, 1981, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1702812 ; E.M. Laska & M. Meisner, plant-capture, as reviewed in Y. Wang, M. Lysy & A. Béliveau, "Plant-Capture Methods for Estimating Population Size from Uncertain Plant Captures", arXiv:2403.04058, 2024, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.04058
techniques.what_it_does: Seed M known defects into the target, run the review, count how many seeds were found (R) alongside real findings (n). Estimate the real population as N_hat = n*M/R (Petersen), or the bias-corrected Chapman form (M+1)(n+R+1)/(R+1)-1. Remaining = N_hat - n. Crucially it is a SINGLE-occasion method: it needs one reviewer, not several, so it is the only technique in this whole area that works for the solo-researcher-with-one-model deployment.
techniques.assumption: The fundamental assumption, named as such in the plant-capture literature (their Assumption 2): plants and real defects have the same detection probability, and plants are indistinguishable from real defects during review. Secondary: closed population, and every seed's capture status known with certainty.
techniques.why: You are already running the mechanism (bench/canary_seeding.py computes p_hat = catches/k per model per domain on a held-out split, with a two-generator requirement and repo-exclusion guards — the hard engineering is done). What is missing is the estimator that converts p_hat into a statement about the unfound population, and the stratification that makes it valid. I computed what your current run gives: with 5 seeds and 5 found, Petersen and Chapman both return exactly zero remaining regardless of how many real findings you have, because R/M = 1. That is not a measurement, it is an arithmetic identity. The exact 95% one-sided lower bound on detection probability from 5-of-5 is 0.549 (verified two ways: closed form 0.05^(1/5) and Clopper-Pearson beta.ppf(0.05,5,1) = 0.549280), so your data are consistent with the panel missing 45% of that defect class. Monte Carlo (100 real defects, p=0.6, true remaining 40) gives 95% intervals for the remaining count of [0, 252] at M=5, [21, 71] at M=50, [26, 61] at M=100, [31, 51] at M=400 and [32, 49] at M=1000 — so a POINT ESTIMATE at the ±20% accuracy bar the inspection literature uses needs on the order of a thousand seeds, and even 5,000 only reaches ±17% because the binomial noise on the real findings becomes the floor. But a DECISION gate is far cheaper: for the question "is residual ≤ 10% of found?", ~10 seeds already decides correctly 99% of the time in the keep-going direction, and ~50 seeds reaches 90% and ~100 seeds 97% in the safe-to-stop direction. Use it as a gate, not as an estimate, and budget roughly 50-100 held-out seeds PER DEFECT CLASS.

techniques.name: Stratified (class-based) plant-capture for heterogeneous detectability
techniques.source: Wang, Lysy & Béliveau, arXiv:2403.04058, 2024, §2.3 "Incorporating Heterogeneity Between Sites (Model M_class)", https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.04058
techniques.what_it_does: When capture probability differs across strata (their case: survey sites), fit the plant-capture model within class and aggregate, rather than assuming one global detection probability.
techniques.assumption: Within each class, plants and targets are exchangeable. Classes must be defined a priori, not chosen after seeing which seeds were found.
techniques.why: This is the fix for your catalogue-1 failure, and it is the right shape rather than a patch. Your plants sitting next to docstrings that state the invariant they break did not make the estimator noisy — I simulated it, and the damage is categorical. With plant detection p=1.0 against real-defect detection p=0.6, the Mills estimator's 95% interval for remaining defects is [0.0, 0.0] with a median of 0.0 against a true value of 40: it is confidently, silently wrong in the reassuring direction. At p_seed=0.9 vs p_real=0.5 it reports a median of 5.3 remaining against a true 50. Stratifying by defect class does not fix a plant that is easier than everything in its own class; it fixes the case where your catalogue over-represents easy classes. Both problems are real and they need different remedies: exchangeability WITHIN class is bought by construction discipline (seed into a history-free copy, strip the adjacent invariant statement, use multiple generators — you already require two), and representativeness ACROSS classes is bought by stratification.

techniques.name: Capture-recapture on reviewer overlap (Mh-JK and the M0/Mt/Mh/Mth model family)
techniques.source: S.G. Eick, C.R. Loader, M.D. Long, L.G. Votta & S. Vander Wiel, "Estimating Software Fault Content Before Coding", ICSE 1992, pp.59-65; L. Briand, K. El Emam & B. Freimut, "A Comprehensive Evaluation of Capture-Recapture Models for Estimating Software Defect Content", IEEE TSE 26(6):518-540, 2000, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/852741/ ; H. Petersson, T. Thelin, P. Runeson & C. Wohlin, "Capture-recapture in Software Inspections after 10 Years Research", J. Systems and Software 72(2):249-264, 2004, full text at https://wohlin.eu/jss04-1.pdf ; K.P. Burnham & W.S. Overton, Biometrika 65:625-633, 1978 (jackknife); A. Chao, Biometrics 43:783-791, 1987
techniques.what_it_does: Uses the OVERLAP between what different reviewers found to estimate what nobody found. Four models: M0 (all defects equally findable, all reviewers equally able), Mt (reviewers differ), Mh (defects differ in findability), Mth (both). The ten-year survey's settled conclusion is that Mh with the second-order jackknife estimator (Mh-JK) is the best for software inspections, that most estimators underestimate, and that Mh-JK is appropriate for FOUR reviewers or more.
techniques.assumption: Reviewers work independently and in parallel — the survey is explicit that fault searching "has to be performed before, and not during, an inspection meeting". Closed population. Some overlap must exist: with zero overlap no estimate is produced at all (the survey lists "Failure Rate — the rate of cases for which no estimate is produced" as a standard evaluation measure).
techniques.why: This is the technique that would directly answer "when does asking another model stop paying", and it is the one your instrumentation currently cannot feed. Two of 2,050 is below the floor. Reading that as 2,048 singletons and 2 doubletons, Chao2 gives 2050 + 2048²/4 = 1,050,626 total findings, i.e. at least 1,048,576 undiscovered and a maximum sample coverage of 0.195% (computed in numpy, cross-checked in sympy). Sensitivity: you need roughly 10% co-discovery to get to 20% estimated coverage, 30% to reach 55%, 50% to reach 80%. No credible artefact has a million defects, so the number is diagnosing your pipeline, not the target. Two candidate causes push in OPPOSITE directions and must be separated before anything else is done. (a) The matcher fails to recognise that two models reported the same defect — this inflates singletons and makes the artefact look far worse than it is. (b) Your round protocol shows round-k findings to round-k+1 reviewers, which removes those defects from the sampling frame by construction and suppresses re-discovery — this is a violation of the constant-abundance assumption in exactly the direction that destroys overlap. Cheap falsification test: compute co-discovery within ROUND 1 ONLY, where models are blind to each other, and compare it to the cross-round figure. If round-1 co-discovery is materially above 0.1%, cause (b) dominates and the 2/2050 headline is an artefact of the protocol rather than a fact about model diversity. If it is still near zero, the matcher is the problem. Note also Scott & Wohlin's industrial pre-study (https://www.wohlin.eu/esem08-1.pdf) hit precisely your situation: three testers handed in results with no overlap at all, and "the pre-study could not produce an estimate since some overlap is a prerequisite". Their main study used a human MEETING to build the overlap matrix — the matching step you have automated is the step they judged needed people.

techniques.name: STADS: software testing as species discovery (Chao1/Chao2, Good-Turing discovery probability, extrapolation)
techniques.source: M. Böhme, "STADS: Software Testing as Species Discovery", ACM TOSEM 27(2), 2018, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.02130 ; underlying estimators A. Chao 1987/1989, Chao, Lee & Jeng, Biometrics 48:201-216, 1992; I.J. Good 1953 (Good-Turing)
techniques.what_it_does: Recasts a testing campaign as ecological sampling. Gives you three things you want: (i) residual risk — Good-Turing U_hat(n) = f1/n, the probability the next sample discovers something new, PROVED to be an upper bound on the probability that an undiscovered error exists; (ii) campaign completeness — S_obs / Chao1, reported as a percentage with an explicit decision table (<95% incomplete, <98% decide on other factors, ≥98% nearly complete); (iii) extrapolation — for incidence data (one sample yielding multiple findings, which is your case), S_hat(n+m*) = S(n) + Q0_hat[1 - (1 - Q1/V)^m*], i.e. how many more reviewer-rounds to discover a given fraction more.
techniques.assumption: Relative species abundances must not change substantially during the campaign. Chao1/Chao2 are LOWER bounds on richness (so coverage is an UPPER bound) and are unbiased point estimators only when undetected and singleton species have approximately equal detection probability. The Bernoulli product / incidence model is the correct one when a single sample yields several findings.
techniques.why: The Bernoulli product model in §7 is a precise structural match: one reviewer pass yields many findings, exactly as one ecological quadrat contains many species. Chao2 and the Eq.30 extrapolator are the right formulas for "how many more model-rounds buy me 10% more findings", and Good-Turing gives you a principled convergence gate to replace a heuristic one. Böhme also falsifies the naive gate you are probably tempted by: AFL's built-in stopping rule (abort when a cycle adds no new path) "would have (incorrectly) aborted openssl already at the 6 hour mark while ffmpeg would (incorrectly) continue even after the 48 hour mark" — a K-consecutive-quiet-rounds rule is empirically demonstrated to fail in both directions. Adaptation needed: everything here is a function of singletons and doubletons, so it inherits the finding-identity problem wholesale, and it inherits your co-discovery pathology directly. Fix the matcher first or these numbers are noise. Practical note: the R packages SpadeR (ChaoSpecies, with 95% CIs) and iNEXT implement all of this, so this is a dependency decision, not an implementation project.

techniques.name: Adaptive-bias-corrected residual risk estimators (reset and mean-local)
techniques.source: M. Böhme, D. Liyanage & V. Wüstholz, "Estimating Residual Risk in Greybox Fuzzing", ESEC/FSE 2021, https://mboehme.github.io/paper/FSE21.pdf ; follow-ups: Liyanage, Böhme, Tantithamthavorn & Lipp, "Reachable Coverage: Estimating Saturation in Fuzzing", ICSE 2023; Liyanage et al., "Extrapolating Coverage Rate in Greybox Fuzzing", ICSE 2024, https://mboehme.github.io/paper/ICSE24.pdf
techniques.what_it_does: Shows that when the search adapts (each round's sampling distribution depends on what earlier rounds found), classical Good-Turing and Laplace estimators "systematically and substantially under-estimate the true risk" — by up to four orders of magnitude — so an engineer who stops when the estimator says the risk is acceptable "is vastly misled". Proposes three corrections: a-reset estimators (reset frequency counts each time the corpus changes; they overestimate with high variance), mean-local estimators (weighted combinations of per-seed local estimates; these performed best, with the Mean Local Good-Turing "almost never" underestimating), and power-law extrapolation of log(n) vs log(discovery probability), which fits with median R² ≥ 97%.
techniques.assumption: That adaptive bias decreases as the campaign lengthens, which they prove under stated conditions and confirm empirically. Requires per-seed (per-sub-campaign) bookkeeping, not just a global singleton count.
techniques.why: Your panel is adaptive in the same formal sense — later rounds are conditioned on earlier findings — so the naive Good-Turing number would be biased, and this paper is the published correction. But be careful about DIRECTION, because your adaptivity is not theirs and I could not find anyone who has analysed your variant. In greybox fuzzing, adaptivity RAISES the probability of discovering neighbouring species, so classical estimators under-report risk. In CDSFL, showing round-k findings to round-k+1 reviewers REMOVES those findings from the sampling frame, which should suppress redundancy and inflate singletons, biasing the other way. The mean-local construction (estimate locally per sub-campaign, then combine) maps naturally onto per-round or per-model local estimates and is the right starting point, but the sign of the residual bias in your setting is an open empirical question you would have to measure, not inherit.

techniques.name: Chao's estimator as a stopping criterion over an ensemble of diverse reviewers
techniques.source: M.P. Bron, P.G.M. van der Heijden, A.J. Feelders & A.P.J.M. Siebes, "Using Chao's Estimator as a Stopping Criterion for Technology-Assisted Review", ACM TOIS, 2025 (arXiv:2404.01176, 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01176
techniques.what_it_does: An ensemble of five heterogeneous classifiers (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, random forest, LGBM, random sampling) each maintains its own labelled set; which methods discovered each relevant item forms a contingency table; Chao's estimator on that table gives N_hat; the review stops when estimated recall |L+|/N_hat meets a target. Conservative variant uses the upper CI bound, optimistic uses the point estimate.
techniques.assumption: Capture probabilities follow zero-truncated Poisson (heterogeneity across documents is allowed); independence between capture events. Active learning biases which items are examined, which the authors mitigate through ensemble diversity rather than eliminate. Chao is acknowledged as a lower bound on the relevant population.
techniques.why: This is the closest published analogue to CDSFL's exact architecture and I would read it before designing anything: a heterogeneous panel used deliberately AS the multiple-reviewer occasions, a contingency table of who-found-what, Chao as the gate, and a recall target as the stopping threshold. It also gives an honest ceiling. At a 95% recall target the conservative Chao(1987) rule used 40% of the corpus, achieved 95.9% mean recall and 56% work saved — but hit the target in only 70% of runs. The Chao(Rivest) variant hit it in 59%. So even a well-instrumented version of this rule misses its guarantee roughly a third of the time. That is the realistic performance envelope for a Chao-based convergence gate, and it is a number worth putting in front of anyone who expects a statistical gate to be a proof.

techniques.name: Mutation adequacy and the coupling of mutants to real faults
techniques.source: R. Just, D. Jalali, L. Inozemtseva, M.D. Ernst, R. Holmes & G. Fraser, "Are Mutants a Valid Substitute for Real Faults in Software Testing?", FSE 2014, pp.654-665, https://doi.org/10.1145/2635868.2635929 ; R. Gopinath, C. Jensen & A. Groce, "Mutations: How Close Are They to Real Faults?", ISSRE 2014, https://agroce.github.io/issre14.pdf ; J.H. Andrews, L.C. Briand & Y. Labiche, "Is Mutation an Appropriate Tool for Testing Experiments?", ICSE 2005
techniques.what_it_does: Just et al. tested whether a test suite's mutant-detection rate predicts its real-fault-detection rate, using 357 real faults across 5 Java applications totalling 321,000 lines. They found a statistically significant correlation independent of coverage (point-biserial and rank-biserial coefficients 0.66-0.81 per project), that 73% of real faults are coupled to mutants from common operators with on average 2 mutants per real fault, and that 27% are not coupled — of which 17% are coupled to NO mutant at all. Gopinath et al. characterised 240,000 changes from 5,000 projects in four languages and found the typical real fault touches three to four tokens, rising to five (ten for insertions/deletions) to cover 80% of real faults, while standard mutation operators are one-token.
techniques.assumption: The Competent Programmer Hypothesis — that real faults are syntactically near-neighbours of correct code — which Gopinath et al. conclude "may not be applicable". Also that mutation score is measured against a fixed operator set.
techniques.why: Do NOT take this as a stopping rule: nothing in this literature maps mutation score to a count of residual defects, and treating it as one would be an invention on your part, not a transfer. Take it instead as the calibration audit your canary catalogue needs. Just et al.'s taxonomy of the 63 real faults coupled to no mutant is the most useful thing here, because it names the classes a seeded catalogue will systematically miss: algorithm modification or simplification (37 of 63), code that must be DELETED (7), calling a wrong but related method (5), context sensitivity (4), violated pre/post-conditions and library invariants (3), numerical analysis errors from overflow, underflow and NaN (4). For a STEM artefact those are not a tail — a wrong derivation, a missing term, a violated precondition and a numerical-stability error are the high-value findings your harness exists to catch. If your catalogue cannot generate them, your p_hat is measured on the wrong population and every downstream residual estimate is optimistic. Andrews, Briand & Labiche add the complementary warning from the other direction: hand-seeded faults tend to be HARDER to detect than real ones, while mutation-generated faults track real faults better — so the bias from hand-seeding is not consistently signed, which is a further argument for stratifying and for your existing two-generator requirement.

techniques.name: Software reliability growth models and cost-based optimal stopping
techniques.source: A.L. Goel & K. Okumoto, NHPP model m(t) = a(1 - e^(-bt)), 1979; J.D. Musa, operational-profile-driven reliability engineering; S.R. Dalal & C.L. Mallows, "When Should One Stop Testing Software?", JASA 83(403):872-879, 1988, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1988.10478676
techniques.what_it_does: Goel-Okumoto fits a cumulative-failure curve in execution time and reads the asymptote a as the total fault content. Dalal & Mallows derive an optimal stopping rule from the trade-off between the cost of continued testing (an arbitrary predictable f(t)) and the expected loss from bugs shipped, given known costs of fixing a bug during versus after release.
techniques.assumption: Goel-Okumoto: failures arrive as a non-homogeneous Poisson process in EXECUTION TIME under a stable operational profile, detection intensity proportional to remaining faults, and perfect immediate debugging. Dalal-Mallows: testing cost perfectly predictable, per-bug costs known constants.
techniques.why: The growth-model half does not transfer and I would not spend effort on it. You have rounds, not execution time; your detection agents are a small heterogeneous panel, not a stochastic input sampler; and there is no operational profile. The curve-fitting analogue that DOES exist for review data is the Detection Profile Method (Wohlin & Runeson 1998), and the inspection literature settled that question against it: Thelin & Runeson found DPM the best of the curve-fitting family but still beaten by Mh-JK, and the Briand et al. selection procedure that chose between enhanced DPM and Mh-JK failed to replicate (Petersson & Wohlin 1999a). Fitting a(1-e^(-bt)) to cumulative findings per round is easy, tempting, and worse than the estimator you should be using. The Dalal-Mallows half is different and worth keeping: it is a decision framework, not an estimator, and once you have a residual estimate from seeding or from Chao it gives you the principled way to convert that estimate into a stop decision using YOUR costs — the price of another panel round versus the cost of shipping an unfalsified claim. That is the piece that answers "decided in a principled way rather than by guess", and it is orthogonal to which estimator supplies the residual.

techniques.name: Confidence intervals for missing mass / maximum unseen probability
techniques.source: A. Colombi, M. Beraha, A. Painsky & S. Favaro, "Confidence intervals for maximum unseen probabilities, with application to sequential sampling design", arXiv:2601.20320; foundational: Robbins 1968 (MSE of Good-Turing < 1/n); Zhang & Zhang (asymptotic normality of Good-Turing)
techniques.what_it_does: Distribution-free, non-asymptotic confidence intervals on the largest probability mass attached to any as-yet-unobserved category, with an explicit sequential-sampling-design application: how many more samples to collect to reach a stated guarantee.
techniques.assumption: Observations from an unknown discrete distribution; a finite sample already collected. Does not assume a parametric abundance model.
techniques.why: A point estimate of residual risk should never drive a gate on its own — the Wohlin survey's whole application section is built on estimate PLUS interval, and Thelin et al. found log-normal intervals best for capture-recapture point estimates. This gives you finite-sample rather than asymptotic coverage, which matters because your sample sizes are small by the standards of every other paper here (2,050 findings across a whole programme, against fuzzing campaigns with 63.6 million inputs). Treat it as the interval machinery for whichever point estimator you adopt, not as a stopping rule in itself.

techniques.name: Sample-size and precision rules for two-occasion capture-recapture
techniques.source: D.S. Robson & H.A. Regier, "Sample Size in Petersen Mark-Recapture Experiments", Transactions of the American Fisheries Society, 1964; D.G. Chapman, 1951 (bias-corrected estimator); G.A.F. Seber, The Estimation of Animal Abundance, 1982
techniques.what_it_does: Gives the operating characteristics: the Chapman estimator's bias is negligible once recaptures R ≥ 7 (at which point there is a 95% chance that Mn/N > 4); precision is conventionally graded good at R ≥ 12, fair at 7-11, poor below 7; and the design criterion n1*n2 > 4N.
techniques.assumption: Two independent sampling occasions, closed population, equal catchability. The rules are about precision only — they say nothing about the bias from unequal catchability, which is the error that actually matters to you.
techniques.why: This is the arithmetic that answers "how large a seeded set". Recaptures R, not seeds M, is the governing quantity, and R = M * p, so the seed count you need scales inversely with how well your panel detects that class: to reach the R ≥ 7 fair threshold you need 7 seeds at p=1.0, 12 at p=0.6, 24 at p=0.3; for R ≥ 12 (good) it is 12, 20 and 40 respectively. Approximate relative precision is 1/sqrt(R), so R=12 gives a coefficient of variation near 29% and R=100 near 10%, which agrees with the Monte Carlo I ran. Blunt reading: your current 5 seeds is below the "poor" threshold of the discipline that invented the method. But pair this with the decision-versus-estimate distinction — the precision rules govern the point estimate, and your gate is a decision, which my simulation says is satisfiable at roughly 50-100 held-out seeds per class rather than the thousand the point estimate demands.

techniques.name: The independence assumption, and its empirical failure
techniques.source: J.C. Knight & N.G. Leveson, "An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming", IEEE TSE SE-12(1), 1986, https://www.csc.kth.se/utbildning/kth/kurser/DA2210/vettig13/Seminarier/KnightLeveson.pdf ; N. Ebrahimi, IEEE TSE 23(8):529-532, 1997 (a capture-recapture estimator without the independence restriction)
techniques.what_it_does: Knight & Leveson prepared 27 program versions independently from one specification at two universities and ran a million test cases: the versions were individually reliable but co-failed far more often than independence predicts. Ebrahimi later derived a defect-content estimator that drops the reviewer-independence restriction, and found results similar to Mt-ML.
techniques.assumption: n/a — this is the falsification of an assumption the other techniques rest on.
techniques.why: Every overlap-based estimator above assumes reviewers are independent, and the 1986 result is the canonical demonstration that independently produced artefacts share correlated blind spots. For a panel of frontier language models the concern is sharper, not weaker: shared pretraining corpora and shared instruction-tuning make correlated blind spots the default expectation rather than a surprise. The practical consequence is directional and worth stating plainly — positive correlation between reviewers inflates overlap, which makes capture-recapture UNDERESTIMATE what remains, which is the dangerous direction for a stopping gate. Note this pushes the opposite way to your suppressed-co-discovery problem, so the two could mask each other. Ebrahimi's estimator exists but the ten-year survey lists replicating it as outstanding work, so it is a research lead, not a dependency.

transfers: Plant-capture (seeding) is the ONLY method in this area that works with a single reviewer, because it is a single-occasion design. That makes it the right backbone for the solo-researcher-one-model deployment, and it means your seeding work is load-bearing for the scaling problem, not a side experiment. Every overlap-based method needs two reviewers minimum and four or more to be trustworthy (Briand et al. 2000, Miller 1999), so the panel-based estimators are only available to the moderate and institutional tiers.

The estimate-versus-decision distinction, which the inspection literature formalised as Relative Decision Accuracy (El Emam et al. 2000; El Emam & Laitenberger 2001; Thelin & Runeson 2000a). You do not need an accurate count of remaining defects, you need a correct answer to "stop or continue". My simulation shows the cost difference is roughly twenty-fold in seeds: ~1,000 seeds for a ±20% point estimate versus ~50-100 for a gate that is right 90-97% of the time.

The specific seed-count arithmetic. Recaptures R, not seeds M, is what governs precision, R = M*p, and the discipline's thresholds are R ≥ 7 (fair) and R ≥ 12 (good). At a plausible panel detection rate of p=0.6 that is 12 and 20 seeds respectively just to leave the "poor" band — so your current 5 is below the floor by the standards of the field that invented the method.

The Bernoulli product / incidence model from STADS §7 is the structurally correct model for CDSFL (one review pass yields many findings), and its Chao2 estimator and Eq.30 extrapolator are the right formulas for "how many more rounds buy 10% more findings". Implementations exist in the R packages SpadeR and iNEXT with 95% confidence intervals.

Good-Turing discovery probability as a residual-risk gate, with Böhme's proof that it upper-bounds the probability that an undiscovered error exists. This is a strictly better convergence criterion than "K consecutive quiet rounds", which Böhme falsified empirically: AFL's equivalent rule aborted openssl 90+ hours too early while refusing to stop ffmpeg long after it was done.

The Bron et al. TOIS 2025 architecture transfers almost unchanged: use the heterogeneous panel AS the multiple capture occasions, build the who-found-what contingency table, apply Chao, stop at a recall target using the conservative upper-CI variant. Their 70%-of-runs success rate at a 95% recall target is the realistic performance envelope you should plan around.

Dalal & Mallows' cost-based optimal stopping is the principled bridge from a residual estimate to a stop decision, using your own costs (panel round versus shipped-unfalsified-claim). It is the part of the SRGM tradition that survives the transfer.

Just et al.'s taxonomy of real faults that couple to NO mutant — algorithmic changes, code deletion, context sensitivity, violated invariants, numerical analysis errors — is directly usable as a coverage checklist for auditing whether your canary catalogue can generate the defect classes that matter in a STEM artefact.

Stratification by defect class (plant-capture Model M_class) is the principled remedy for heterogeneous detectability and should be built in from the start rather than retrofitted, because a global p_hat over a mixed-difficulty catalogue is uninterpretable.
does_not_transfer: Software reliability growth models as such — Goel-Okumoto, Musa, the NHPP family. They require a failure process in execution time under a stable operational profile with detection intensity proportional to remaining faults. You have discrete rounds, a small heterogeneous panel, and no operational profile. Do not fit a(1-e^(-bt)) to cumulative findings per round.

Curve fitting to the finding-accumulation curve more generally. The review analogue exists (Wohlin & Runeson's Detection Profile Method, 1998) and the inspection literature spent years testing it: DPM is the best of the curve-fitting family and still loses to Mh-JK, the derivative-DPM improvement did not beat Mh-JK either, and the Briand et al. model-selection procedure between enhanced DPM and Mh-JK failed replication (Petersson & Wohlin 1999a).

Mutation score as a stopping criterion in the sense of estimating residual population. It is an adequacy criterion, and Just et al. establish only a moderate correlation (0.66-0.81) with real-fault detection. There is no published mapping from mutation score to a count of remaining real defects; constructing one would be invention, not transfer.

"No new findings for K consecutive rounds" as a convergence gate. Empirically falsified in the closest analogous setting: Böhme (TOSEM 2018) shows AFL's equivalent rule stopping ~90 hours too early on openssl and failing to stop on ffmpeg long after saturation. The gate is wrong in both directions and the direction is not predictable from the artefact.

Capture-recapture on your CURRENT co-discovery record. At 2 doubletons in 2,050, Chao2 returns 1,050,626 total findings and 0.195% coverage. The literature is explicit that with zero or near-zero overlap no estimate is produced at all, and Scott & Wohlin's industrial pre-study aborted for exactly this reason. Applying any overlap estimator before diagnosing the matcher and the round protocol would produce a number with the shape of evidence and none of the content.

Mills' estimator at your current 5 seeds. It returns exactly zero remaining as an arithmetic identity whenever all seeds are found, and the honest bound from 5-for-5 is that detection could be as low as 55%.

The claim that executing a falsifier gives you ground truth that rescues these methods. It individuates each finding soundly, which is genuinely valuable and better than a label. It does not tell you whether two findings from two models are THE SAME finding, and every estimator here is a function of that judgement.
open: The species-identity problem under a noisy matcher. Every estimator in this literature is a function of f1 and f2 (or Q1 and Q2) — singletons and doubletons — and every one assumes species identity is given. In ecology it is; in inspections it is decided by a human coordinator or a meeting (Wohlin's process explicitly requires someone to 'identify which faults noted by the individual reviewers may actually be regarded as the same', and Scott & Wohlin ran a dedicated meeting step to build the overlap matrix). I found NO published analysis of how Chao1/Chao2/Mh-JK behave when the species-identity function itself has a measurable error rate. Given that your own records show a parser dropping ~10% of real replies and that dedup has been a recurring blocker, this is not a theoretical concern — and characterising estimator bias as a function of matcher precision and recall would be a genuine contribution, not just a fix.

Your specific direction of adaptive bias. Böhme, Liyanage & Wüstholz analysed adaptivity that RAISES the discovery probability of neighbouring species. CDSFL's rounds do something structurally different: showing round-k findings to round-k+1 reviewers REMOVES those defects from the sampling frame, which should suppress redundancy and inflate singletons. Nobody has analysed a review protocol that actively deletes discovered species from the frame. The sign and magnitude of the resulting estimator bias are unknown and would need to be measured, most cheaply by comparing round-1-only co-discovery (models blind to each other) against the cross-round figure.

Species estimation applied to a panel of LLM reviewers producing open-ended findings. Bron et al. (TOIS 2025) is the closest published work and it uses five classifiers ranking a fixed corpus, where the item set is enumerable and identity is trivial. Nobody has done it where the reviewers generate free-form findings over an artefact and the population is not enumerable. Searching for this combination directly returned nothing.

How to allocate a fixed seed budget across defect classes when the classes have unequal prior probability AND unequal detection difficulty. Stratified plant-capture tells you to stratify; it does not tell you the optimal allocation, and the optimal-allocation question interacts with your routing ladder in a way nothing in this literature addresses.

Estimator behaviour when the number of reviewers spans orders of magnitude between deployments — one model versus five versus effectively unlimited. The inspection literature is explicit that Mh-JK needs four or more reviewers, that results for two are 'ambiguous' with Mt-Ch recommended by one study and contradicted by another on real inspection data, and that at N=2 experience-based methods (bias around 20%) beat capture-recapture. Nobody has produced a coherent estimator LADDER that degrades gracefully from many reviewers to one. Since your explicit design goal is usefulness at every scale, this is your problem to solve and the literature will not hand you the answer — though the fact that plant-capture works at N=1 while overlap methods need N≥4 gives you the natural seam to build it across.

Whether panel co-discovery, once correctly measured, is high enough for overlap estimators at all. If frontier models genuinely share blind spots (the Knight-Leveson concern, sharpened by shared pretraining), a corrected matcher might reveal correlated overlap that biases capture-recapture toward UNDERestimating what remains — the dangerous direction. That correlation could also mask the suppression effect. Separating these three signals (matcher error, protocol suppression, genuine correlation) requires a deliberately designed experiment, not a re-analysis of existing logs.

synthesis:
## 1. WHICH QUESTIONS ARE ALREADY SOLVED

### Q1 — "when does another model stop paying" — SOLVED, in two halves, and you cannot currently run either.

**Half one: the marginal-value question.** Chao & Jost (2012, *Ecology* 93(12):2533–2547) prove the identity that answers it directly. I extracted the paper text and confirmed both forms verbatim:

- theoretical, their Eq. 3: `1 − E(C_m) = E(S_{m+1}) − E(S_m)`, "the slope of the expected SAC for a sample of size m is equal to the expected coverage deficit of the sample";
- empirical, their Eq. 6: `1 − Ĉ_m = Ŝ_{m+1} − Ŝ_m`.

The estimated fraction of the finding population you would add by running one more reviewer **is** the estimated coverage deficit, and coverage is estimable from the sample itself with no knowledge of the population — Turing's estimator `1 − f₁/n` (Good 1953), improved by Chao & Shen's Eq. 4a `Ĉ_n = 1 − (f₁/n)·[(n−1)f₁ / ((n−1)f₁ + 2f₂)]`. Robbins (1968) puts the MSE under `1/n`; McAllester & Schapire (COLT 2000) give the finite-sample concentration bound. You compute a derivative, not an asymptote — which is why this needs far less data than "how many findings exist". Source: https://www.davidzeleny.net/wiki/lib/exe/fetch.php/vegecol:materials:chao-jost2012_ecology.pdf, https://www.learningtheory.org/colt2000/papers/McAllesterSchapire.pdf

**Half two: the stopping rule.** Chao & Jost name it explicitly — "When a sample reaches a predetermined value of this coverage estimate… sampling stops. This stopping rule was theoretically justified by an optimal stopping theory (Rasmussen and Starr 1979)" (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1979.10481667). The economic version, with an explicit exchange rate between the cost of one more occasion and the loss from a missed defect, is Dalal & Mallows, "When Should One Stop Testing Software?", *JASA* 83(403), 1988 (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1988.10478676).

**Error seeding answers a different question, and you need it too.** Every overlap estimator is blind to findings whose detection probability is zero for every reviewer. Chao's estimator is a *lower bound* for exactly that reason. Seeding is the only instrument that bounds the shared blind spot, and it is the only one that works with **one** reviewer — no overlap required. Origin: Mills (1972), cited in Petersson et al. as the technique used jointly with capture–recapture in testing. **Severe caveat:** Andrews, Briand & Labiche (ICSE 2005) found hand-seeded faults are *not* a valid substitute for real faults while mechanically generated mutants are; Just et al. (FSE 2014, https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~mernst/pubs/mutation-effectiveness-fse2014.pdf) confirm mutant detection correlates with real-fault detection independent of coverage. So your seeded corpus must be generated by mechanical operators, not written by hand or by a model. The literature disagrees with itself here: Gopinath et al. (ISSRE 2014, https://agroce.github.io/issre14.pdf) and the 2023 coupling study question how tightly common operators couple to real faults.

**Do the two together answer "when does another model stop paying"? Yes — plainly yes — for the population your panel can in principle see, subject to three inputs you do not currently record. Not for the class none of them can see; only seeding bounds that.**

### The reductio you can compute today

I ran your numbers through the incidence-based estimators (T = 5 occasions, S_obs = 2050, Q₂ = 2, Q₁ = 2048), cross-checked Chao2 against a homogeneous-detection back-out in SymPy:

```
Chao2 lower bound on total findings   = 840,911
Chao–Shen incidence coverage Ĉ_T      = 0.0024   (deficit 99.76%)
Turing form 1 − Q₁/U                  = 0.0020
implied per-model per-finding p       = 0.000488  → N ≈ 840,090  (agrees)
```

Two independent routes agree: at 2-in-2050, **every estimator in this family says your panel has seen a quarter of one percent of the finding population.** For coverage to reach 0.8 at 2050 observed findings you would need 1,078 of them (52.6%) seen by two or more occasions; for 0.5, you need 533 (26.0%). You have 2.

That is either true — the finding space over an artefact really is effectively unbounded, which is a substantive possibility, not a joke — or your matcher is under-merging. **Until that is settled, none of the machinery above produces an actionable number.** This is why matcher accuracy is instrumentation item #1 and not item #4. Fraysse et al. (2023, arXiv:2304.00885, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.00885) show the misidentification models will not converge below ~0.2 capture rate without an informative prior on the identification probability — so a *measured* matcher accuracy is a required input, not a refinement.

### Q2 — allocation — PARTLY SOLVED, in pieces, none a drop-in.

**The one that genuinely fits: adaptive submodularity.** Golovin & Krause, *JAIR* 42:427–486, 2011 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.3967). Coverage of a finding set is submodular; allocation under uncertainty with observed outcomes is adaptive stochastic maximisation / min-cost cover; adaptive greedy is provably competitive with the optimal policy. It transfers **because** your ground truth comes from execution: the framework requires observing the realised outcome of each action before choosing the next, which is exactly what a falsifier gives you and exactly what a vote does not. This is the best-fitting formal frame for your allocation problem and it is off the shelf.

**Close precedent for the routing ladder: per-instance algorithm selection.** SATzilla (Xu, Hutter, Hoos & Leyton-Brown, *JAIR* 32, 2008, https://jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/10556) and algorithm portfolios (Gomes & Selman, *Artificial Intelligence* 126, 2001). Portfolio selection is trained against a *runtime oracle* — did the solver solve it — not against agreement. Same epistemic shape as yours. Its founding premise is that **there is no total order on solvers**, which is precisely the assumption your ladder violates. Gomes, Selman, Crato & Kautz (*JAR*, 2000) on heavy-tailed runtimes gives the additional result you need at the solo tier: **restarting the same solver with a different seed is a rational escalation**, often better than a "stronger" one.

**Difficulty-conditioned allocation: real and quantified.** Snell, Lee, Xu & Kumar (arXiv:2408.03314, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314) — allocating test-time compute per-prompt by difficulty beats uniform best-of-N by >4×. LLM routing and cascades (FrugalGPT; RouteLLM; survey at https://arxiv.org/html/2603.04445v2) give the mechanism. What transfers: predict sub-problem difficulty from features, allocate accordingly, and use the falsifier outcome as the training label. You have a better label than any of these papers do.

**What does NOT transfer, said plainly:** best-arm identification and OCBA (Audibert & Bubeck 2010; Karnin et al. 2013; Chen's OCBA line, https://mason.gmu.edu/~cchen9/ocba.html) solve *identify the best arm under a budget*. That is not your objective. You want to cover a set, not crown a model. Their transfer is confined to the narrow sub-problem "which model should class-X claims be routed to" — and even there, they assume stationary arm rewards, which model-version churn breaks. Do not build the allocator on them.

Crowdsourcing budget-allocation (Karger, Oh & Shah, *Operations Research* 2014, https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/opre.2013.1235; bandit task assignment, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.05800) assumes **ground truth is recovered by aggregating worker labels**. That assumption is exactly what your falsifier removes. The aggregation half does not transfer; the budget-per-item half does. Note the field disagrees with itself on whether adaptivity even helps: some results find adaptive assignment needs similar label counts to random, others find it wins when the worker distribution is diverse or tasks heterogeneous (https://www.jennwv.com/papers/repeatedlabel.pdf).

### Q3 — measuring diversity and pricing it — MEASUREMENT SOLVED, PRICING NOT.

**Measurement.** The Kish design effect gives one number: `n_eff = k / (1 + (k−1)ρ̄)`, with ρ̄ the mean pairwise correlation. "Nine Judges, Two Effective Votes" (arXiv:2605.29800, **unrefereed preprint**, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29800) measures it on nine frontier models from seven families: ρ̄ = 0.391, **n_eff = 2.18 [2.07, 2.31]**, independence ratio 24.2%, asymptotic ceiling `1/ρ̄ = 2.56` regardless of panel size. Majority-vote accuracy falls 7.6–22.0 points short of the independent-voting prediction. I reproduced their arithmetic exactly (k=9, ρ̄=0.391 → 2.180; ceiling 2.558).

Two of their results aim straight at CDSFL's design:

- **"Family diversity alone does not recover independence."** Same-family pairs ϕ = 0.437 against a cross-family mean of 0.389 — nearly identical. Selecting one judge per family *reduced* n_eff to 1.93. **Four vendors does not mean four independent reviewers, and your architecture currently assumes it does.**
- Diminishing returns are brutal and land exactly at your panel size. On my computation from their ρ̄, the first five occasions deliver 61% of all achievable independence; occasions 6 through 9 add 0.23 effective votes between them.

**Transfer caveat, and it is a real one:** they measure three-way NLI label agreement — a low-entropy classification task where every model sees identical input and emits one of three tokens. You run open-ended generative search. Correlation structure on classification need not carry to generative search, and it may well be *lower* for you. Do not import 0.391. Measure your own ρ̄ off the overlap matrix. The transferable claim is the architectural one — vendor identity is a poor proxy for independence — not the number.

**Honest report on the diversity-metric literature: it has a bad track record.** Kuncheva & Whitaker (*Machine Learning* 51(2):181–207, 2003, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1022859003006) studied ten diversity statistics and concluded with "doubts about the usefulness of diversity measures in building classifier ensembles in real-life pattern recognition problems." Do not sell a diversity metric as a solved instrument. The exception is that in your setting the overlap matrix *is* the measurement — generalized diversity `GD = 1 − p(2)/p(1)` is computed from the same spectrum as coverage, so it costs nothing extra.

**Pricing.** The only theorem I found is Littlewood, Popov, Strigini & Shryane (2000) Result 7: if two reviewers have equal squared efficacy, one-of-each strictly beats two-of-either. It is Cauchy–Schwarz and **assumes nothing about the sign of their correlation**. I verified numerically (1M draws, Beta(2,3) marginals): E[θ²] = 0.20002 vs E[θ_Aθ_B] = 0.16007. That converts "buy diversity" from taste into a theorem — *when candidates are comparable*. Establishing comparability, and pricing when they are not, is unsolved. Nothing prices a vendor against a seat against a prompt-role.

Also relevant to Q1 and unhelpful for optimism: Chen et al., "Are More LLM Calls All You Need?" (arXiv:2403.02419, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02419) prove performance of a Vote system is **non-monotone** in the number of calls — more calls help easy items and *hurt* hard ones, so a task with both has an interior optimum. Your gate must be able to say "fewer", not only "more".

## 2. WHAT GENUINELY REQUIRES INVENTION

**Your candidate — allocation where ground truth comes from tool execution rather than agreement — is NOT novel, and it is the easy regime, not the hard one.** Verifier-in-the-loop allocation is well populated:

- Brown et al., "Large Language Monkeys" (arXiv:2407.21787, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21787) explicitly partition verifier-present from verifier-absent. With a verifier, SWE-bench Lite goes 15.9% → 56% from 1 to 250 samples, coverage log-linear over four orders of magnitude. Without one, majority voting and reward models plateau in the hundreds.
- SATzilla's entire training signal is execution.
- Adaptive submodularity requires observed realised outcomes.
- Snell et al. search against verifiers.

Claiming novelty here would be wrong, and it would put you on the defensive against four well-known lines of work. Say instead: *CDSFL operates in the verifier-present regime, which the literature identifies as the regime where scaling actually pays.* That is a strength claim, and it is true.

**What is genuinely open, strictly:**

**(N1) Open-population capture–recapture where the artefact is edited between rounds.** Every estimator above assumes a closed population. Yours is not closed: findings are born and die as the artefact changes. Petersson, Thelin, Runeson & Wohlin (2004, https://wohlin.eu/jss04-1.pdf) name this in §6 and I quote them exactly: *"there are still areas that have not been explored, e.g. open models and change-in-ratio models… This has been regarded as not useful for software inspections, but none has actually explored this subject."* Twenty-two years on, sweep 1 found nothing that has. You are forced into this by your own multi-round design. **This is a real gap and CDSFL is unusually well positioned to work it.**

**(N2) Capture histories labelled by an oracle.** Each of your captures carries CONFIRMED / REFUTED from falsifier execution. No capture–recapture formulation uses a per-capture validity label. The inspection literature handled false positives by *luck*, and again I quote Petersson et al. exactly: *"most models underestimate. However, this may not be a big problem since false positives are often included in the inspection data, which would increase the estimation result."* That is two errors cancelling, not a method. A three-state capture history — not-found / found-refuted / found-confirmed — with a partially observed validity process is uninvented. It is also a *small* problem: a latent-class extension of M_th, not a research programme. **This is your strongest novelty claim and your cheapest.**

**(N3) A common currency for units of diversity.** Pricing a vendor against a seat against a prompt-role against a resample, validated against a verifier. n_eff supplies the currency; nothing supplies the exchange rate. Modest novelty — a calibration study plus engineering, not a theory gap.

**(N4) Not novel, but unoccupied: coverage-based convergence gating for AI reviewer panels.** Sweep 1 reports zero arXiv hits for capture–recapture ∧ LLM and for species-richness ∧ LLM. The nearest neighbour is UCS (arXiv:2604.12015, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12015), which uses smoothed Good–Turing to pick in-context examples — a different problem. So: mature technique, empty application. That is an opportunity *and* a warning — there is no prior calibration to lean on, and your first results become the calibration.

## 3. MINIMUM INSTRUMENTATION, RANKED BY WHAT IT UNLOCKS

1. **A measured finding-matcher.** Sample finding pairs, adjudicate same/different by tool or human, report precision and recall with a confidence interval. Nothing downstream means anything without it — see the reductio above. The inspection process design already names this step: *"it is important that the person tries to identify which faults noted by the individual reviewers may actually be regarded as the same"* (Petersson et al. 2004 §5). Estimated cost: a few hundred adjudications.

2. **The full occasion × finding incidence matrix.** Attributing each finding to exactly one model destroys the only statistic every technique here consumes. Record, per finding, the set of occasions that reported it, where **occasion = (model, prompt-role, seed, round)**. This single change unlocks Q₁/Q₂, Chao2, coverage, the deficit gate, ρ̄, n_eff, generalized diversity, and DPM — all from the same object.

3. **Per-occasion and per-falsifier-execution cost.** Wall-clock, tokens, tool time, split by confirmed / refuted / not-executable. Without this, "when does another model stop paying" has no numerical answer even with perfect overlap data. Rasmussen & Starr and Dalal & Mallows both require the exchange rate.

4. **Falsifier outcome attached to the capture, not to the finding.** CONFIRMED / REFUTED / NOT-EXECUTABLE per (occasion, finding) pair. This is the raw material for N2.

5. **A mechanically generated seeded-defect corpus.** Mutation-operator style, never hand-written, planted per run, undisclosed to reviewers. The **only** instrument that bounds the shared blind spot, and the only one that yields a detection-rate estimate at T = 1. Ranked fifth because it is the most expensive to build, not because it matters least — start it in parallel.

6. **Round index and artefact version hash per occasion.** The prerequisite for any open-population work (N1). Cheap now, impossible to backfill.
