## 4. THE SCALE LADDER

**One model, one vendor.** Capture–recapture across models is *impossible* — you need at least two occasions for any overlap at all. The fix is to change the sampling unit: **the occasion, not the model.** Repeated samples at temperature > 0 and distinct prompt roles are trapping occasions, which is precisely what Brown et al. measure. Available at this tier: Good–Turing coverage over the sample axis; **error seeding, the only estimator needing no overlap whatsoever**; experience-based estimation (Wohlin et al. 2001 report ~20% absolute bias and ~20% SD, less bias than any capture–recapture estimator at two reviewers though not significantly so); curve-fitting (DPM) over samples rather than reviewers. Routing ladder fix: **escalation at this tier is re-conditioning — different role, different seed, different decomposition — not "a stronger model"**, justified by Gomes et al.'s heavy-tail restart result. Expect high intra-model ρ̄, so a low n_eff ceiling; the gate should *tell the solo researcher honestly that coverage C is unreachable* rather than silently converging.

**~5 seats across 4 vendors.** This is exactly the boundary where the inspection literature says the estimators begin to work: *"at least four to five reviewers should participate in order to make the accuracy acceptable"* (Briand et al. 2000; Miller 1999), with Mh-JK the consensus recommendation for four or more (Biffl 2000; Briand et al. 1997, 2000; Miller 1999; Thelin et al. 2002). It is also the point where, on the Nine Judges ρ̄, five occasions have already bought 61% of all achievable independence and seats six through nine would add 0.23 effective votes. **So: run Mh-JK plus the coverage gate, measure your own ρ̄ and n_eff, and spend the marginal pound on conditioning diversity rather than a sixth seat.** Do not build a two-reviewer gate: the literature contradicts itself there — El Emam & Laitenberger (2001) recommend Mt-Ch for two reviewers from simulation, Thelin et al. (2002) find Mt-Ch does not estimate well on real inspection data, and Mh-JK is explicitly non-robust and underestimates at two.

**Effectively unlimited.** The binding constraint stops being seats and becomes ρ̄ — you cannot buy past `1/ρ̄` effective votes no matter how much you spend, and nine frontier models across seven families bought 2.56. At this tier the rational spend is: (a) adaptive submodular allocation across sub-problems rather than more reviewers per sub-problem; (b) a seeded corpus large enough to actually characterise the blind spot; (c) buying *conditioning* diversity and measuring whether ρ̄ falls — treat every claimed diversity purchase as a hypothesis and test it; (d) respect the extrapolation ceiling — Orlitsky, Suresh & Wu (*PNAS* 113(47):13283–13288, 2016, https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1607774113) show you cannot reliably extrapolate more than ~n log n beyond your sample, so unlimited access still does not license estimating a distant asymptote from a small run.

**What is invariant across all three tiers:** the gate. "Estimated coverage reached C" means the same thing at one occasion and at five hundred, and comparably-scaled outputs are what let a solo result be read against an institutional one. "N models ran" and "K rounds elapsed" do not have that property.

**One structural warning that governs the whole ladder.** I checked the marginal-return decay under the Eckhardt–Lee difficulty model with Beta(2,3) difficulty (mean detection 60%), by exact Beta moments and by 2M-draw Monte Carlo (agreement to 2×10⁻⁵). Residual undetected fraction after 8 occasions: **1.82% under the correct model vs 0.066% under an independence model — a 28× understatement.** Marginal yield per occasion runs 0.600, 0.200, 0.086, 0.043, 0.024, 0.014, 0.009, 0.006; the local decay exponent is −2.5 at n≈4, −3.1 at n≈8, tending to −(b+1) = −4. **The decay is polynomial, not geometric, and its exponent is set entirely by the shape of the difficulty distribution near θ → 1 — the hardest findings — which is the region you have least data about.** Any scaling projection you publish is a claim about that tail. Say so.

## 5. THE THREE THINGS TO BUILD FIRST

**1. The occasion × finding incidence matrix, plus a measured matcher.**
*Buys:* every other technique on this page, and an immediate verdict on whether 2-in-2050 measures your panel or your parser. This is the highest-leverage item by a wide margin, because if the matcher is the cause, **Q1 becomes a solved problem requiring no invention at all — only recording.** That is the single biggest lever available to you and it is a recording change, not a research project.

**2. The coverage-deficit gate, run in shadow against historical runs.**
Compute `1 − Ĉ_T` per round from the incidence spectrum; stop when the estimated marginal yield of the next occasion falls below its cost. Run it *alongside* the current gate, and include a naive knee-detector as a control — sweep 1 reports that the crowned inspection estimators lost badly to a naive knee-detector in an open environment, and you sit between the closed and open regimes, so this is an empirical question you must settle rather than assume. **Select on Relative Decision Accuracy, not estimation error** (El Emam & Laitenberger, *IEEE TSE* 27(9):851–864, 2001, https://www.ehealthinformation.ca/web/default/files/wp-files/1068.pdf): an estimator can be poor at estimating and good at deciding, and deciding is all a gate does. Report the output as a dependence-robust confidence set, not a point estimate (Sun et al., arXiv:2008.00127, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.00127) — you cannot assert reviewer independence, and a bounded set is more falsifiable than a point anyway.
*Buys:* a scale-invariant stop criterion; one number that means the same thing at every tier; an honest "unreachable" for the solo researcher.

**3. The mechanically seeded-defect corpus.**
*Buys:* the only bound on findings no model can see; per-model detection-rate calibration that works at T = 1 and therefore at every tier; and the ground truth needed to price diversity purchases. Start it in parallel with (1) — it is the slowest to build and it is independent of the other two.

Deliberately **not** in the first three: the routing-ladder rewrite. Fix its immediate bug now — replace "escalate to a stronger writer" with "re-condition and retry", which costs nothing and removes the single-model failure — but do not rebuild it on adaptive submodularity until the incidence matrix exists, because the allocator's objective function is coverage and you cannot currently measure coverage.

## WHERE THE LITERATURE DISAGREES WITH ITSELF

- **Two-reviewer estimators:** El Emam & Laitenberger (2001) recommend Mt-Ch from simulation; Thelin et al. (2002) find it fails on real inspection data. Unresolved.
- **Subjective vs capture–recapture:** Biffl (2000) — subjective has smaller bias, larger variance. Thelin (2002) — capture–recapture is significantly more accurate on both point estimates and confidence intervals. Directly contradictory.
- **Whether the assumptions hold for inspections at all:** Ekros et al. (1998) say capture–recapture models are not suitable; Miller (2002) finds no empirical evidence for that and finds no reviewer dependence. Petersson et al.'s own verdict: "There is no agreement of the result found in this subject."
- **Panels of judges vs the best single judge:** Verga et al. (2024) PoLL — three small models from different providers beat a single large judge on six datasets at ~7× lower cost (https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/panel-of-llm-evaluators-poll). arXiv:2605.29800 — nine judges yield 2.18 effective votes and individual top judges match or exceed the full panel. The stated methodological reason for the split: PoLL benchmarks the panel against the *average* judge, the newer work against the *best* judge. **Which comparison you adopt determines whether your panel looks like a success.** Both are preprints or recent; treat with care.
- **Mutants as proxies for real faults:** Andrews/Briand/Labiche and Just et al. say yes; Gopinath et al. and the 2023 coupling work say the coupling is looser than claimed.
- **Replication failure:** Briand et al. (2000)'s EDPM/Mh-JK selection procedure showed a small improvement; Petersson & Wohlin (1999a) did not confirm it.
- **Adaptivity in crowdsourced allocation:** some results find adaptive assignment needs similar label counts to random assignment; others find it wins when workers or tasks are heterogeneous.

**Flags.** arXiv:2605.29800, arXiv:2606.30931, arXiv:2604.12015 and arXiv:2603.04445 are unrefereed preprints [VERIFY:current]. The Chao et al. (2009) sufficient-sampling effort multipliers (90% of the estimated population at a median 0.80× current effort; 100% at 2.23× and up to 10.67×) are passed through from sweep 1 as reported — I did not re-derive them. The Porter et al. team-size F-statistics are likewise passed through unverified.
